children.title: Log-Concave Density Estimation
children.top_down_role: Distribution-estimation templates using log-concave density structure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Equivariance of the Log-Concave MLE
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transformation law for the unrestricted log-concave maximum-likelihood estimator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T(x)=Ax+b\) with nonsingular \(A\). If \(\widehat f\) is the log-concave MLE for \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), then the MLE for \(T(x_1),\ldots,T(x_n)\) is \(\widehat f_T(y)=|\det A|^{-1}\widehat f(A^{-1}(y-b))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The log-concave MLE transforms equivariantly under invertible affine coordinate changes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat f_T(y)=|\det A|^{-1}\widehat f(A^{-1}(y-b)).
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Equivariance of the Log-Concave MLE

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tent-Function Structure of the Log-Concave MLE
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sample representation for an unrestricted Lebesgue log-concave MLE.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C=\operatorname{conv}\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\) has nonempty interior, the log-concave MLE is zero outside \(C\). On \(C\), its log-density is a polyhedral concave tent function: for suitable observation heights it is the least upper-semicontinuous concave function majorizing those heights. Thus the infinite-dimensional likelihood problem admits a finite height parameterization, although evaluating its normalization still requires integration over the induced polyhedral subdivision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The log-concave MLE is supported on the sample convex hull and has a polyhedral tent-function log-density determined by finitely many heights.
assumptions_latex: The unrestricted model uses densities relative to \(d\)-dimensional Lebesgue measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{supp}(\widehat f)=C,\qquad \log\widehat f\text{ is polyhedral and concave on }C.
knowledge_statements.title: Tent-Function Structure of the Log-Concave MLE

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence and Essential Uniqueness of the Log-Concave MLE
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp existence boundary for unrestricted log-concave densities relative to ambient Lebesgue measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The unrestricted log-concave MLE over Lebesgue densities on \(\mathbb R^d\) exists if and only if the sample convex hull has nonempty interior. When it exists, the maximizing density is unique up to Lebesgue-null sets. If the observations lie in a proper affine subspace, no \(d\)-dimensional Lebesgue-density maximizer exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ambient log-concave density MLE exists and is essentially unique exactly when the observations have a full-dimensional convex hull.
assumptions_latex: The model uses densities relative to \(d\)-dimensional Lebesgue measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat f\text{ exists}\iff\operatorname{int}\operatorname{conv}\{x_i\}_{i=1}^n\ne\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.title: Existence and Essential Uniqueness of the Log-Concave MLE

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat f=e^{\widehat\phi}/\int e^{\widehat\phi}\) is a log-concave maximum-likelihood density whenever an optimizer exists.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional observations with an unrestricted concave log-density potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given observations \(x_1,ldots,x_n\in\mathbb{R}^d\), log-concave density estimation chooses an upper-semicontinuous concave function \(\phi:\mathbb{R}^d\to[-\infty,\infty)\) by solving
\[
\widehat\phi\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{\phi}\left\{\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\phi(x_i)-\log\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}e^{\phi(u)}\,du\right\}.
\]
The associated estimate is
\[
\widehat f(x)=\frac{e^{\widehat\phi(x)}}{\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}e^{\widehat\phi(u)}\,du}.
\]
Because the log-integral-exponential functional is convex and the feasible set of concave potentials is convex, the displayed maximization is a concave optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Estimate a density by maximizing normalized log-likelihood over concave log-density potentials; exponentiating and normalizing the optimizer yields a log-concave density.
knowledge_statements.title: Log-Concave Density Estimation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The log-concave MLE formulation is plausible, but no inspectable source supports the infinite-dimensional likelihood template or its convexity characterization. The observation list also contains the malformed token “ldots”.

children.title: Shape-Constrained Likelihood Interface
children.top_down_role: Likelihood models organized by convexly representable shape restrictions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order certificate specialized to a convexly parameterized shape-constrained likelihood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=-\sum_i\ell_i\). If \(L\) is proper convex, \(\widehat\theta\in C\), and the subdifferential sum rule applies to \(L+\delta_C\), then \(\widehat\theta\) maximizes \(\sum_i\ell_i\) over \(C\) if and only if \(0\in\partial L(\widehat\theta)+N_C(\widehat\theta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible shape-constrained parameter is likelihood-optimal exactly when a loss subgradient is canceled by a normal to the shape set.
assumptions_latex: The convex subdifferential sum rule applies at \(\widehat\theta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in\partial L(\widehat\theta)+N_C(\widehat\theta).

notation.meaning: Convex normal cone to the shape set

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Likelihood Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic existence and uniqueness conditions for the convex shape-constrained likelihood interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be nonempty and closed and let \(L=-\sum_i\ell_i\) be proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex on \(C\). If \(C\) is compact or \(L+\delta_C\) is coercive, a minimizer exists. If \(L\) is strictly convex on \(C\), the minimizer is unique. Convexity alone guarantees neither attainment nor uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compactness or coercivity yields likelihood attainment, and strict convexity yields uniqueness; convexity alone yields neither.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[C\text{ compact or }L+\delta_C\text{ coercive}\bigr]\Longrightarrow\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta\in C}L(\theta)\ne\varnothing.

notation.meaning: Convex indicator of the shape-constraint set

knowledge_statements.title: Attainment and Uniqueness Conditions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the abstract convex-programming interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A statistically meaningful shape restriction does not by itself define a convex program. If its image \(C\) in the chosen parameterization is nonconvex, or if the log-likelihood is not concave in that parameter, maximizing likelihood over \(C\) falls outside this convex interface even when a different parameterization might be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shape meaning alone does not imply convexity; feasibility and likelihood curvature must be convex-compatible in the actual optimization parameterization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\text{ nonconvex or }\ell\text{ nonconcave}\Longrightarrow\text{the displayed parameterization is not a convex program}.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameterization-Dependent Convexity Boundary

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmax}_{\theta\in C}\sum_{i=1}^n\ell_i(\theta)\) is a convex-programming likelihood interface.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract interface for likelihood models whose shape restrictions form a convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A shape-constrained likelihood problem has the convex-programming representation
\[
\widehat\theta\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{\theta\in C}\sum_{i=1}^n\ell_i(\theta),
\]
where \(\Theta\) is convex, \(C\subseteq\Theta\) is convex, and every log-likelihood contribution \(\ell_i\) is concave on \(C\). Equivalently, it minimizes the convex objective \(-\sum_{i=1}^n\ell_i(\theta)\) over \(C\). The interface covers shape restrictions expressible through convex constraints, including monotonicity or concavity inequalities, but does not assert convexity when the chosen parameterization makes either the feasible set nonconvex or the log-likelihood nonconcave.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shape-constrained likelihood is convex-programmable when its parameter set and shape constraints are convex and its log-likelihood is concave.
knowledge_statements.title: Shape-Constrained Likelihood Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The abstract representation fits the interface leaf and is mathematically plausible, but it has no cited source for the asserted shape-constrained likelihood scope.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact first-order certificate for finite-dimensional convex regularized likelihood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(\theta)=L(\theta)+\lambda R(\theta)+\delta_C(\theta)\), with proper closed convex terms, and suppose the subdifferential sum rule applies at \(\widehat\theta\). Then \(\widehat\theta\) is optimal if and only if \(0\in\partial L(\widehat\theta)+\lambda\partial R(\widehat\theta)+N_C(\widehat\theta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameter is regularized-likelihood optimal exactly when likelihood and penalty subgradients plus a feasible-set normal sum to zero.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) and \(R\) are proper, closed, and convex.
The subdifferential sum rule applies at \(\widehat\theta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in\partial L(\widehat\theta)+\lambda\partial R(\widehat\theta)+N_C(\widehat\theta).

notation.meaning: Normal cone of the parameter domain

knowledge_statements.title: Regularized-Likelihood Optimality Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment and uniqueness qualifications for finite-dimensional convex regularized likelihood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F=L+\lambda R+\delta_C\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and level-bounded, then its minimizer set is nonempty and compact. If \(F\) is strictly convex on its effective domain, the minimizer is unique. A coercive regularizer with \(\lambda>0\) can provide level-boundedness, whereas a merely convex penalty need provide neither attainment nor uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proper closed level-bounded regularized likelihoods attain compact solution sets, and strict convexity gives uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ level-bounded}\Longrightarrow\operatorname*{argmin}F\ne\varnothing;\qquad F\text{ strictly convex}\Longrightarrow|\operatorname*{argmin}F|\le1.
knowledge_statements.title: Existence and Uniqueness Regimes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic relation between regularized likelihood and a likelihood problem with a regularizer budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{\theta\in C}\{L(\theta):R(\theta)\le\tau\}\). Under a relative-interior Slater condition, any optimal solution \(\widehat\theta\) and optimal multiplier \(\lambda^\star\ge0\) satisfy \(\widehat\theta\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta\in C}\{L(\theta)+\lambda^\star R(\theta)\}\) and \(\lambda^\star(R(\widehat\theta)-\tau)=0\). No one-to-one correspondence between \(\tau\) and \(\lambda\) follows without additional uniqueness and sensitivity conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A qualified budget multiplier yields a matching penalized-likelihood solution, but penalty and budget parameters need not correspond one-to-one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat\theta\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta\in C}\{L(\theta)+\lambda^\star R(\theta)\},\quad \lambda^\star(R(\widehat\theta)-\tau)=0.
knowledge_statements.title: Penalty-Budget Multiplier Relation

assumptions_latex: \(R:C\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is a proper convex regularizer and \(\lambda\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\theta_\lambda\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta\in C}\{L(\theta)+\lambda R(\theta)\}\) is a convex regularized-likelihood estimator.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Penalized maximum likelihood in a convex parameterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a convex parameter set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\), convex negative log-likelihood \(L\), proper convex regularizer \(R\), and weight \(\lambda\geq0\), a regularized likelihood estimator is any solution of
\[
\widehat\theta_\lambda\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta\in C}\bigl\{L(\theta)+\lambda R(\theta)\bigr\}.
\]
Equivalently, when \(L=-\ell\), it maximizes \(\ell(\theta)-\lambda R(\theta)\). Extended values may encode additional convex constraints. The regularizer can promote structure such as sparsity, smoothness, or low complexity; existence and uniqueness require additional coercivity, compactness, or strict-convexity assumptions and are not part of the template.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regularized likelihood estimator minimizes convex negative log-likelihood plus a nonnegative multiple of a convex structural penalty.
knowledge_statements.title: Regularized Likelihood Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The convex penalized-likelihood definition is standard and appropriately qualified, but the record supplies no source or locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: MAP estimation as regularized likelihood maximization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents Bayesian MAP estimation through posterior, likelihood-prior, joint-density, and log-additive objectives, including the log-concavity condition and the uniform-prior reduction to constrained maximum likelihood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) have joint density \(p_{X,Y}(x,y)\), let \(p_X\) be the prior density, and observe a value \(y\) with \(p_Y(y)>0\). Then any MAP estimate satisfies
\[
\widehat{x}_{\mathrm{MAP}}\in\operatorname*{argmax}_x p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)
=\operatorname*{argmax}_x p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)p_X(x)
=\operatorname*{argmax}_x p_{X,Y}(x,y),
\]
and, with zero densities assigned logarithm \(-\infty\), equivalently
\[
\widehat{x}_{\mathrm{MAP}}\in\operatorname*{argmax}_x\left\{\log p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)+\log p_X(x)\right\}.
\]
If both terms in the logarithmic objective are concave in \(x\), the MAP problem is a convex optimization problem. If \(p_X\) is uniform on a set \(C\) and zero outside \(C\), its MAP estimates coincide with maximum-likelihood estimates constrained to \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an observation having positive marginal density, MAP estimation maximizes the posterior density of the unknown parameter. Factors independent of the parameter can be removed, so this is equivalently maximization of likelihood times prior, the joint density, or log-likelihood plus log-prior. If the log-likelihood and log-prior are concave in the parameter, this maximization is a convex optimization problem. A prior that is uniform on a set and zero outside it reduces MAP to maximum likelihood constrained to that set.
assumptions_latex: p_{X,Y}(x,y)\text{ is a joint density of }(X,Y)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat{x}_{\mathrm{MAP}}\in\operatorname*{argmax}_x\left\{\log p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)+\log p_X(x)\right\};\quad \log p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid\cdot)\text{ and }\log p_X\text{ concave}\Longrightarrow\text{a convex optimization problem}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constrained maximum-likelihood estimation and its convexity condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines maximum-likelihood estimation from one observed sample, including explicit and implicit parameter constraints and the sufficient condition for a convex formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{p_x\}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\) be a family of densities on \(\mathbb{R}^m\), let \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) be observed, and define \(\ell_y(x)=\log p_x(y)\). For an admissible set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), a maximum-likelihood estimate satisfies \(\widehat{x}_{\mathrm{ML}}\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}p_x(y)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\ell_y(x)\). The constraint can equivalently be encoded by setting \(p_x(y)=0\) for every \(y\) when \(x\notin C\), hence \(\ell_y(x)=-\infty\) there. If \(\ell_y\) is concave in \(x\) for every \(y\), and \(C\) is described by linear equalities and convex inequalities, then computing \(\widehat{x}_{\mathrm{ML}}\) is a convex optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a density family indexed by x and an observed sample y, maximum likelihood chooses an admissible parameter maximizing the likelihood, equivalently the log-likelihood. Parameter constraints may be imposed explicitly or by assigning zero likelihood, and thus log-likelihood minus infinity, outside the feasible set. If every fixed-observation log-likelihood is concave in x and the feasible set has linear-equality and convex-inequality constraints, the estimation problem is convex.
assumptions_latex: C\text{ is representable by linear equalities and convex inequalities}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat{x}_{\mathrm{ML}}\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\ell_y(x),\qquad \text{and this maximization is a convex optimization problem under the stated concavity and constraint assumptions.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization template over an infinite-dimensional probability class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X_1,ldots,X_n\) be observations in a measurable space and let \(\mathcal P\) be an infinite-dimensional class of probability measures. A nonparametric distribution estimator specified by optimization has the form
\[
\widehat P\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{P\in\mathcal P}\left\{\Phi(P;X_1,ldots,X_n)+\lambda J(P)\right\},
\]
where \(\Phi\) measures data fit, \(J\) imposes structural regularity, and \(\lambda\geq0\). The problem is convex when \(\mathcal P\) is convex and both \(\Phi(\,cdot\,;X_1,ldots,X_n)\) and \(J\) are convex under mixtures of probability measures. A finite-dimensional discretization is an implementation, not part of the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonparametric distribution estimation optimizes data fit and structural regularity over an infinite-dimensional class of probability measures.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonparametric Distribution Estimation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Probability-simplex representation of a finite distribution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of all probability distributions on a fixed finite support, used as the parameter domain in nonparametric distribution estimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X take values in a fixed finite set \{\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}, and define p_k=\operatorname{Prob}(X=\alpha_k). Then p\succeq 0 and \mathbf{1}^Tp=1. Conversely, every p\in\mathbb{R}^n satisfying p\succeq0 and \mathbf{1}^Tp=1 defines such a distribution by \operatorname{Prob}(X=\alpha_k)=p_k. Hence the probability simplex is in one-to-one correspondence with the probability distributions on this finite set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a random variable supported on a fixed finite set, its probabilities form a nonnegative vector whose entries sum to one. Conversely, every such vector defines a probability distribution on that set, so the probability simplex is in one-to-one correspondence with all distributions on the finite support.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left\{p\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid p\succeq0,\ \mathbf{1}^Tp=1\right\}\ \longleftrightarrow\ \left\{\text{probability distributions on }\{\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n\}\right\}\text{ bijectively}.

children.top_down_role: Convex templates for estimating covariance structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence boundary for the unstructured Gaussian covariance MLE.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[L(\Sigma)=\log\det\Sigma+\operatorname{tr}(S\Sigma^{-1}),\qquad\Sigma\succ0,\] if \(S\succ0\), the unique minimizer is \(\widehat\Sigma=S\). If \(S\) is singular, the infimum is approached as covariance eigenvalues in null directions of \(S\) tend to zero and is not attained in \(\mathbb S_{++}^p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unstructured covariance MLE equals the sample covariance when it is positive definite; a singular sample covariance gives no positive-definite MLE.
assumptions_latex: \(S\in\mathbb S_+^p\) is the centered sample covariance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\succ0\Rightarrow\widehat\Sigma=S\); singular \(S\Rightarrow\operatorname*{argmin}_{\Sigma\succ0}L(\Sigma)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Gaussian Covariance MLE Existence Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear shrinkage toward a positive-definite target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S\succeq0\), \(T\succ0\), and \(0\leq\alpha\leq1\), \[\widehat\Sigma_\alpha=(1-\alpha)S+\alpha T\succeq0.\] It is positive definite whenever \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shrinking a sample covariance toward a positive-definite target preserves PSD structure and restores positive definiteness for positive shrinkage.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\Sigma_\alpha\succeq0\), and \(\alpha>0\Rightarrow\widehat\Sigma_\alpha\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Definite Covariance Shrinkage

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex least-squares covariance estimation under convex structural restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty closed convex \(C\subseteq\mathbb S_+^p\), \[\widehat\Sigma=P_C(S)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\Sigma\in C}\tfrac12\|\Sigma-S\|_F^2\] exists uniquely. It is characterized by \[\langle S-\widehat\Sigma,\Sigma-\widehat\Sigma\rangle\leq0\qquad\forall\Sigma\in C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection of the sample covariance onto a closed convex PSD model is a unique convex covariance estimator with an exact variational-inequality certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb S_+^p\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\Sigma=P_C(S)\) exists uniquely and satisfies the displayed variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Covariance Projection Estimator

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb S_+^p\) is a convex structural constraint set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\Sigma\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\Sigma\in C\cap\mathbb S_{++}^p}\{\log\det\Sigma+\operatorname{tr}(S\Sigma^{-1})+\lambda R(\Sigma)\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For centered Gaussian observations with sample covariance \(S\), direct covariance-matrix estimation minimizes
\[
\widehat\Sigma\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\Sigma\in C\cap\mathbb S_{++}^p}\left\{\log\det\Sigma+\operatorname{tr}(S\Sigma^{-1})+\lambda R(\Sigma)\right\},
\]
where \(C\subseteq\mathbb S_+^p\) represents structural restrictions and \(R\) is a selected penalty. The unpenalized expression is the Gaussian negative log-likelihood up to constants. In the covariance variable, \(\log\det\Sigma\) is concave, so the displayed objective is not generally convex; convex programming commonly requires a suitable special structure or reparameterization by the precision matrix \(\Theta=\Sigma^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gaussian covariance estimation minimizes log determinant plus an inverse-covariance trace term, but direct covariance parameterization is generally not convex.

knowledge_statements.title: Precision-Matrix Estimation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian precision parameterization with convex constraints and regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a sample covariance matrix \(S\in\mathbb S_+^p\), Gaussian precision-matrix estimation over a convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb S_{++}^p\) has the representation
\[
\widehat\Theta\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\Theta\in C}\left\{-\log\det\Theta+\operatorname{tr}(S\Theta)+\lambda R(\Theta)\right\},
\]
where \(R\) is convex and \(\lambda\geq0\). The objective is convex because \(-\log\det\Theta\) is convex on the positive-definite cone and the trace term is affine. The corresponding covariance estimate is \(\widehat\Sigma=\widehat\Theta^{-1}\). Existence or uniqueness requires additional assumptions on \(C\), \(S\), and \(R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gaussian precision estimation is convex: minimize negative log determinant, a sample-covariance trace term, and an optional convex penalty.
assumptions_latex: \(S\in\mathbb S_+^p\) is a sample covariance matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\Theta\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\Theta\in C}\{-\log\det\Theta+\operatorname{tr}(S\Theta)+\lambda R(\Theta)\}\) is a convex precision estimator.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The negative log determinant makes every attained convex precision estimate unique.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is convex on its effective domain and \(\lambda\geq0\).

children.title: Sparse Graphical Estimation Interface
children.top_down_role: Precision-estimation applications emphasizing sparse conditional-dependence structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact first-order certificate for the off-diagonal graphical-Lasso objective, conditional on attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix \(\widehat\Theta\succ0\) minimizes \(-\log\det\Theta+\langle S,\Theta\rangle+\lambda\|\Theta\|_{1,\mathrm{off}}\) if and only if there is a symmetric matrix \(Z\) such that \(Z_{ii}=0\), \(Z_{ij}=\operatorname{sign}(\widehat\Theta_{ij})\) when \(\widehat\Theta_{ij}\ne0\), \(Z_{ij}\in[-1,1]\) otherwise, and \(-\widehat\Theta^{-1}+S+\lambda Z=0\). Any attained optimum is unique because \(-\log\det\) is strictly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An off-diagonal l1 subgradient stationarity equation exactly certifies the unique attained graphical-Lasso optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in-\widehat\Theta^{-1}+S+\lambda\partial\|\widehat\Theta\|_{1,\mathrm{off}}.
knowledge_statements.title: Graphical-Lasso KKT Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual covariance representation when diagonal precision entries are unpenalized.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The primal problem \(\min_{\Theta\succ0}\{-\log\det\Theta+\langle S,\Theta\rangle+\lambda\|\Theta\|_{1,\mathrm{off}}\}\) has the dual representation \(\max_{W\succ0}\{\log\det W+p:W_{ii}=S_{ii},\ |W_{ij}-S_{ij}|\le\lambda\ (i\ne j)\}\). Whenever primal and dual optima are attained, \(W^\star=(\Theta^\star)^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The graphical Lasso is dual to log-determinant maximization over covariance matrices in an off-diagonal box around the sample covariance.
assumptions_latex: The stated primal and dual optima are attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W^\star=(\Theta^\star)^{-1},\quad W^\star_{ii}=S_{ii},\quad |W^\star_{ij}-S_{ij}|\le\lambda.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic regimes in which the precision objective can fail to attain a finite minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\lambda=0\) and \(S\) is singular, the objective is unbounded below along a positive-definite sequence expanding in a null direction of \(S\). If \(S\succeq0\), \(\lambda>0\), and every \(S_{ii}>0\), the off-diagonal graphical-Lasso objective is level-bounded and attains its unique minimum. A zero diagonal entry of a positive-semidefinite \(S\) leaves the corresponding diagonal precision direction uncontrolled and can again cause unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Singular unpenalized covariance data, or a zero-variance coordinate, can destroy attainment; positive coordinate variances and a positive off-diagonal penalty ensure it.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A sparse Gaussian graphical estimator may be represented by
\[
\widehat\Theta\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\Theta\in\mathbb S_{++}^p}\left\{-\log\det\Theta+operatorname{tr}(S\Theta)+\lambda\lVert\Theta\rVert_{1,\mathrm{off}}\right\},
\]
or by imposing the hard linear constraints \(\Theta_{ij}=0\) for every \((i,j)\notin E\). Both interfaces are convex. For a nondegenerate multivariate Gaussian distribution, \(\Theta_{ij}=0\) is equivalent to conditional independence of coordinates \(i\) and \(j\) given all remaining coordinates. Thus the off-diagonal support of \(\widehat\Theta\) supplies the estimated undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sparse Gaussian graph estimation uses zeros or an off-diagonal lasso penalty in the precision matrix; nonzero off-diagonal entries define estimated edges.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact certificate for binary Bayes-detector optimality and suboptimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(a(x)=\pi_0c_{10}p_0(x)\) and \(b(x)=\pi_1c_{01}p_1(x)\). For any measurable randomized detector \(0\leq\delta\leq1\), and a Bayes rule \(\delta^*\) choosing one where \(b>a\) and zero where \(a>b\), \[R(\delta)-R(\delta^*)=\int|a(x)-b(x)|\,|\delta(x)-\delta^*(x)|\,d\mu(x)\geq0.\] Decisions are arbitrary on \(a=b\); equality holds exactly when \(\delta\) agrees with a Bayes decision almost everywhere off the tie set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Excess Bayes risk is the weighted disagreement with the likelihood-ratio decision, giving an exact optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(\delta)-R(\delta^*)=\int|\pi_0c_{10}p_0-\pi_1c_{01}p_1|\,|\delta-\delta^*|\,d\mu\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Achievable error tradeoffs for randomized mixtures of detectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If detectors \(\delta_1,\delta_2\) have false-positive and true-positive pairs \((u_1,v_1)\) and \((u_2,v_2)\), then \(\delta_\lambda=\lambda\delta_1+(1-\lambda)\delta_2\), \(0\leq\lambda\leq1\), satisfies \[\bigl(E_0\delta_\lambda,E_1\delta_\lambda\bigr)=\lambda(u_1,v_1)+(1-\lambda)(u_2,v_2).\] Hence randomized detectors convexify the achievable ROC region, and threshold randomization fills line segments or jumps between deterministic operating points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mixing detectors linearly mixes their false-positive and detection probabilities, making the randomized ROC region convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((E_0\delta_\lambda,E_1\delta_\lambda)=\lambda(E_0\delta_1,E_1\delta_1)+(1-\lambda)(E_0\delta_2,E_1\delta_2)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bayes-optimal detector for two simple dominated hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For simple hypotheses \(H_0:P_0\) and \(H_1:P_1\), define the Bayes risk of a measurable detector \(\delta:\mathcal X\to\{0,1\}\) by
\[
R(\delta)=\pi_0c_{10}P_0(\delta=1)+\pi_1c_{01}P_1(\delta=0).
\]
Initialize no state. On observing \(x\), output
\[
\delta^*(x)=\mathbf 1\!\left\{\pi_1c_{01}p_1(x)\geq\pi_0c_{10}p_0(x)\right\},
\]
with either decision permitted on equality. This pointwise likelihood-ratio rule minimizes \(R(\delta)\) over all measurable binary detectors. The rule terminates after evaluating the two weighted likelihoods.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two simple hypotheses, compare weighted likelihoods and choose the hypothesis with smaller conditional Bayes loss.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines finite deterministic detectors, maximum-likelihood detection, and the column-stochastic representation of randomized detectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For observations \(k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and hypotheses \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), a deterministic detector is a map \(\psi:\{1,\ldots,n\}\to\{1,\ldots,m\}\), with \(\widehat\theta=\psi(k)\) after observing \(X=k\). A maximum-likelihood detector chooses any \(\psi_{\mathrm{ml}}(k)\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}}p_{kj}\). A randomized detector is represented by \(T=(t_{ik})\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), where \(t_{ik}=\Pr(\widehat\theta=i\mid X=k)\); consequently, each column satisfies \(t_k\succeq0\) and \(\mathbf1^Tt_k=1\). Unit-vector columns represent deterministic detectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic detector maps each observation to one hypothesis, and maximum likelihood selects a hypothesis maximizing the likelihood of that observation. A randomized detector assigns a probability distribution over hypotheses to each observation, so every column of its matrix lies in the probability simplex. Unit-vector columns give deterministic rules.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \psi_{\mathrm{ml}}(k)\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{j}p_{kj},\qquad t_k\succeq0,\quad\mathbf1^Tt_k=1\quad(k=1,\ldots,n).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Robust Minimax Detector and LP Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines worst-case detector performance and gives linear-programming formulations for finite and columnwise polyhedral ambiguity sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\in\mathcal P\) be an uncertain conditional-distribution matrix and let \(T\in\mathbb{R}^{m	imes n}\) be a randomized detector whose columns lie in the probability simplex. Define \(D^{\mathrm{wc}}_{ij}=\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}(TP)_{ij}\) for \(i
e j\), \(D^{\mathrm{wc}}_{ii}=\inf_{P\in\mathcal P}(TP)_{ii}\), and \(P_i^{\mathrm{wce}}=1-D^{\mathrm{wc}}_{ii}\). A robust minimax detector minimizes \(\max_iP_i^{\mathrm{wce}}\), equivalently maximizing \(\min_i\inf_{P\in\mathcal P}(TP)_{ii}\). Because its entries can be attained at different members of \(\mathcal P\), \(D^{\mathrm{wc}}\) need not have columns summing to one. If \(\mathcal P=\{P_1,\ldots,P_K\}\), an equivalent LP is \(\max_{T,\gamma}\gamma\) subject to \((TP_j)_{ii}\ge\gamma\) for all \(i=1,\ldots,m\) and \(j=1,\ldots,K\), together with the simplex constraints on every column of \(T\). Replacing this finite set by its convex hull leaves all relevant worst-case values and the robust minimax solutions unchanged. If the ambiguity set separates by hypothesis as \(p_i\in\{p:A_ip=b_i,\ \mathbf1^Tp=1,\ p\succeq0\}\), with each such set nonempty, LP duality yields the equivalent constraints \(
u_i^Tb_i+\mu_i\ge\gamma\) and \(A_i^T
u_i+\mu_i\mathbf1\preceq\widetilde t_i\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), where \(\widetilde t_i^T\) is row \(i\) of \(T\), along with the column-simplex constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A robust minimax detector minimizes the largest error probability over all hypotheses and all distributions in an ambiguity set. Its worst-case matrix uses infima for correct detections and suprema for errors and therefore need not be stochastic. Finite ambiguity sets give a direct linear program and may be replaced by their convex hull. Independent polyhedral ambiguity sets for the hypothesis distributions also give a linear program after dualizing the worst-case constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_T\max_i\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\bigl(1-(TP)_{ii}\bigr)=1-\max_T\min_i\inf_{P\in\mathcal P}(TP)_{ii},\quad\text{with the stated finite-set and polyhedral LP representations.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Binary Likelihood-Ratio Detectors and the ROC
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the binary error representation, likelihood-ratio scalarization rule, and the boundary that threshold rules give ROC vertices rather than every Pareto-optimal detector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p,q\in\mathbb{R}^n\) be the observation distributions under hypotheses \(1\) and \(2\). With false-positive and false-negative probabilities \(P_{\mathrm{fp}}\) and \(P_{\mathrm{fn}}\), the detection matrix is \(D=\begin{bmatrix}1-P_{\mathrm{fp}}&P_{\mathrm{fn}}\\P_{\mathrm{fp}}&1-P_{\mathrm{fn}}\end{bmatrix}\). For positive scalarization weights \(W_{12},W_{21}\), an optimal deterministic detector uses \(\widehat\theta(k)=1\) when \(W_{21}p_k>W_{12}q_k\) and \(\widehat\theta(k)=2\) otherwise. Whenever the ratio is defined, this is the likelihood-ratio test \(p_k/q_k>W_{12}/W_{21}\). Varying the threshold produces deterministic Pareto-optimal detectors corresponding to vertices of the piecewise-linear optimal trade-off curve, or ROC. These likelihood-ratio detectors do not constitute every Pareto-optimal detector; randomized detectors can occupy nonvertex points of the trade-off curve.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two hypotheses, performance is described by false-positive and false-negative probabilities. A positive weighted scalarization yields a likelihood-ratio threshold rule, with equality assigned to hypothesis 2 under the stated convention. Changing the threshold produces deterministic Pareto-optimal vertices of the piecewise-linear ROC, but threshold rules do not give every Pareto-optimal detector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat\theta(k)=\begin{cases}1,&W_{21}p_k>W_{12}q_k,\\2,&W_{21}p_k\le W_{12}q_k,\end{cases}\quad\text{and the resulting likelihood-ratio rules give deterministic Pareto vertices, not all Pareto-optimal detectors.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a finite observation alphabet with \(n\geq1\) outcomes, deterministic tests form \(\{0,1\}^n\), which is nonconvex. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision-space convexity of worst-case binary testing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal D\) be a convex set of measurable randomized tests \(\delta:\mathcal X\to[0,1]\). For arbitrary nonempty distribution families \(\mathcal P_0,\mathcal P_1\), define \[\alpha(\delta)=\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_0}E_P\delta,\qquad \beta(\delta)=\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_1}E_P(1-\delta).\] Both are convex in \(\delta\), being suprema of affine functionals. Therefore minimizing \(\max\{\alpha,\beta\}\), or any coordinatewise nondecreasing convex function of \((\alpha,\beta)\), over \(\mathcal D\) is convex. Convexity of the distribution families is unnecessary for this decision-space claim, though finite-dimensional tractability requires additional representation assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Worst-case errors are convex in a randomized detector; tractable finite reformulations require further distributional structure.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P_0,\mathcal P_1\) are nonempty families for which the displayed expectations exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are convex on \(\mathcal D\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional formulation for finite observations and finite hypothesis families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\mathcal X=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with null probability vectors \(p_i^0\), \(i=1,\ldots,r\), and alternative probability vectors \(p_j^1\), \(j=1,\ldots,s\). Equal-error minimax testing is the linear program \[\min_{\delta,t}t\quad\text{s.t.}\quad (p_i^0)^{\mathsf T}\delta\leq t\ \forall i,\quad (p_j^1)^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf1-\delta)\leq t\ \forall j,\quad 0\leq\delta\leq\mathbf1.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With finite observations and finitely many candidate distributions, minimax randomized testing is exactly a linear program.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimax testing between convex composite parameter families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For composite hypotheses \(H_0:\theta\in C_0\) and \(H_1:\theta\in C_1\), a randomized detector \(\delta:\mathcal X\to[0,1]\) has worst-case type-I and type-II errors
\[
\alpha(\delta)=\sup_{\theta\in C_0}E_\theta[\delta(X)],\qquad
\beta(\delta)=\sup_{\theta\in C_1}E_\theta[1-\delta(X)].
\]
A minimax hypothesis-testing model minimizes \(\max\{\alpha(\delta),\beta(\delta)\}\), or a specified convex weighted combination, over an admissible convex class of randomized tests. Convexity of \(C_0\) and \(C_1\) alone does not make the finite-dimensional reformulation convex; that conclusion additionally requires suitable concavity, affine expectation structure, or a valid saddle-point representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex hypothesis-testing template minimizes worst-case error over randomized tests, provided the distributional model admits the needed convex or saddle-point structure.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Hypothesis-Testing Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The minimax error expression is plausible, but convex parameter sets alone do not produce a convex hypothesis-testing model. A model-specific source is needed to identify sufficient distributional or saddle-point assumptions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: E-optimal design and its semidefinite representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous experiment design under the worst-direction covariance criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v_1,\ldots,v_p\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\Delta_p=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^p:\mathbf1^T\lambda=1\}\), and \(M(\lambda)=\sum_{i=1}^p\lambda_i v_i v_i^T\). Assume that \(M(\lambda)\succ0\) for at least one \(\lambda\in\Delta_p\). E-optimal design minimizes \(\|M(\lambda)^{-1}\|_2\) over \(\lambda\in\Delta_p\) with \(M(\lambda)\succ0\). Equivalently, if \[t_\star=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_p,\,t\in\mathbb R}\{t:M(\lambda)\succeq tI\},\] then \(t_\star>0\) and the optimal inverse-norm value is \(1/t_\star\). Thus the equivalent design selection is given by the SDP \[\begin{array}{ll}\operatorname{maximize}_{\lambda,t}&t\\\operatorname{subject\ to}&M(\lambda)\succeq tI,\\&\lambda\succeq0,\quad\mathbf1^T\lambda=1.\end{array}\] The inverse-norm objective is convex. If \(E=cM(\lambda)^{-1}\) for fixed \(c>0\), the criterion also minimizes the confidence-ellipsoid diameter and \(\max_{\|q\|_2=1}\operatorname{var}(q^Te)=\|E\|_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: E-optimal design minimizes the largest eigenvalue of the error covariance, equivalently maximizing the smallest eigenvalue of the information matrix. The latter formulation is an SDP. With fixed covariance scaling, the criterion minimizes both confidence-ellipsoid diameter and the largest estimation-error variance over unit directions.
assumptions_latex: E=cM(\lambda)^{-1},\quad c>0\text{ fixed, for the covariance interpretations}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: t_\star=\max\{t:M(\lambda)\succeq tI,\ \lambda\in\Delta_p\}>0,\qquad\min_{\lambda\in\Delta_p,\,M(\lambda)\succ0}\|M(\lambda)^{-1}\|_2=t_\star^{-1},\quad\text{and the minimization problem is convex.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A-optimal design and its semidefinite representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous experiment design under the total mean-square estimation-error criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v_1,\ldots,v_p\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\Delta_p=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^p:\mathbf1^T\lambda=1\}\), and \(M(\lambda)=\sum_{i=1}^p\lambda_i v_i v_i^T\). Assume that \(M(\lambda)\succ0\) for at least one \(\lambda\in\Delta_p\). A-optimal design solves \[\min_{\lambda\in\Delta_p,\,M(\lambda)\succ0}\operatorname{tr}\bigl(M(\lambda)^{-1}\bigr),\] which is a convex problem. If \(E=cM(\lambda)^{-1}\) is the estimation-error covariance for fixed \(c>0\), then \(\mathbb E\|e\|_2^2=\operatorname{tr}E\), so the criterion minimizes total mean-square error. With \(e_k\) denoting the \(k\)-th coordinate vector, an equivalent SDP is \[\begin{array}{ll}\operatorname{minimize}_{\lambda,u}&\mathbf1^Tu\\\operatorname{subject\ to}&\begin{bmatrix}M(\lambda)&e_k\\e_k^T&u_k\end{bmatrix}\succeq0,\quad k=1,\ldots,n,\\&\lambda\succeq0,\quad\mathbf1^T\lambda=1.\end{array}\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A-optimal design minimizes the trace of the inverse information matrix, a convex criterion proportional to the total mean-square estimation error. Introducing one epigraph variable for each coordinate yields an equivalent semidefinite program.
assumptions_latex: E=cM(\lambda)^{-1},\quad c>0\text{ fixed, for the mean-square-error interpretation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{\lambda\in\Delta_p,\,M(\lambda)\succ0}\operatorname{tr}(M(\lambda)^{-1})=\min_{\lambda,u}\left\{\mathbf1^Tu:\begin{bmatrix}M(\lambda)&e_k\\e_k^T&u_k\end{bmatrix}\succeq0\ (k=1,\ldots,n),\ \lambda\in\Delta_p\right\},\quad\text{and the problem is convex.}

knowledge_statements.title: A-Optimality Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate linear-design formulation with normalized nonnegative weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given candidate regressors \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb{R}^p\), an approximate design is a weight vector \(w\in\Delta_m\) with information matrix
\[
M(w)=\sum_{i=1}^m w_i a_i a_i^{\mathsf T}.
\]
An A-optimal design is any
\[
w_A\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{w\in\Delta_m,\,M(w)\succ0}\operatorname{tr}\bigl(M(w)^{-1}\bigr).
\]
Under homoscedastic linear estimation, this criterion minimizes the sum of componentwise estimator variances, up to the common noise factor. Since the inverse-trace function is convex on \(\mathbb S_{++}^p\) and \(M(w)\) is affine in \(w\), the design problem is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A-optimal design minimizes the trace of the inverse information matrix, corresponding to the total variance of linear parameter estimates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w_A\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{w\in\Delta_m,\,M(w)\succ0}\operatorname{tr}(M(w)^{-1})\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate dependence of the unweighted A criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under \(\beta=T\gamma\) with nonsingular \(T\), the information matrix becomes \(T^{\mathsf T}M(w)T\), and \[\operatorname{tr}((T^{\mathsf T}M(w)T)^{-1})=\operatorname{tr}(T^{-1}M(w)^{-1}T^{-\mathsf T}).\] Thus ordinary A-optimality is invariant under orthogonal coordinate changes and common scalar rescaling, but not under arbitrary nonsingular reparameterization.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{tr}((T^{\mathsf T}MT)^{-1})\) is generally not proportional to \(\operatorname{tr}(M^{-1})\).

knowledge_statements.title: D-Optimality Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate linear-design formulation maximizing information volume.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given candidate regressors \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb{R}^p\), define \(M(w)=\sum_{i=1}^m w_i a_i a_i^{\mathsf T}\) for \(w\in\Delta_m\). A D-optimal design is any
\[
w_D\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{w\in\Delta_m,\,M(w)\succ0}\log\det M(w),
\]
equivalently, any minimizer of \(-\log\det M(w)\). In a homoscedastic linear model, maximizing the determinant minimizes the volume of the usual covariance ellipsoid, up to constants independent of \(w\). The problem is convex-programmable because \(\log\det\) is concave on \(\mathbb S_{++}^p\) and \(M(w)\) depends affinely on \(w\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: D-optimal design maximizes the log determinant of the information matrix, thereby minimizing generalized covariance or confidence-ellipsoid volume.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w_D\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{w\in\Delta_m,\,M(w)\succ0}\log\det M(w)\).

source_refs.locator: 2.3.8 Convex real-valued functions of matrices p. 26

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.8 Convex real-valued functions of matrices p. 26

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-design-space general equivalence theorem for D-optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M^\star=M(w^\star)\succ0\). Then \(w^\star\) is D-optimal if and only if \[a_i^{\mathsf T}(M^\star)^{-1}a_i\leq p,\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.\] Equality holds whenever \(w_i^\star>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A design is D-optimal exactly when every candidate leverage is at most the parameter dimension, with equality at support points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w^\star\text{ is D-optimal}\iff a_i^{\mathsf T}(M^\star)^{-1}a_i\leq p\ \forall i\).

notation.meaning: Information matrix of the candidate design

knowledge_statements.title: D-Optimality General Equivalence Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonsingular linear parameter-coordinate invariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonsingular \(T\), \[\log\det(T^{\mathsf T}M(w)T)=\log\det M(w)+2\log|\det T|.\] The added term is independent of \(w\), so the maximizing designs are unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: D-optimal designs are invariant under every nonsingular linear reparameterization.
assumptions_latex: The transformed information matrix is \(T^{\mathsf T}M(w)T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmax}_w\log\det(T^{\mathsf T}M(w)T)=\operatorname*{argmax}_w\log\det M(w)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Reparameterization Invariance of D-Optimality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous experiment-design weights under the information-volume criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v_1,\ldots,v_p\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\Delta_p=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^p:\mathbf 1^T\lambda=1\}\), and \(M(\lambda)=\sum_{i=1}^p\lambda_i v_i v_i^T\). On the domain \(M(\lambda)\succ0\), a D-optimal design solves \[\min_{\lambda\in\Delta_p}\log\det\bigl(M(\lambda)^{-1}\bigr).\] This is a convex optimization problem. If the estimation-error covariance is \(E=m^{-1}M(\lambda)^{-1}\) for fixed \(m>0\), this problem has the same minimizers as minimizing \(\det E\), and hence the volume of a fixed-confidence ellipsoid, whose volume is proportional to \((\det E)^{1/2}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For continuous design weights on the probability simplex, D-optimal design minimizes the log determinant of the inverse information matrix over designs for which that matrix is positive definite. The problem is convex and, for fixed sample scaling and confidence level, minimizes confidence-ellipsoid volume.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{\lambda\in\Delta_p,\,M(\lambda)\succ0}\log\det(M(\lambda)^{-1})\text{ is convex and has the same minimizers as the fixed-confidence ellipsoid volume.}

knowledge_statements.title: E-Optimality Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate linear-design formulation maximizing worst-direction information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given candidate regressors \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb{R}^p\), define \(M(w)=\sum_{i=1}^m w_i a_i a_i^{\mathsf T}\) for \(w\in\Delta_m\). An E-optimal design is any
\[
w_E\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{w\in\Delta_m}\lambda_{\min}\bigl(M(w)\bigr).
\]
Equivalently, it maximizes \(t\) subject to
\[
M(w)\succeq tI,\qquad w\in\Delta_m.
\]
Thus E-optimality maximizes information in the least-informed parameter direction and minimizes the largest eigenvalue of the covariance matrix when \(M(w)\succ0\). The semidefinite representation is convex because \(M(w)\) is affine in the design weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: E-optimal design maximizes the smallest information eigenvalue, protecting the least-informed parameter direction through a semidefinite constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w_E\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{w\in\Delta_m}\lambda_{\min}(M(w))\).

source_refs.locator: 3.4.1 The Multiplicity of Optimal Eigenvalues p. 55

source_witnesses.locator: 3.4.1 The Multiplicity of Optimal Eigenvalues p. 55

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General equivalence and complementary-slackness certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M^\star=M(w^\star)\) and \(t^\star=\lambda_{\min}(M^\star)\). The design is E-optimal if and only if some \(Z^\star\succeq0\) satisfies \[\operatorname{tr}Z^\star=1,\quad (M^\star-t^\star I)Z^\star=0,\quad a_i^{\mathsf T}Z^\star a_i\leq t^\star\ \forall i.\] Equality holds when \(w_i^\star>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: E-optimality is certified by a trace-one PSD matrix supported on the least-eigenvalue eigenspace and satisfying candidate sensitivity bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed PSD, eigenspace, and sensitivity conditions are necessary and sufficient for E-optimality.

notation.meaning: Dual matrix supported on the least-eigenvalue eigenspace

knowledge_statements.title: E-Optimality General Equivalence Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-design-space minimax dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: E-optimality satisfies \[\max_{w\in\Delta_m}\lambda_{\min}(M(w))=\min_{Z\succeq0,\,\operatorname{tr}Z=1}\max_{1\leq i\leq m}a_i^{\mathsf T}Za_i.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The E-optimal value equals the minimum, over trace-one PSD direction mixtures, of the largest candidate directional information.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_w\lambda_{\min}(M(w))=\min_{Z\succeq0,\operatorname{tr}Z=1}\max_i a_i^{\mathsf T}Za_i\).
knowledge_statements.title: Minimax Dual of E-Optimality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonsmoothness caused by multiplicity of the smallest eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The superdifferential of the concave minimum-eigenvalue map is \[\partial^+\lambda_{\min}(M)=\{Z\succeq0:\operatorname{tr}Z=1,\ (M-\lambda_{\min}(M)I)Z=0\}.\] It is a singleton exactly when the smallest eigenvalue is simple. With multiplicity greater than one, the criterion is nonsmooth and worst-direction certificates need not be unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A repeated smallest eigenvalue makes E-optimality nonsmooth and permits mixtures of worst directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^+\lambda_{\min}(M)\) is a singleton if and only if \(\lambda_{\min}(M)\) is simple.

notation.meaning: Concave superdifferential of the minimum eigenvalue

knowledge_statements.title: Least-Eigenvalue Multiplicity Boundary

children.title: Optimality-Criterion Tradeoff Regimes
children.top_down_role: Design consequences arising from the choice among competing optimality criteria.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A convex information segment on which A-, D-, and E-optimality disagree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the attainable compound-experiment information segment \[M(t)=\operatorname{diag}(1+9t,4-3t),\qquad0\leq t\leq1,\] E-optimality selects \(t_E=1/4\), A-optimality selects \(t_A=(4\sqrt3-1)/(9+3\sqrt3)\), and D-optimality selects \(t_D=11/18\). These points are distinct.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex information region can have three distinct A-, D-, and E-optimal points.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M=\{\operatorname{diag}(1+9t,4-3t):0\leq t\leq1\}\) is the feasible information region.
Each endpoint may represent the information supplied by a compound experiment.

notation.meaning: Allocation parameter between two compound experiments

knowledge_statements.title: Criterion-Disagreement Counterexample

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epsilon-constraint representation of alphabetic-criterion Pareto designs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every Pareto-optimal design \(w^\star\) solves, for example, \[\min_{w\in W}\Phi_A(w)\quad\text{subject to}\quad \Phi_D(w)\leq\Phi_D(w^\star),\quad \Phi_E(w)\leq\Phi_E(w^\star).\] Conversely, a unique optimizer is Pareto optimal; more generally one must select a nondominated optimizer of the epsilon-constraint problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pareto designs solve epsilon-constraint problems; uniqueness or a nondominance refinement excludes merely weakly efficient optimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}\{\Phi_A(w):\Phi_D(w)\leq\Phi_D(w^\star),\ \Phi_E(w)\leq\Phi_E(w^\star)\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Epsilon-Constraint Tradeoff Representation
Optimality-Criterion Tradeoff Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto tradeoffs among A-, D-, and E-optimal approximate-design criteria.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let candidate regressors be \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R^p\), and let \(M(w)=\sum_{i=1}^m w_i a_i a_i^{\mathsf T}\succ0\) for \(w\) in the probability simplex. Define \(\Phi_A(w)=\operatorname{tr}(M(w)^{-1})\), \(\Phi_D(w)=-\log\det M(w)\), and \(\Phi_E(w)=\lambda_{\max}(M(w)^{-1})\). These criteria respectively emphasize average variance, generalized variance, and worst-direction variance and need not have a common minimizer. For any \(\alpha_A,\alpha_D,\alpha_E>0\), every minimizer of \(\alpha_A\Phi_A+\alpha_D\Phi_D+\alpha_E\Phi_E\) is Pareto optimal for the three-criterion minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A-, D-, and E-optimality control average, generalized, and worst-direction variance. They may select different designs; positive weighted scalarizations produce Pareto-optimal tradeoffs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_w(\alpha_A\Phi_A+\alpha_D\Phi_D+\alpha_E\Phi_E)\) consists of Pareto-optimal designs when \(\alpha_A,\alpha_D,\alpha_E>0\).

notation.meaning: information matrix of design weights w
A-, D-, and E-optimality loss criteria

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard convex optimal-design criteria and positive scalarization property

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property and content kind fit the tradeoff-regime leaf, but no cited source with an inspectable locator supports the optimal-design criteria or scalarization claim.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistent finite-grid approximation of continuous approximate design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let finite grids \(\mathcal X_k\subset\mathcal X\) satisfy \(\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}\inf_{y\in\mathcal X_k}\|x-y\|\to0\). If \(\Phi\) is continuous on \(\mathcal I\), then \[v_k=\min_{\xi\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X_k)}\Phi(M(\xi))\longrightarrow v=\min_{\xi\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X)}\Phi(M(\xi)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimizing on increasingly dense finite grids converges in optimal value when the regression map and criterion are continuous.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\) is compact and \(f\) is continuous.
\(\mathcal X_k\) are finite and converge to \(\mathcal X\) in one-sided Hausdorff distance.
\(\Phi\) is continuous on the compact information region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_k\to v\).
knowledge_statements.title: Convergent Finite-Grid Approximation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Information Region, Existence, and Finite Support
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact convex information region, existence, and Carathéodory reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For compact \(\mathcal X\) and continuous \(f\), \[\mathcal I=\left\{\int_{\mathcal X}f(x)f(x)^{\mathsf T}\,d\xi(x):\xi\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X)\right\}=\operatorname{conv}\{f(x)f(x)^{\mathsf T}:x\in\mathcal X\}\] is compact and convex. Every \(M\in\mathcal I\) is generated by a design supported on at most \(p(p+1)/2+1\) points. Every lower-semicontinuous criterion \(\Phi\) on \(\mathcal I\) that is finite somewhere attains its minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous designs generate a compact convex information region; finite-support designs suffice, and lower-semicontinuous information criteria attain their optima.
assumptions_latex: \(\Phi:\mathcal I\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is lower semicontinuous and finite somewhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every attainable or optimal information matrix has a representing design with at most \(p(p+1)/2+1\) support points, and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{M\in\mathcal I}\Phi(M)\neq\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Borel probability measures on the design space

knowledge_statements.title: Information Region, Existence, and Finite Support
Continuous Design Measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate optimal designs represented by probability measures on a design space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be a compact design space and \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^p\) a continuous regression map. A continuous, or approximate, design is a Borel probability measure \(\xi\) on \(\mathcal X\). Its information matrix is \[M(\xi)=\int_{\mathcal X} f(x)f(x)^{\mathsf T}\,d\xi(x).\] For a finite design space \(\mathcal X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\), this reduces to \(M(\xi)=\sum_{i=1}^m w_i f(x_i)f(x_i)^{\mathsf T}\), where \(w_i=\xi(\{x_i\})\ge0\) and \(\sum_iw_i=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous design allocates probability mass across experimental settings; integrating the rank-one regression information gives its information matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\xi\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X)\) and \(M(\xi)=\int_{\mathcal X}ff^{\mathsf T}\,d\xi\).

notation.meaning: Borel probability measures on the design space
information matrix of the approximate design

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The approximate-design definition is mathematically standard and fits the container, but it has no authoritative source reference with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relaxation bound and equality certificate for minimization-form exact design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an information loss \(\Phi\), \[v_{\mathrm{app}}=\min_{w\in\Delta_m}\Phi(M(w))\leq\min_{n\in\mathbb Z_+^m,\,\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}n=N}\Phi(M(n/N))=v_{\mathrm{ex}}.\] An exact design attaining \(v_{\mathrm{app}}\) is globally optimal for the fixed run budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The approximate optimum is a global lower bound for exact minimization, and equality certifies exact optimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_{\mathrm{app}}\leq v_{\mathrm{ex}}\), with equality attained by an exact design certifying global exact optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximate-Relaxation Bound Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact count of unrestricted replication vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The number of vectors \(n\in\mathbb Z_+^m\) satisfying \(\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}n=N\) is \[\binom{N+m-1}{m-1}.\] Exhaustive evaluation is therefore globally exact but has this candidate count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: There are binomial(N+m-1,m-1) exact replication vectors.
assumptions_latex: \(m\) candidate experiments and run budget \(N\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\{n\in\mathbb Z_+^m:\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}n=N\}|=\binom{N+m-1}{m-1}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Design Enumeration Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp rank-loss example at the approximate-to-exact boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a_1=e_1,a_2=e_2\in\mathbb R^2\) and \(N=1\), the approximate design \(w=(1/2,1/2)\) has \(M(w)=I/2\succ0\). The only exact weights, \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\), yield rank-one information matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With two orthogonal regressors and one run, a full-rank approximate design exists but every exact design is singular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M((1/2,1/2))\succ0\), while every exact one-run information matrix is singular.
knowledge_statements.title: One-Run Rank-Loss Counterexample
Discrete Experiment-Design Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between convex approximate designs and exact finite-run designs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m\) candidate experiments and a fixed run budget \(N\in\mathbb N\), an exact design has replication counts \(n\in\mathbb Z_+^m\) satisfying \(\sum_i n_i=N\), hence weights \(w_i=n_i/N\). The approximate relaxation replaces these weights by the simplex \(\{w\in\mathbb R_+^m:\sum_iw_i=1\}\). Although a convex information criterion may yield a tractable approximate-design problem, the exact feasible set is discrete and nonconvex. Consequently, an approximate optimum need not be exactly implementable, and rounding its weights need not preserve feasibility, nonsingularity, or optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-run replication counts impose an integer grid. Convex approximate-design solutions may be unrealizable, and rounding can destroy information-matrix rank or optimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w\in N^{-1}\mathbb Z_+^m\cap\{w:\sum_iw_i=1\}\), a generally nonconvex proper subset of the approximate-design simplex.

notation.meaning: replication count for candidate experiment i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact-design integrality versus approximate-design convexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and integrality distinction are appropriate, but the exact-design and rounding claims lack a cited source with an inspectable locator.
