children.title: Blur-Kernel Mismatch Boundary
children.top_down_role: Restoration degradation caused by inaccurate forward-blur models.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp best-fit residual floor caused by an incorrect fixed blur operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With noiseless data \(f=K_0u_0\) but assumed operator \(K\), \[\inf_u\|Ku-f\|_2=\operatorname{dist}\bigl((K_0-K)u_0,\operatorname{range}K\bigr).\] Kernel error therefore has an irreducible data-space signature exactly when \((K_0-K)u_0\notin\operatorname{range}K\). If it lies in \(\operatorname{range}K\), another image can absorb the mismatch and achieve exact fit, so zero residual does not certify that the assumed kernel is correct.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The irreducible residual from a wrong kernel is the distance of its induced error to the assumed operator's range; some kernel errors can be absorbed by changing the image.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) and \(K_0\) are linear maps between finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_u\|Ku-f\|_2=\operatorname{dist}((K_0-K)u_0,\operatorname{range}K).

notation.meaning: True and assumed forward blur operators.

knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Kernel-Mismatch Residual Floor
Blur-Kernel Mismatch Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic data-error floor induced by using an incorrect blur operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose noiseless data satisfy \(f=K_0u_0\), but restoration uses a different operator \(K\). At the true image, the modeled residual equals \[Ku_0-f=(K-K_0)u_0.\] Therefore exact modeled data fit by \(u_0\) is impossible whenever \((K-K_0)u_0\ne0\). Moreover, \(\|(K-K_0)u_0\|\le\|K-K_0\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|u_0\|\), so operator-norm control gives only an upper bound on the mismatch residual, not identifiability of both image and kernel. Fixed-kernel convex TV restoration does not correct an unknown kernel; joint image-kernel estimation is generally a different, typically nonconvex problem.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An image \(x\) minimizes \[\frac12\|P_\Omega x-b\|_2^2+\lambda\|Gx\|_{2,1}\] if and only if there is a field \(p\) with \(p_i\in\partial\|\cdot\|_2((Gx)_i)\) such that \[P_\Omega^T(P_\Omega x-b)+\lambda G^Tp=0.\] Restricting this equation to missing coordinates gives \[P_{\Omega^c}G^Tp=0,\] so unobserved coordinates satisfy pure TV equilibrium, whereas observed coordinates also balance the data residual.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete convex reconstruction from a partially observed image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) be an image, let \(P_\Omega\) retain coordinates indexed by the observed set \(\Omega\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(b\in\mathbb R^{|\Omega|}\) contain the observations. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Poisson count-data variant of finite-dimensional TV tomography.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For independent Poisson measurements with means \((Ax)_i\), a TV reconstruction solves \[\min_{x\in C}\sum_{i=1}^m\left((Ax)_i-b_i\log((Ax)_i)\right)+\lambda\operatorname{TV}(x),\qquad \lambda>0.\] The extended-valued objective is convex when \(A\) is linear, \(C\subseteq\mathbb R_+^n\) is convex, and its effective domain requires \((Ax)_i>0\) whenever \(b_i>0\). Unlike weighted least squares, this fidelity models signal-dependent Poisson counting noise.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) stack the retained horizontal and vertical differences and let \(R(x)=\|Dx\|_1\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kernel characterization for anisotropic TV on the graph induced by retained differences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the retained finite differences be the oriented edges of \(G=(V,E)\). Then \[\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{aniso}}(x)=0\iff x\text{ is constant on every connected component of }G.\] On a connected rectangular grid its nullspace is \(\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1\}\), so it induces a norm on \(\mathbb R^V/\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Anisotropic TV vanishes exactly on componentwise-constant images and becomes a norm after constants are factored out on a connected grid.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) contains precisely the pixel adjacencies represented by \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ker(\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{aniso}})=\{x:x\text{ is constant on each component of }G\}\).

notation.meaning: Difference graph of pixels and retained adjacencies.

knowledge_statements.title: Nullspace on a Difference Graph
Anisotropic Total Variation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward-difference anisotropic TV on a rectangular scalar-image grid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an image \(x\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), define forward differences \((D_1x)_{ij}=x_{i+1,j}-x_{ij}\) for \(i<m\) and \((D_2x)_{ij}=x_{i,j+1}-x_{ij}\) for \(j<n\). Its anisotropic discrete total variation is \[\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{aniso}}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n}|(D_1x)_{ij}|+\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}|(D_2x)_{ij}|.\] Equivalently, after omitting unavailable boundary differences, it is the \(\ell_1\)-norm of the stacked discrete gradient. This functional is convex, positively homogeneous, and invariant under addition of a constant image.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Anisotropic TV sums absolute horizontal and vertical finite differences separately, making it the entrywise one-norm of the discrete gradient.
assumptions_latex: Forward differences are omitted at the corresponding grid boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{aniso}}(x)=\|Dx\|_1\) for the stacked forward-difference operator \(D\).

children.title: Isotropic Total Variation
children.top_down_role: Total-variation models using rotationally aggregated local variation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Isotropic TV for a fixed discrete gradient partitioned into local two-component blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write \(R(x)=\sum_v\|(Dx)_v\|_2\). Then \[R(x)=\max_{\|p_v\|_2\leq1\ \forall v}\sum_v\langle(Dx)_v,p_v\rangle=\max_{\|p_v\|_2\leq1\ \forall v}\langle x,D^{\mathsf T}p\rangle.\] A vector \(s\) lies in \(\partial R(x)\) exactly when \(s=D^{\mathsf T}p\), \(\|p_v\|_2\leq1\), and \(p_v=(Dx)_v/\|(Dx)_v\|_2\) whenever \((Dx)_v\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Isotropic TV is supported by pixelwise Euclidean unit balls; aligned dual blocks give its exact subgradient certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a fixed linear discrete-gradient operator.
The components of \(Dx\) are partitioned into local gradient blocks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(x)=\max_{\|p_v\|_2\leq1}\langle x,D^{\mathsf T}p\rangle\) with the stated subgradient characterization.
knowledge_statements.title: Block-Dual Representation and Subgradient Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kernel of isotropic TV under a fixed difference graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the graph formed by all retained directional differences, \[\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{iso}}(x)=0\iff x\text{ is constant on every connected component}.\] Thus a connected grid has nullspace \(\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1\}\), and isotropic TV induces a norm modulo constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Isotropic TV vanishes precisely on componentwise-constant images.
assumptions_latex: Every retained difference is included in a local Euclidean block.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ker(\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{iso}})=\{x:x\text{ is constant on each component of the difference graph}\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Connected-Grid Nullspace
Isotropic Total Variation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward-difference isotropic TV on a rectangular scalar-image grid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), let \(D_1x\) and \(D_2x\) be forward differences, extended by zero where a forward neighbor is unavailable. The isotropic discrete total variation is \[\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{iso}}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sqrt{(D_1x)_{ij}^2+(D_2x)_{ij}^2}.\] It applies the Euclidean norm to the two directional differences at each pixel and then sums across pixels. The functional is convex, positively homogeneous, and unchanged by adding a constant image.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Isotropic TV sums the Euclidean magnitudes of pixelwise horizontal and vertical finite-difference vectors.
assumptions_latex: Unavailable forward differences are set to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{iso}}(x)=\sum_{i,j}\|(D_1x,D_2x)_{ij}\|_2\).

children.title: Grid-Orientation Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Directional artifacts and invariance differences across the two variants.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes invariance of the local norm from invariance of the sampled finite-difference functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Although \(\|Qg\|_2=\|g\|_2\) for every planar orthogonal \(Q\), a fixed Cartesian finite-difference operator generally does not commute with arbitrary image rotation and resampling. Thus Euclidean local aggregation removes norm-induced axis preference but does not make the complete discrete isotropic-TV functional invariant under arbitrary rotations. Exact invariance follows only for transformations preserving the grid, stencil, and boundary convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Euclidean local norm is rotation invariant, but a Cartesian discretization generally is not.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a fixed Cartesian-grid difference operator.
A rotation not preserving the sampled grid requires a specified resampling map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|Qg\|_2=\|g\|_2\) does not generally imply \(\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{iso}}(T_Qx)=\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{iso}}(x)\).

notation.meaning: Chosen discrete rotation and resampling transformation.

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete Rotation-Invariance Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative comparison of anisotropic and isotropic aggregation for a two-direction gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(g=(g_1,g_2)\in\mathbb R^2\), \[\|g\|_2\leq\|g\|_1\leq\sqrt2\,\|g\|_2.\] Equality on the left holds exactly when \(g_1g_2=0\); for \(g\neq0\), equality on the right holds exactly when \(|g_1|=|g_2|\). Consequently, for matching stencils, \[\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{iso}}(x)\leq\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{aniso}}(x)\leq\sqrt2\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{iso}}(x),\] with both constants sharp.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Anisotropic TV lies sharply between isotropic TV and √2 times isotropic TV; aligned and diagonal gradients attain the extremes.
assumptions_latex: Both TV functionals use the same local gradient vectors and boundary convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{iso}}(x)\leq\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{aniso}}(x)\leq\sqrt2\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{iso}}(x)\), sharply.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Local Norm Comparison
Grid-Orientation Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orientation dependence induced by the local gradient norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g\in\mathbb R^2\) be a local discrete-gradient vector and define \(\phi_1(g)=|g_1|+|g_2|\) and \(\phi_2(g)=\sqrt{g_1^2+g_2^2}\). For every orthogonal matrix \(Q\), \(\phi_2(Qg)=\phi_2(g)\), whereas \(\phi_1(Qg)\) need not equal \(\phi_1(g)\). In particular, for \(g=(1,0)\) and a rotation \(Q\) through \(\pi/4\), \[\phi_1(g)=1,\qquad \phi_1(Qg)=\sqrt2,\qquad \phi_2(g)=\phi_2(Qg)=1.\] Hence anisotropic TV has intrinsic axis preference at the local norm level, while isotropic TV removes that particular norm-induced orientation bias, apart from discretization effects.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The anisotropic gradient norm changes under rotation, while the Euclidean gradient norm does not; consequently anisotropic TV favors grid-aligned edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi_2(Qg)=\phi_2(g)\) for every \(Q\), but generally \(\phi_1(Qg)\neq\phi_1(g)\).

children.title: Vectorial Total Variation
children.top_down_role: Total-variation models coupling multiple image channels or fields.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic vectorial TV formed from a matrix norm at each pixel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R(x)=\sum_v\|G_v(x)\|_\star\), and let \(\|\cdot\|_{\star,*}\) be the dual matrix norm under the Frobenius pairing. Then \[R(x)=\max_{\|P_v\|_{\star,*}\leq1\ \forall v}\sum_v\langle G_v(x),P_v\rangle_F=\max_{\|P_v\|_{\star,*}\leq1\ \forall v}\langle x,G^*P\rangle.\] A field \(G^*P\) is a subgradient exactly when each local pairing attains \(\|G_v(x)\|_\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every matrix-norm vectorial TV has a local dual-matrix-ball representation and a saturation-based subgradient certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(x)=\max_{\|P_v\|_{\star,*}\leq1}\langle x,G^*P\rangle\).

notation.meaning: Adjoint of the full multichannel-gradient map.

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Norm Dual Representation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kernel for a genuine matrix norm and common channelwise differences on a connected grid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\|\cdot\|_\star\) is a norm and the spatial difference graph is connected, then \[\operatorname{VTV}_\star(x)=0\iff x^{(r)}\text{ is spatially constant for every channel }r.\] Hence the nullspace has dimension \(c\) and consists of arbitrary constant channel vectors replicated over the grid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a connected grid, vectorial TV vanishes exactly when every channel is constant, though the channel constants may differ.
assumptions_latex: The local penalty is a true matrix norm.
Every channel uses the same connected spatial difference graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ker(\operatorname{VTV}_\star)=\{\mathbf1\otimes a:a\in\mathbb R^c\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Vectorial-TV Nullspace
Vectorial Total Variation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint first-order TV for multichannel discrete images.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in\mathbb R^{m\times n\times c}\) be a \(c\)-channel image. At pixel \((i,j)\), collect its directional differences into the matrix \(G_{ij}(x)\in\mathbb R^{c\times2}\), whose channel \(r\) row is \(((D_1x^{(r)})_{ij},(D_2x^{(r)})_{ij})\). For any matrix norm \(\|\cdot\|_\star\), the associated vectorial total variation is \[\operatorname{VTV}_\star(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\|G_{ij}(x)\|_\star.\] It is convex and positively homogeneous. Choosing a nonseparable matrix norm couples channels by charging their colocated directional changes jointly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vectorial TV sums a matrix norm of all channel gradients at each pixel, allowing edges in different channels to be coupled.
assumptions_latex: \(D_1\) and \(D_2\) are fixed linear difference operators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{VTV}_\star(x)=\sum_{i,j}\|G_{ij}(x)\|_\star\) is a convex multichannel regularizer.

notation.meaning: Matrix of all channel gradients at one pixel.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard matrix-norm formulation of discrete vectorial TV

children.title: Higher-Order Total Variation
children.top_down_role: Total-variation extensions based on higher-order spatial structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support representation for a fixed order-k difference operator and local norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_k(x)=\sum_v\|(D^kx)_v\|\), with dual local norm \(\|\cdot\|_*\). Then \[R_k(x)=\max_{\|p_v\|_*\leq1\ \forall v}\langle D^kx,p\rangle=\max_{\|p_v\|_*\leq1\ \forall v}\langle x,(D^k)^{\mathsf T}p\rangle.\] Thus \(s\in\partial R_k(x)\) exactly when \(s=(D^k)^{\mathsf T}p\) for a locally dual-feasible field whose pairing with each derivative block attains that block's norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Higher-order TV is supported by the adjoint higher-difference operator applied to local dual balls, yielding an exact subgradient certificate.
assumptions_latex: The penalty is a sum of norms of local derivative blocks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_k(x)=\max_{\|p_v\|_*\leq1}\langle x,(D^k)^{\mathsf T}p\rangle\).

notation.meaning: Local dual field for an order-k derivative block.

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order Dual Representation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limitation on identifying the kernel of discrete higher-order TV with polynomial samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The identity \(R_k(x)=0\iff x\in\ker(D^k)\) is unconditional, but identifying \(\ker(D^k)\) with sampled polynomials of degree below \(k\) is not boundary-convention invariant. The ordinary unpadded one-dimensional \(k\)-th forward difference on a connected interval annihilates exactly the discrete polynomial sequences of degree at most \(k-1\); zero padding, periodic closure, or additional boundary rows can shrink or otherwise alter that kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The operator kernel is exact, but a polynomial-nullspace description requires a specified stencil and boundary treatment.
assumptions_latex: \(D^k\) is a discrete order-k derivative operator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ker(D^k)\) depends on the full stencil, including its boundary rows.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Dependent Polynomial Nullspace
Higher-Order Total Variation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete order-k variation defined by higher finite differences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an integer \(k\geq2\) and a linear discrete derivative operator \(D^k:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^q\) collecting all prescribed finite differences of total order \(k\). The order-\(k\) discrete total-variation seminorm associated with a norm \(\|\cdot\|_{1,\mathrm{loc}}\) is \[\operatorname{HOTV}_k(x)=\|D^k x\|_{1,\mathrm{loc}},\] where the local norm groups derivative components at each grid site and sums the resulting magnitudes. It is convex and positively homogeneous, and \(\operatorname{HOTV}_k(x)=0\) exactly when \(x\in\ker(D^k)\). Under a standard consistent stencil, sampled polynomials of degree below \(k\) belong to this kernel away from boundary modifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Higher-order TV penalizes grouped finite differences of order k and vanishes on the nullspace of that higher-derivative operator.
assumptions_latex: \(D^k:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^q\) is a fixed linear order-k difference operator.
\(\|\cdot\|_{1,\mathrm{loc}}\) is a norm formed by summing local norms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{HOTV}_k(x)=\|D^kx\|_{1,\mathrm{loc}}\) is convex and has kernel \(\ker(D^k)\).

notation.meaning: Chosen discrete derivative operator of order k.

boundary convention must be fixed by implementation

children.title: Cross-Channel Coupling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Alternative coupling choices for multichannel variation models.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual representation of separable and jointly coupled channel-gradient magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At each site let \(a=(a_1,\ldots,a_c)\in\mathbb R_+^c\) contain channel-gradient magnitudes. For \(1\leq p\leq\infty\) and conjugate exponent \(q\), \[\|a\|_p=\max_{\|z\|_q\leq1}\langle a,z\rangle.\] Hence a sum of local \(\ell_p\) aggregators has independent local \(\ell_q\)-ball constraints in the dual. For \(c\geq2\), \(p=1\) gives channel-separable addition, whereas every \(p>1\) uses a shared local dual budget and is nonseparable across channel magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cross-channel coupling is dual to sharing one local dual-norm budget; p=1 is separable, while p>1 couples two or more channels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|a\|_p=\max_{\|z\|_q\leq1}\langle a,z\rangle\); for \(c\geq2\), the aggregation is channel-separable exactly when \(p=1\).
review_flags: corrected_builder_claim: added c>=2 condition to the separability boundary
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Norm Dual Coupling

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of coupling regimes on orthogonal changes of channel coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\in\mathbb R^{c\times d}\) be a local channel-gradient matrix and let \(U\in\mathbb R^{c\times c}\) be orthogonal. Every unitarily invariant matrix norm satisfies \(\|UG\|=\|G\|\); in particular, Frobenius and Schatten norms are invariant under orthogonal mixing of channels. By contrast, the row-separable penalty \(\sum_{r=1}^c\|G_{r,:}\|_2\) generally changes under such mixing when \(c>1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Schatten and Frobenius couplings are invariant to orthogonal channel mixing, while channelwise summed TV generally is not.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a local channel-by-direction gradient matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|UG\|=\|G\|\) for unitarily invariant norms, but generally \(\sum_r\|(UG)_{r,:}\|_2\neq\sum_r\|G_{r,:}\|_2\).
knowledge_statements.title: Channel-Basis Invariance Boundary
Cross-Channel Coupling Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separable and joint norm regimes for multichannel gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a multichannel image, let \(g_{ijr}\in\mathbb R^2\) be the gradient of channel \(r\) at pixel \((i,j)\). Two principal convex coupling regimes are \[R_{\mathrm{sep}}(x)=\sum_{i,j}\sum_{r=1}^c\|g_{ijr}\|_2\] and \[R_{\mathrm{joint}}(x)=\sum_{i,j}\left(\sum_{r=1}^c\|g_{ijr}\|_2^p\right)^{1/p},\qquad 1<p<\infty.\] The separable regime adds channelwise TV penalties independently. The joint regime uses a mixed norm at each pixel, so simultaneous channel gradients share one local penalty. More generally, Schatten norms of the channel-gradient matrix can additionally couple edge directions across channels.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Channelwise TV penalizes each channel independently; mixed or Schatten norms jointly penalize colocated multichannel gradients and can encourage shared edges.
assumptions_latex: \(g_{ijr}\in\mathbb R^2\) is the discrete gradient of channel \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_{\mathrm{sep}}\) is channel-separable, whereas \(R_{\mathrm{joint}}\) couples channel-gradient magnitudes at each pixel.

notation.meaning: Gradient of channel r at pixel (i,j).

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard separable-versus-mixed-norm multichannel coupling taxonomy

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The separable and mixed-norm formulas are convex and fit a representation of coupling regimes, but the shared-edge interpretation and Schatten-norm extension need authoritative support.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Higher-dimensional geometric form of TV edge preservation for a two-phase image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\subset\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) have finite perimeter in \(\Omega\), and let \(u=a\mathbf1_E+b\mathbf1_{\Omega\setminus E}\). Then \[\operatorname{TV}(u;\Omega)=|a-b|\operatorname{Per}(E;\Omega).\] Thus first-order TV charges an ideal edge by its contrast times its geometric perimeter and does not require the transition to be spatially diffuse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a two-phase image, TV equals jump contrast times interface perimeter, explaining why sharp edges can be retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{TV}(u;\Omega)=|a-b|\operatorname{Per}(E;\Omega).

notation.meaning: perimeter of E relative to Omega

knowledge_statements.title: Jump-Set Cost of Total Variation
Edge-Preservation Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why first-order TV does not intrinsically penalize edge sharpness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u\in BV((0,1))\) be monotone with one-sided endpoint values \(u(0+)=a\) and \(u(1-)=b\). Then \[\operatorname{TV}(u;(0,1))=|b-a|.\] The same value is attained by a step function having a single jump from \(a\) to \(b\), and by any monotone continuous transition between those levels. Consequently, first-order TV charges contrast magnitude but not transition width. In a data-fitting model, this creates an edge-preservation regime: when the data term supports a discontinuity strongly enough, replacing it by a wider monotone ramp yields no intrinsic TV reduction, although contrast may still be biased.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For monotone transitions, TV depends on endpoint contrast rather than transition width, so sharp edges are not intrinsically more expensive than ramps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{TV}(u;(0,1))=|b-a|\), independently of whether the transition is sharp or diffuse.

notation.meaning: Functions of bounded variation on the unit interval.
Total variation of u on the interval.

children.title: Staircasing Artifacts
children.top_down_role: Piecewise-constant artifacts arising in total-variation reconstructions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact one-dimensional ROF example producing artificial plateaus from a smooth ramp.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=x\) on \([0,1]\), consider \[\min_{u\in BV(0,1)}\frac12\int_0^1(u(x)-x)^2\,dx+\lambda\operatorname{TV}(u).\] If \(0<\lambda\le 1/8\) and \(a=\sqrt{2\lambda}\), the unique minimizer is \[u_\lambda(x)=\begin{cases}a,&0\le x<a,\\x,&a\le x\le1-a,\\1-a,&1-a<x\le1.\end{cases}\] Thus first-order TV replaces portions of a strictly varying signal by artificial constant plateaus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: ROF denoising of a linear ramp creates constant boundary plateaus of width square root of twice the regularization weight.
assumptions_latex: The continuum one-dimensional ROF problem uses the natural boundary condition for its TV subgradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unique minimizer has positive-length constant boundary intervals although \(f(x)=x\) is strictly increasing.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Ramp Staircasing Example
Staircasing Artifacts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational failure signature of first-order TV reconstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be observed data on a connected domain \(\Omega\), and let \(u_\lambda\) minimize a first-order TV model \[\frac12\|u-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\lambda\operatorname{TV}(u),\qquad \lambda>0.\] Staircasing is present relative to a nonconstant reference \(f_\star\) when there exists a measurable set \(E\subseteq\Omega\) of positive measure such that \(u_\lambda=c\) almost everywhere on \(E\), while \(f_\star\) is not essentially constant on \(E\). The artifact therefore consists of spurious plateaus separated by jumps. It marks a failure of first-order TV to represent smoothly varying regions without piecewise-constant bias; higher-order regularization can alter this failure mode.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Staircasing occurs when first-order TV replaces a genuinely varying region by positive-area constant plateaus separated by artificial jumps.
assumptions_latex: \(u_\lambda\) minimizes the displayed first-order TV objective.
\(f_\star\) is the nonconstant reference image used to assess the reconstruction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A positive-measure plateau of \(u_\lambda\) over a nonconstant region of \(f_\star\) is a staircasing artifact.

notation.meaning: Region on which a spurious plateau occurs.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard operational characterization of TV staircasing
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, and the plateau criterion is a plausible operational characterization, but it is not a universally self-evident definition and needs a supporting source.

children.title: Contrast-Bias Effects
children.top_down_role: Systematic attenuation or distortion of reconstructed contrast.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complementary constant-solution regime of the two-region ROF model in the immutable seed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the two-region assumptions of the seed, if \[b-a\le\lambda\left(\ell^{-1}+(1-\ell)^{-1}\right),\] the ROF minimizer is the constant \[u(t)=\bar f:=\ell a+(1-\ell)b\quad\text{a.e. on }(0,1).\] Hence the reconstructed contrast is zero. Equality is the threshold at which the positive-contrast formula reaches zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Once the TV weight reaches the explicit two-region threshold, the two levels merge into their weighted mean and contrast vanishes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u\equiv\ell a+(1-\ell)b\quad\text{and the recovered contrast is }0.

notation.meaning: spatial mean of the two-level datum

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Region Contrast-Extinction Threshold
Contrast-Bias Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact contrast shrinkage in a two-region one-dimensional ROF model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(0<\ell<1\), let \(a<b\), and define \(f=a\) on \((0,\ell)\) and \(f=b\) on \((\ell,1)\). Minimize \[\frac12\int_0^1(u-f)^2\,dt+\lambda\operatorname{TV}(u),\qquad \lambda>0.\] If \(b-a>\lambda(\ell^{-1}+(1-\ell)^{-1})\), the minimizer is constant on the two regions with values \[u=a+\frac{\lambda}{\ell}\quad\text{and}\quad u=b-\frac{\lambda}{1-\ell}.\] Its reconstructed contrast is therefore \[b-a-\lambda\left(\frac1\ell+\frac1{1-\ell}\right)<b-a.\] Thus TV preserves the jump location in this regime but systematically shrinks its amplitude.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a two-region ROF problem, TV shifts both levels toward each other, reducing contrast by an explicit amount while retaining the jump.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recovered contrast equals \(b-a-\lambda(\ell^{-1}+(1-\ell)^{-1})\), strictly below \(b-a\).

notation.meaning: Length of the first constant region.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value-function structure for the TV regularization parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(v(\lambda)=\inf_u\{D(u)+\lambda T(u)\}\) for \(\lambda>0\), with \(T\ge0\). Then \(v\) is nondecreasing and concave. Whenever \(u_\lambda\) is a minimizer, \(T(u_\lambda)\) is a supergradient of \(v\) at \(\lambda\): \[v(\mu)\le v(\lambda)+T(u_\lambda)(\mu-\lambda)\quad(\mu>0).\] If \(v\) is differentiable at \(\lambda\), all minimizers have the same variation and \(v'(\lambda)=T(u_\lambda)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The optimal value is an increasing concave function of the TV weight, and its slope equals the attained total variation when differentiable.
assumptions_latex: A minimizer exists at each parameter where a supergradient is asserted
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v\text{ is nondecreasing and concave, with }T(u_\lambda)\in\partial^+v(\lambda).

notation.meaning: superdifferential of the concave value function

knowledge_statements.title: Concavity of the Regularization-Path Value

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lexicographic limiting behavior of TV-penalized minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be finite-dimensional, let \(D,T:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions with \(T\ge0\), and suppose the relevant minimizers exist and the considered minimizer sequences are bounded. For \(u_\lambda\in\operatorname*{argmin}(D+\lambda T)\): (i) every cluster point as \(\lambda\downarrow0\) minimizes \(D\) and, among minimizers of \(D\), minimizes \(T\); (ii) every cluster point as \(\lambda\to\infty\) minimizes \(T\) and, among minimizers of \(T\), minimizes \(D\). For ordinary TV on a connected domain with shift-invariant boundary conditions, the minimum-TV signals are constants, so a unique best-fitting constant is the large-\(\lambda\) limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vanishing TV weight selects a least-TV data-fit minimizer, while diverging weight selects a best-fitting minimum-TV signal, usually a constant.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) and \(T\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions
The considered minimizers exist and form bounded sequences
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda\downarrow0\text{ and }\lambda\to\infty\text{ produce the stated lexicographic cluster points.}

notation.meaning: a minimizer of the penalized objective at weight lambda

review_flags: The cluster-point conclusions require the stated attainment and boundedness assumptions.
knowledge_statements.title: Small- and Large-Regularization Limits
Regularization-Strength Tradeoff
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonic fidelity–variation tradeoff for penalized total-variation reconstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be a proper convex data-fidelity function and let \(T(u)=\operatorname{TV}(u)\). For each \(\lambda>0\), suppose \(u_\lambda\in\arg\min_u\{D(u)+\lambda T(u)\}\). If \(0<\lambda_1<\lambda_2\), then
\[
T(u_{\lambda_2})\le T(u_{\lambda_1})
\quad\text{and}\quad
D(u_{\lambda_1})\le D(u_{\lambda_2}).
\]
Thus increasing regularization strength cannot increase the selected solution's total variation or improve its achieved data fit, although either inequality may be an equality when minimizers are nonunique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stronger TV regularization produces a minimizer with no greater total variation and no better data fit, with possible equality under nonuniqueness.
assumptions_latex: A minimizer \(u_\lambda\) exists for each considered \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(u_{\lambda_2})\le T(u_{\lambda_1})\) and \(D(u_{\lambda_1})\le D(u_{\lambda_2})\) whenever \(0<\lambda_1<\lambda_2\).

notation.meaning: a minimizer at regularization strength lambda

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The monotonic tradeoff is mathematically standard and fits the property container, but no inspectable source supports it.

children.title: Image-Boundary Conditions
children.top_down_role: Effects of alternative domain-edge treatments in total-variation models.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nullspaces and offset invariance induced by common discrete-TV boundary closures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) collect horizontal and vertical forward differences on a connected rectangular grid. Under periodic or homogeneous Neumann closure, \[D(u+c\mathbf1)=Du\quad\text{and}\quad\ker D=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1\}.\] Under homogeneous Dirichlet closure to exterior value zero, with boundary differences included, \(D(u+c\mathbf1)\ne Du\) generally for \(c\ne0\), and every nonzero constant image incurs a boundary penalty. Thus periodic and Neumann TV are invariant under global intensity shifts, whereas zero-Dirichlet TV is not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Periodic and Neumann TV ignore global offsets, while Dirichlet anchoring penalizes them through boundary differences.
assumptions_latex: Dirichlet boundary differences are included in \(D\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \ker D=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1\}\text{ for periodic or Neumann closure, whereas zero-Dirichlet anchoring removes nonzero constants from the kernel.}
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Condition Nullspaces
Image-Boundary Conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard closures of a forward-difference TV operator at an image boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an image \(u\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), define the interior horizontal difference by \((D_xu)_{i,j}=u_{i+1,j}-u_{i,j}\) for \(i<m\). Its last-row value is fixed by a boundary convention: periodic closure sets \((D_xu)_{m,j}=u_{1,j}-u_{m,j}\); homogeneous Neumann closure sets \((D_xu)_{m,j}=0\); and Dirichlet closure with exterior value \(c_j\) sets \((D_xu)_{m,j}=c_j-u_{m,j}\). The vertical operator is defined analogously. The selected closure is part of the discrete TV model because it changes the boundary penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Periodic, Neumann, and Dirichlet closures connect, suppress, or externally anchor boundary differences; consequently they define different discrete TV objectives.
assumptions_latex: \(u\) is a finite rectangular image array.
Forward differences are used in each coordinate direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The boundary convention uniquely specifies the missing edge differences and therefore the associated discrete TV functional.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The boundary closures are coherent and fit a definition, but the record supplies no source or locator.

children.title: Discretization-Scheme Effects
children.top_down_role: Imaging behavior associated with alternative discrete gradient constructions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure mode created by a centered-difference TV stencil.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a periodic one-dimensional grid of even size \(N\), define \((D_cu)_i=(u_{i+1}-u_{i-1})/(2h)\), with indices modulo \(N\). For the nonconstant alternating signal \(u_i=(-1)^i\), \[(D_cu)_i=0\quad\text{for every }i.\] Consequently, a TV seminorm constructed only from \(D_c\) assigns zero variation to this mode, whereas forward-difference TV assigns it positive variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Centered differences can miss an alternating checkerboard signal entirely, unlike forward differences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u_i=(-1)^i\not\equiv\mathrm{constant}\quad\text{but}\quad D_cu=0.
knowledge_statements.title: Centered-Difference Checkerboard Null Mode
Discretization-Scheme Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative difference between anisotropic and isotropic pixelwise TV discretizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For forward differences \(p_{i,j}=(D_xu)_{i,j}\) and \(q_{i,j}=(D_yu)_{i,j}\) under one fixed boundary convention, define
\[
\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{iso}}(u)=\sum_{i,j}\sqrt{p_{i,j}^2+q_{i,j}^2},\qquad
\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{aniso}}(u)=\sum_{i,j}(|p_{i,j}|+|q_{i,j}|).
\]
Then
\[
\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{iso}}(u)\le \operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{aniso}}(u)\le \sqrt{2}\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{iso}}(u).
\]
The anisotropic integrand depends on grid-axis orientation, whereas the isotropic integrand is invariant under orthogonal rotations of each two-component discrete gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Anisotropic and isotropic TV differ by at most a factor of square root two, but anisotropic TV preferentially reflects the grid axes.
assumptions_latex: Both discretizations use the same forward differences and boundary closure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{iso}}(u)\le\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{aniso}}(u)\le\sqrt{2}\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{iso}}(u)\).

notation.meaning: horizontal and vertical differences at a pixel

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The norm comparison and orientation distinction are correct for the stated discretizations, but they are unsupported by an inspectable citation.

children.title: Grid-Resolution Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of reconstruction geometry on spatial resolution.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion between continuum-scaled and raw-pixel-sum ROF parameters in two dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a square grid of spacing \(h\), consider \[\frac{h^2}{2}\sum_{i,j}(u_{ij}-f_{ij})^2+\alpha h\sum_{i,j}\|\Delta u_{ij}\|_2.\] Multiplication by \(h^{-2}>0\) leaves its minimizers unchanged and yields \[\frac12\sum_{i,j}(u_{ij}-f_{ij})^2+\frac{\alpha}{h}\sum_{i,j}\|\Delta u_{ij}\|_2.\] Therefore a formulation using unnormalized pixel sums must choose \(\lambda_h=\alpha/h\) to represent a fixed continuum weight \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With unnormalized two-dimensional pixel sums, the raw TV weight scales inversely with grid spacing to represent the same continuum model.
assumptions_latex: The grid is square with spacing \(h>0\)
Both fidelity and TV use raw pixel sums in the second formulation
The boundary and difference conventions are fixed across grids
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda_h=\alpha/h.

notation.meaning: weight multiplying the raw difference sum

knowledge_statements.title: Resolution-Consistent Regularization Scaling
Grid-Resolution Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mesh scaling required for consistent two-dimensional discrete TV values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(u\in C^1([0,1]^2)\) be sampled on a square grid of spacing \(h\), and use forward differences away from the boundary. The quadrature-consistent isotropic TV is
\[
T_h(u)=h^2\sum_{i,j}\sqrt{\left(\frac{u_{i+1,j}-u_{i,j}}{h}\right)^2+\left(\frac{u_{i,j+1}-u_{i,j}}{h}\right)^2}
=h\sum_{i,j}\sqrt{(\Delta_xu_{i,j})^2+(\Delta_yu_{i,j})^2}.
\]
As \(h\to0\), this is a Riemann-sum approximation to \(\int_{[0,1]^2}\|\nabla u(x)\|_2\,dx\). Omitting the factor \(h\) makes the raw sum typically grow like \(h^{-1}\) for a nonconstant smooth image.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In two dimensions, the raw sum of pixel differences must be multiplied by grid spacing to approximate continuum TV across resolutions.
assumptions_latex: The grids are uniform and square with spacing \(h\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_h(u)\to\int_{[0,1]^2}\|\nabla u(x)\|_2\,dx\), while the unscaled difference sum generally has order \(h^{-1}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-dimensional mesh scaling is plausible, but a source and a precise summation/boundary convention are needed to validate the convergence statement.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential update for nonnegative growth vectors; the return ratios, barrier values, and maximizers must be well-defined at each iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, let $F$ be a $\nu$-self-concordant barrier for $P$, let $x_0\in\operatorname{int}P$, and let $c_k\in\mathbb{R}_+^n$ for $k\ge0$. For $k=0,1,2,\ldots$, select
\[
x_{k+1}\in\arg\max_{x\in P}\left\{\frac{1}{k+1}\sum_{i=0}^{k}\frac{\langle c_i,x-x_i\rangle}{\langle c_i,x_i\rangle}-\frac{\sqrt{\nu}+\sqrt{k+1}}{\sqrt{\nu(k+1)}}\bigl(F(x)-F(x_0)\bigr)\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each period, update the portfolio by maximizing the average linearized relative return observed so far, penalized by an iteration-dependent self-concordant-barrier displacement from the initial portfolio.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{k+1}\in\arg\max_{x\in P}\left\{\frac{1}{k+1}\sum_{i=0}^{k}\frac{\langle c_i,x-x_i\rangle}{\langle c_i,x_i\rangle}-\frac{\sqrt{\nu}+\sqrt{k+1}}{\sqrt{\nu(k+1)}}(F(x)-F(x_0))\right\},\quad k\ge0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimal Constant-Share Portfolio and Average Growth Rate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon benchmark over a feasible subset of the simplex, assuming the product maximization attains its optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $P\subseteq\Delta_n$ and $c_k\in\mathbb{R}_+^n$ for $k=0,\ldots,N$. Choose
\[
x_N^\star\in\arg\max_{x\in P}\prod_{k=0}^{N}\langle c_k,x\rangle.
\]
The corresponding optimal average growth rate is
\[
\psi_N^\star:=\left(\prod_{k=0}^{N}\langle c_k,x_N^\star\rangle\right)^{1/(N+1)}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The optimal constant-share portfolio is a single feasible portfolio maximizing cumulative multiplicative return over the observed horizon; its optimal average growth is the geometric mean of those returns.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_N^\star\in\arg\max_{x\in P}\prod_{k=0}^{N}\langle c_k,x\rangle,\qquad \psi_N^\star=\left(\prod_{k=0}^{N}\langle c_k,x_N^\star\rangle\right)^{1/(N+1)}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Component and fractional contributions for covariance volatility and variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\sigma(x)=\sqrt{x^{\mathsf T}\Sigma x}>0\), Euler's identity gives \[\sigma(x)=\sum_i x_i\frac{(\Sigma x)_i}{\sigma(x)}.\] Thus the component volatility contribution is \(RC_i^\sigma=x_i(\Sigma x)_i/\sigma(x)\), its fraction of total volatility is \(x_i(\Sigma x)_i/(x^{\mathsf T}\Sigma x)\), and the component variance contribution \(RC_i^v=x_i(\Sigma x)_i\) sums to total variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Covariance risk decomposes into Euler component contributions whose normalized values are the fractions prescribed by risk budgets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed contributions sum exactly to total volatility or variance, respectively.

notation.meaning: component contribution of asset \(i\) to portfolio volatility
component contribution of asset \(i\) to portfolio variance

knowledge_statements.title: Euler Risk Contributions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of interiority, coercivity, or strict convexity in the standard convex construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The seeded logarithmic formulation uses \(b_i>0\) and \(\Sigma\succ0\). If \(b_i=0\), the logarithmic term does not force coordinate \(i\) to remain positive, so its budget equation is replaced by a boundary KKT condition. If \(\Sigma\succeq0\) is singular and some \(d>0\) lies in \(\ker\Sigma\), then along \(y+td\) the quadratic term remains bounded while \(-\sum_i b_i\log(y_i+td_i)\to-\infty\); hence no minimizer exists. Positive definiteness excludes this recession failure and yields strict convexity and coercivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero budgets require boundary conditions, and a singular covariance can make the logarithmic risk-budget construction unbounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Positive budgets and positive-definite covariance ensure the seeded interior construction, while the displayed positive-null-vector case has no minimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary of the Logarithmic Construction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneity of fractional covariance risk contributions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(a>0\), \[\frac{(ax_i)(\Sigma(ax))_i}{(ax)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma(ax)}=\frac{x_i(\Sigma x)_i}{x^{\mathsf T}\Sigma x}.\] Hence fractional risk-budget equations determine a positive ray. Any positive homogeneous normalization that intersects this ray, such as \(\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}x=1\) for a positive portfolio, selects exactly one point on it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fractional risk contributions are scale invariant, so a risk-budget solution is a ray until a portfolio normalization is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fractional covariance risk contributions are homogeneous of degree zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Scale Invariance and Normalization
Risk-Budget Portfolio Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Long-only covariance risk budgeting through a convex logarithmic formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^n\), let \(b\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\) satisfy \(\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}b=1\), and choose \(\kappa>0\). The strictly convex problem
\[
\min_{y\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n}\ \frac12 y^{\mathsf T}\Sigma y-\kappa\sum_{i=1}^n b_i\log y_i
\]
has a unique minimizer \(y^\star\) satisfying \(y_i^\star(\Sigma y^\star)_i=\kappa b_i\). After normalization \(x=y^\star/(\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}y^\star)\), the fractional volatility contributions obey
\[
\frac{x_i(\Sigma x)_i}{x^{\mathsf T}\Sigma x}=b_i,
\]
so \(x\) realizes the prescribed risk budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex log-barrier problem constructs a positive portfolio whose component contributions to variance equal prescribed budget fractions after normalization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The normalized optimizer satisfies \(x_i(\Sigma x)_i/(x^{\mathsf T}\Sigma x)=b_i\) for every \(i\).

notation.meaning: target fractional risk budget of asset i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The logarithmic risk-budget representation and normalization calculation fit the container, but no supporting source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical single-period Markowitz models with known return mean and covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widehat r=\mathbb E[r]\), \(\Sigma=\mathbb E[(r-\widehat r)(r-\widehat r)^\top]\succeq0\), and \(\varrho(x)=r^\top x\). Then \(\mathbb E[\varrho(x)]=\widehat r^\top x\) and \(\operatorname{var}(\varrho(x))=x^\top\Sigma x\). For a feasible portfolio set \(\mathcal X\), Markowitz optimization may be written either as \(\max_{x\in\mathcal X}\{\widehat r^\top x:x^\top\Sigma x\leq\bar\sigma^2\}\) or as \(\min_{x\in\mathcal X}\{x^\top\Sigma x:\widehat r^\top x\geq\mu\}\). Both are convex quadratic programs. Varying \(\bar\sigma\) or \(\mu\) traces the efficient frontier; a feasible portfolio whose risk-return pair lies on that frontier is efficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With known expected returns and a positive-semidefinite covariance matrix, portfolio expected return is linear and variance is quadratic. One may maximize return subject to a variance limit or minimize variance subject to a required return. Both models are convex quadratic programs, and their optimal risk-return pairs form the efficient frontier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_{x\in\mathcal X,\,x^\top\Sigma x\leq\bar\sigma^2}\widehat r^\top x\quad\text{and}\quad\min_{x\in\mathcal X,\,\widehat r^\top x\geq\mu}x^\top\Sigma x\text{ are convex quadratic programs defining the efficient frontier.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: KKT Certificate for a Return Target
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary-and-sufficient optimality system with a general convex holdings set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a relative-interior constraint qualification holds. A feasible \(x^\star\) is optimal for the return-target problem if and only if there exist \(\eta^\star\ge0\), \(\tau^\star\in\mathbb R\), and \(s^\star\in N_C(x^\star)\) such that \[\Sigma x^\star-\eta^\star\mu+\tau^\star\mathbf1+s^\star=0,\qquad \eta^\star(\mu^{\mathsf T}x^\star-r)=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasibility, normal-cone stationarity, and return complementary slackness exactly certify a minimum-variance target portfolio.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed KKT system is necessary and sufficient for optimality.

notation.meaning: normal cone of the holdings set at \(x^\star\)

knowledge_statements.title: KKT Certificate for a Return Target

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment and uniqueness for return-target minimum variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_r=C\cap\{x:\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}x=1,\ \mu^{\mathsf T}x\ge r\}\). If \(F_r\) is nonempty and either compact or the quadratic objective is level-bounded on \(F_r\), then a minimizer exists. It is unique if \((x-y)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma(x-y)>0\) for every distinct \(x,y\in F_r\). A nonzero feasible difference in \(\ker\Sigma\) can cause nonuniqueness, and closedness alone does not guarantee attainment without level-boundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Existence requires compactness or level-bounded risk, while uniqueness requires positive covariance curvature between distinct feasible portfolios.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated compactness or level-boundedness condition ensures existence, and positive curvature on feasible differences ensures uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.title: Existence and Uniqueness Boundary
Return-Target Portfolio Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex Markowitz minimum-variance model with a required expected return.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given expected returns \(\mu\in\mathbb{R}^n\), covariance matrix \(\Sigma\in\mathbb{S}_+^n\), target return \(r\in\mathbb{R}\), and a nonempty closed convex constraint set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), the return-target portfolio model is
\[
\min_{x\in C}\ \frac12 x^{\mathsf T}\Sigma x
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}x=1,
\qquad \mu^{\mathsf T}x\ge r.
\]
It is a convex quadratic program. Writing \(M=\sup\{\mu^{\mathsf T}x:x\in C,\ \mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}x=1\}\), the model is feasible when \(r<M\), infeasible when \(r>M\), and feasible at \(r=M\) exactly when the supremum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The model minimizes portfolio variance over convex holdings constraints, full investment, and an expected-return floor. A target below the supremum attainable return is feasible; equality additionally requires attainment of that supremum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed return-target model is a convex quadratic program, and its feasibility has the stated attainment-qualified characterization.

notation.meaning: supremum expected return under the holdings and full-investment constraints

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Connection between return-constrained frontier points and risk-return scalarization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a return-target optimum \(x^\star\) satisfies a constraint qualification and its return constraint is active with multiplier \(\eta^\star\ge0\), then \(x^\star\) also minimizes \[\frac12x^{\mathsf T}\Sigma x-\eta^\star\mu^{\mathsf T}x\] over the same holdings and full-investment constraints. Conversely, every optimizer of this scalarization is weakly mean-variance efficient; strict improvement in one criterion without worsening the other is impossible when \(\eta^\star>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A return-constraint multiplier is the supporting risk-return tradeoff selecting the same frontier portfolio.
assumptions_latex: A constraint qualification holds at the return-target optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An active constrained optimum is supported by the scalarization determined by its return multiplier.

notation.meaning: return multiplier and supporting tradeoff coefficient

knowledge_statements.title: Supporting Scalarization of Frontier Points

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundaries of efficient interpretation and of the classical frontier formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the inequality-defined value function, targets below the expected return of a global minimum-variance portfolio can share the same optimizer and value; those target labels do not describe distinct efficient criterion points unless the return constraint is active. In the unconstrained formula with \(\Sigma\succ0\), \(D=AC-B^2\ge0\), with \(D=0\) exactly when \(\mu\) is proportional to \(\mathbf1\). Then every fully invested portfolio has the same expected return and the nondegenerate frontier parabola collapses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Flat inactive-target segments are not distinct efficient outcomes, and identical asset means collapse the classical two-dimensional frontier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Active return constraints delimit the efficient branch, while \(D=0\) exactly characterizes collapse of the classical frontier.
knowledge_statements.title: Inactive-Target and Degenerate-Frontier Boundaries

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Efficient-frontier equation with full investment and no holdings restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Sigma\succ0\), define \(A=\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf1\), \(B=\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}\mu\), \(C=\mu^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}\mu\), and \(D=AC-B^2\). If \(D>0\), the minimum variance subject to \(\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}x=1\) and \(\mu^{\mathsf T}x=r\) is \[v(r)=\frac{Ar^2-2Br+C}{D}=\frac1A+\frac A D\left(r-\frac BA\right)^2,\] attained uniquely at \[x(r)=\Sigma^{-1}\left(\frac{C-Br}{D}\mathbf1+\frac{Ar-B}{D}\mu\right).\] The branch \(r\ge B/A\) is mean-variance efficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without holdings restrictions, the return-variance frontier is an explicit parabola whose upper branch begins at the global minimum-variance portfolio.
assumptions_latex: Only full-investment and expected-return equalities constrain the portfolio.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimum variance and unique optimizer are given by the displayed formulas.

notation.meaning: standard frontier scalars formed from \(\Sigma^{-1}\), \(\mathbf1\), and \(\mu\)

knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Form Unconstrained Markowitz Frontier
Efficient-Frontier Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex value-function geometry of the constrained mean–variance frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex, let \(\Sigma\succeq0\), and define
\[
v(r)=\inf\{x^{\mathsf T}\Sigma x:x\in C,\ \mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}x=1,\ \mu^{\mathsf T}x\ge r\}.
\]
On its effective domain, \(v\) is convex and nondecreasing in \(r\). Hence its epigraph \(\{(r,s):s\ge v(r)\}\) is convex, and the lower boundary gives the minimum-variance efficient frontier in return–variance coordinates. If \(\Sigma\) is positive definite on feasible directions, each attained frontier point has a unique portfolio optimizer, although different targets may share an optimizer over flat segments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum attainable variance is a convex, nondecreasing function of the return target; its graph forms the efficient boundary in return–variance coordinates.
assumptions_latex: The value is considered on targets for which the constraints are feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The frontier value function \(v(r)\) is convex and nondecreasing on its effective domain.

notation.meaning: minimum variance attainable at return floor r
epigraph of the frontier value function

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The value-function geometry is consistent with the container, but the convexity and uniqueness assertions have no supporting citation.

children.title: Tracking-Error Portfolio Models
children.top_down_role: Benchmark-relative portfolio risk objectives and constraints.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}(x-b)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma(x-b)\iff0\in2\Sigma(x^\star-b)+N_C(x^\star).

notation.meaning: normal cone of the feasible portfolio set at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality and uniqueness conditions for covariance tracking-error minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min_{x\in C}(x-b)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma(x-b)\), a feasible \(x^\star\) is optimal if and only if \(0\in2\Sigma(x^\star-b)+N_C(x^\star)\). If \(\Sigma\) is positive definite on \(\operatorname{span}(C-C)\), the minimizer is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible portfolio is tracking-error optimal exactly when its covariance-weighted active position is balanced by a feasible-set normal. Definiteness on feasible directions gives uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.title: Tracking-Error Optimality Certificate

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x-b)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma(x-b)=0\iff x-b\in\ker\Sigma.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of portfolio identification by tracking error under singular covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\Sigma\succeq0\) is singular, then \((x-b)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma(x-b)=0\) if and only if \(x-b\in\ker\Sigma\). Hence zero tracking error need not imply \(x=b\). For \(\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\), every active position \((0,t)\) has zero tracking error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular covariance matrix cannot distinguish active positions in its nullspace, so zero tracking error need not identify the benchmark.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular-Covariance Identification Boundary

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x-b)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma(x-b)\le\gamma^2\iff\lVert L(x-b)\rVert_2\le\gamma.

notation.meaning: square-root factor of the covariance matrix

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact conic representation of a covariance tracking-error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Sigma=L^{\mathsf T}L\succeq0\). For \(\gamma\ge0\), \((x-b)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma(x-b)\le\gamma^2\) if and only if \(\lVert L(x-b)\rVert_2\le\gamma\). Thus a tracking-error standard-deviation objective or budget is second-order-cone representable when the remaining restrictions are conic representable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Factoring the covariance matrix converts a tracking-error budget exactly into a second-order-cone constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order-Cone Tracking-Error Form
Tracking-Error Portfolio Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex portfolio selection relative to a fixed benchmark under covariance tracking error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(b\in\mathbb{R}^n\) be benchmark weights, let \(\Sigma\in\mathbb{S}_+^n\) be the return covariance matrix, and let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a convex portfolio set. A quadratic tracking-error model is
\[
\min_{x\in C}\ (x-b)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma(x-b)
\quad\text{subject to}\quad \mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}x=1,
\]
possibly augmented by convex return, turnover, or exposure constraints. Its objective is the variance of active return \((x-b)^{\mathsf T}R\) when the random return vector \(R\) has covariance \(\Sigma\). Thus the formulation is a convex quadratic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tracking-error optimization minimizes the variance of return relative to a benchmark while enforcing full investment and convex portfolio restrictions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The tracking-error objective equals \(\operatorname{Var}((x-b)^{\mathsf T}R)\) and is convex in \(x\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tracking-error formulation is mathematically coherent and correctly identified as a definition, but it lacks an inspectable source.

children.title: Factor-Risk Portfolio Models
children.top_down_role: Portfolio risk expressed through factor exposures and residual components.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Factor-Exposure Lift and Conic Volatility Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lifted formulation of factor-model variance and volatility constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Sigma=BF B^{\mathsf T}+D\), choose factors \(F=L_FL_F^{\mathsf T}\) and \(D=L_DL_D^{\mathsf T}\), and introduce \(y=B^{\mathsf T}x\). Then \[x^{\mathsf T}\Sigma x=\|L_F^{\mathsf T}y\|_2^2+\|L_D^{\mathsf T}x\|_2^2=\left\|\begin{bmatrix}L_F^{\mathsf T}y\\L_D^{\mathsf T}x\end{bmatrix}\right\|_2^2.\] Consequently, for \(\sigma\ge0\), \[x^{\mathsf T}\Sigma x\le\sigma^2\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists y:\ y=B^{\mathsf T}x,\ \left\|\begin{bmatrix}L_F^{\mathsf T}y\\L_D^{\mathsf T}x\end{bmatrix}\right\|_2\le\sigma.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Introducing factor exposures gives an exact lift of factor-model variance and an exact second-order-cone formulation of a volatility limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^{\mathsf T}\Sigma x\le\sigma^2\iff\exists y:\ y=B^{\mathsf T}x,\ \|[L_F^{\mathsf T}y;L_D^{\mathsf T}x]\|_2\le\sigma.

notation.meaning: Factors of the positive-semidefinite covariance components.

knowledge_statements.title: Factor-Exposure Lift and Conic Volatility Form
Factor-Risk Portfolio Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Low-rank-plus-specific covariance representation for convex portfolio risk.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose asset returns satisfy \(R=Bf+\varepsilon\), where \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}\), \(\operatorname{Cov}(f)=F\succeq0\), \(\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon)=D\succeq0\), and \(\operatorname{Cov}(f,\varepsilon)=0\). Then
\[
\Sigma=BF B^{\mathsf T}+D,
\qquad
x^{\mathsf T}\Sigma x=(B^{\mathsf T}x)^{\mathsf T}F(B^{\mathsf T}x)+x^{\mathsf T}Dx.
\]
Consequently, minimizing portfolio variance over any convex feasible set is a convex optimization problem expressed as the sum of factor risk and specific risk. When \(D\) is diagonal, the specific-risk term is separable across assets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A factor covariance model decomposes portfolio variance into systematic factor-exposure risk and asset-specific risk while preserving convexity.
assumptions_latex: Factors and specific returns are uncorrelated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{\mathsf T}\Sigma x=(B^{\mathsf T}x)^{\mathsf T}F(B^{\mathsf T}x)+x^{\mathsf T}Dx\) with \(\Sigma\succeq0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The factor-risk decomposition is correct under the stated covariance assumptions and fits a representation, but no citation is supplied.

children.title: Benchmark–Factor Interaction Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cases where benchmark exposure and factor structure jointly shape portfolio risk.

knowledge_statements.title: Benchmark–Factor Interaction Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Factor decomposition of benchmark-relative risk and active-exposure regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(a=x-b\) be active weights and let \(\Sigma=BF B^{\mathsf T}+D\) be a factor covariance model. Benchmark-relative variance decomposes as
\[
a^{\mathsf T}\Sigma a=(B^{\mathsf T}a)^{\mathsf T}F(B^{\mathsf T}a)+a^{\mathsf T}Da.
\]
If \(B^{\mathsf T}a=0\), tracking error contains only specific active risk. If instead \(Da=0\), it contains only active factor risk. In the general interaction regime both terms are nonnegative and additive; therefore constraints of the form \(\ell\le B^{\mathsf T}(x-b)\le u\) directly limit benchmark-relative factor deviations while leaving the model convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tracking error splits into active factor risk and active specific risk; factor-neutral and specific-neutral portfolios are limiting regimes of this decomposition.
assumptions_latex: The benchmark \(b\) is represented in the same asset universe as \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x-b)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma(x-b)=(B^{\mathsf T}(x-b))^{\mathsf T}F(B^{\mathsf T}(x-b))+(x-b)^{\mathsf T}D(x-b)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The active-risk decomposition and limiting regimes are coherent, but the record has no source locator supporting the claims.

children.title: Downside-Risk Portfolio Models
children.top_down_role: Portfolio templates focused on losses below a target or reference level.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u\mapsto(u)_+^q\text{ is not convex, so lower-partial-moment portfolio objectives of order }q<1\text{ are not convex in general}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp curvature boundary for the target-shortfall power model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<q<1\), let \(f(u)=(u)_+^q\). Then \(f(0)=0\), \(f(1)=1\), and \(f(1/2)=2^{-q}>1/2\). Thus \(f\) is not convex, and lower-partial-moment portfolio objectives of order below one are not generally convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard lower-partial-moment criterion loses convexity below order one.
knowledge_statements.title: Subunit Lower-Partial-Moment Nonconvexity

assumptions_latex: Scenario portfolio returns are affine in \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho_q(x)=\sum_s p_s(\tau-r_s^{\mathsf T}x)_+^q\text{ is convex for }q\ge1.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex fixed-target lower-partial-moment portfolio models of order at least one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For scenario returns \(r_s\), probabilities \(p_s\ge0\), target \(\tau\), and order \(q\ge1\), define \(\rho_q(x)=\sum_s p_s(\tau-r_s^{\mathsf T}x)_+^q\). This function is convex in \(x\). For \(q=1\), it has the linear representation \(\min_z\{\sum_s p_sz_s:z_s\ge\tau-r_s^{\mathsf T}x,\ z_s\ge0\}\); for \(q=2\), it is the convex quadratic shortfall model in the immutable seed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower partial moments of order at least one are convex fixed-target criteria; first-order shortfall has an LP form and second-order shortfall has a QP form.
knowledge_statements.title: General Lower-Partial-Moment Portfolio Model
Downside-Risk Portfolio Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex lower-partial-moment model for returns falling below a target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given scenario returns \(r_s\in\mathbb{R}^n\), probabilities \(p_s>0\) with \(\sum_s p_s=1\), and a target return \(\tau\in\mathbb{R}\), define the second-order downside risk of portfolio \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) by
\[
\rho_2(x)=\sum_s p_s\bigl(\tau-r_s^{\mathsf T}x\bigr)_+^2.
\]
For each fixed \(x\), it has the quadratic representation
\[
\rho_2(x)=\min_z\left\{\sum_s p_sz_s^2: z_s\ge\tau-r_s^{\mathsf T}x,\ z_s\ge0\ \text{for every }s\right\}.
\]
Consequently, minimizing \(\rho_2(x)\) together with convex portfolio constraints is a convex quadratic program. At every optimum of the slack formulation, \(z_s=(\tau-r_s^{\mathsf T}x)_+\) for every scenario.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Squared downside risk penalizes only scenario returns below a target and has a convex quadratic slack-variable representation. Positive scenario probabilities ensure every optimal slack equals its scenario shortfall.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every fixed \(x\), the slack formulation has value \(\rho_2(x)=\sum_s p_s(\tau-r_s^{\mathsf T}x)_+^2\), and every optimal slack satisfies \(z_s=(\tau-r_s^{\mathsf T}x)_+\).

notation.meaning: positive part, equal to the maximum of t and zero

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gaussian Portfolio VaR and Its SOC Constraint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-return value-at-risk model and conic portfolio formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(r\sim\mathcal N(\widehat r,\Sigma)\), \(\varrho(x)=r^\top x\), and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). Define \(\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(x)=-F_{\varrho(x)}^{-1}(\alpha)\). Thus \(\mathbb P(-\varrho(x)>\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(x))\leq\alpha\). For \(\alpha\in(0,1/2)\), \(\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(x)\leq\gamma\) if and only if \(\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha)\|\Sigma^{1/2}x\|_2\leq\widehat r^\top x+\gamma\). Consequently, maximizing \(\widehat r^\top x\) over \(x\in\mathcal X\) subject to this inequality is an SOCP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For normally distributed returns, portfolio VaR is the negative lower return quantile. At levels below one half, an upper VaR bound is exactly a second-order cone constraint involving expected return and portfolio standard deviation, so expected-return maximization under that bound is an SOCP.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(x)\leq\gamma\iff\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha)\|\Sigma^{1/2}x\|_2\leq\widehat r^\top x+\gamma.

children.title: Conditional-Value-at-Risk Portfolios
children.top_down_role: Portfolio templates organized around conditional tail-loss exposure.

knowledge_statements.title: Conditional-Value-at-Risk Portfolios
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rockafellar–Uryasev convex representation for portfolio loss CVaR.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L(x,\xi)\) be a loss convex in portfolio weights \(x\) for every outcome \(\xi\), and let \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). Conditional value at risk has the representation
\[
\operatorname{CVaR}_\alpha(L(x,\xi))=\n\inf_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\left[t+\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\mathbb{E}(L(x,\xi)-t)_+\right].
\]
For scenario losses \(L_s(x)\) with probabilities \(p_s\), introduce \(z_s\ge0\) and impose \(z_s\ge L_s(x)-t\). Minimizing \(t+(1-\alpha)^{-1}\sum_s p_sz_s\), together with convex portfolio constraints, is a convex program and is linear when every \(L_s\) and all portfolio constraints are affine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Portfolio CVaR equals a convex threshold-plus-tail-excess minimization and becomes a linear program for affine scenario losses and constraints.
assumptions_latex: Each scenario loss \(L_s(x)\) is convex in \(x\).
Scenario probabilities are nonnegative and sum to one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{CVaR}_\alpha(L)=\inf_t\{t+(1-\alpha)^{-1}\mathbb{E}(L-t)_+\}\), with the stated finite-scenario convex formulation.

notation.meaning: scenario excess loss above the threshold

source_refs.locator: 5.3 From Bernstein approximation to Conditional Value at Risk and back p. 121

source_witnesses.locator: 5.3 From Bernstein approximation to Conditional Value at Risk and back p. 121

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: t^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_t\left\{t+(1-\alpha)^{-1}\mathbb E(L-t)_+\right\}\iff\mathbb P(L<t^\star)\le\alpha\le\mathbb P(L\le t^\star).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantile characterization of minimizers in the CVaR threshold representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) be integrable and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). A threshold \(t^\star\) minimizes \(t+(1-\alpha)^{-1}\mathbb E(L-t)_+\) if and only if \(\mathbb P(L<t^\star)\le\alpha\le\mathbb P(L\le t^\star)\). The optimal-threshold set can contain more than one point when these inequalities hold throughout a nontrivial interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The auxiliary CVaR threshold is an alpha-quantile; all optimal thresholds are characterized by two probability inequalities.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimal CVaR Threshold Characterization

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{CVaR}_\alpha(\ell)=\max\left\{\sum_s q_s\ell_s:0\le q_s\le p_s/(1-\alpha),\ \sum_s q_s=1\right\}.

notation.meaning: adversarial probability assigned to scenario s

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual representation of portfolio CVaR for a finite scenario distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For losses \(\ell_s\), probabilities \(p_s\ge0\) summing to one, and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), \(\operatorname{CVaR}_\alpha(\ell)=\max_q\{\sum_s q_s\ell_s:0\le q_s\le p_s/(1-\alpha),\ \sum_s q_s=1\}\). For affine scenario losses, portfolio CVaR is therefore the worst expected loss over this capped probability envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-scenario CVaR is the worst expected loss over probability vectors whose scenario masses satisfy tail-dependent caps.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Scenario CVaR Risk Envelope

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{CVaR}_\alpha\text{ is monotone, translation equivariant, positively homogeneous, and subadditive on integrable losses}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Core coherent-risk properties used by CVaR portfolio models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integrable losses \(L,M\), constants \(c\), and \(\lambda\ge0\), CVaR satisfies \(L\le M\Rightarrow\operatorname{CVaR}_\alpha(L)\le\operatorname{CVaR}_\alpha(M)\), \(\operatorname{CVaR}_\alpha(L+c)=\operatorname{CVaR}_\alpha(L)+c\), \(\operatorname{CVaR}_\alpha(\lambda L)=\lambda\operatorname{CVaR}_\alpha(L)\), and \(\operatorname{CVaR}_\alpha(L+M)\le\operatorname{CVaR}_\alpha(L)+\operatorname{CVaR}_\alpha(M)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: CVaR is a coherent loss-risk measure: it is monotone, cash additive, positively homogeneous, and subadditive.
knowledge_statements.title: Coherence of Portfolio CVaR

children.title: Tail-Risk Comparison Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural distinctions among downside-sensitive and tail-sensitive portfolio choices.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E[(L_B)_+]<\mathbb E[(L_A)_+]\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{CVaR}_{0.9}(L_A)<\operatorname{CVaR}_{0.9}(L_B).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of a distribution-free ordering between fixed-target downside risk and CVaR.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L_A\equiv1\), and let \(L_B\) equal \(0\) with probability \(0.9\) and \(5\) with probability \(0.1\). Then \(\mathbb E[(L_A)_+]=1\), \(\mathbb E[(L_B)_+]=1/2\), \(\operatorname{CVaR}_{0.9}(L_A)=1\), and \(\operatorname{CVaR}_{0.9}(L_B)=5\). Hence first-order target shortfall prefers \(B\), while CVaR prefers \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-target downside risk and CVaR can rank the same two loss distributions oppositely.
knowledge_statements.title: Target-Shortfall and CVaR Incomparability

assumptions_latex: VaR uses the lower-quantile convention \(\inf\{t:\mathbb P(L\le t)\ge\alpha\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{VaR}_{1/2}(L(x))=\min\{x_1,x_2\}\text{ is not convex in }x.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-scenario failure of convexity for portfolio value-at-risk.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let two equally likely scenarios have affine losses \(L_1(x)=x_1\) and \(L_2(x)=x_2\). Then \(\operatorname{VaR}_{1/2}(L(x))=\min\{x_1,x_2\}\). Its values at \((0,1)\) and \((1,0)\) are zero, while its value at \((1/2,1/2)\) is \(1/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-scenario affine-loss instance shows that portfolio VaR need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvexity of Portfolio VaR
Tail-Risk Comparison Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of value-at-risk, conditional value-at-risk, and chance constraints for portfolio loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L(x,\xi)\) be an integrable portfolio loss and let \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). Define \(\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(L)=\inf\{t:\mathbb P(L\le t)\ge\alpha\}\) and \(\operatorname{CVaR}_{\alpha}(L)=\inf_{t\in\mathbb R}\{t+(1-\alpha)^{-1}\mathbb E[(L-t)_+]\}\). Then \(\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(L)\le\operatorname{CVaR}_{\alpha}(L)\). Consequently, \(\operatorname{CVaR}_{\alpha}(L(x,\xi))\le b\) implies \(\mathbb P(L(x,\xi)\le b)\ge\alpha\), whereas the converse need not hold. If \(L(\cdot,\xi)\) is convex almost surely, its conditional-value-at-risk is convex in \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conditional value-at-risk dominates value-at-risk, so a CVaR bound safely enforces the corresponding chance constraint. CVaR also preserves convexity of scenario-wise convex losses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}(L)\le\operatorname{CVaR}_{\alpha}(L)\), and a CVaR bound implies the corresponding chance constraint.

knowledge_statements.title: Robust Portfolio Counterpart Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional robust counterpart for uncertain convex portfolio constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) denote portfolio weights and let the uncertainty satisfy \(u\in U\). An uncertain constraint \(f(x,u)\le0\) for every \(u\in U\) is equivalently represented by \(\sup_{u\in U}f(x,u)\le0\). Thus the robust portfolio problem has the interface \(\min_{x\in X}\sup_{u\in U}F(x,u)\) subject to \(\sup_{u\in U}f_i(x,u)\le0\) for each \(i\). If every \(f_i(\cdot,u)\) and \(F(\cdot,u)\) is convex, the robust objective and feasible set are convex; tractability depends on representations of the suprema.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace every uncertain inequality by its worst-case supremum over the uncertainty set. Pointwise suprema preserve convexity, while the uncertainty-set geometry determines tractability.
assumptions_latex: For each \(u\in U\), the functions \(F(\cdot,u)\) and \(f_i(\cdot,u)\) are convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The robust constraints are \(\sup_{u\in U}f_i(x,u)\le0\), and they define a convex feasible set.
