children.title: Convex Transaction-Cost Models
children.top_down_role: Convex costs associated with changes in portfolio positions.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Transaction-Cost Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex penalties on trades relative to a pre-trade portfolio.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given pre-trade holdings \(x^0\in\mathbb R^n\) and post-trade holdings \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), let \(z=x-x^0\). A convex transaction-cost model is a proper convex function \(C:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) with \(C(0)=0\) and usually \(C(z)\ge0\). Standard instances are proportional cost \(C(z)=\sum_{i=1}^n c_i|z_i|\), quadratic impact \(C(z)=\sum_{i=1}^n q_i z_i^2\), and their sum, where \(c_i,q_i\ge0\). Adding \(C(x-x^0)\) to a convex minimization objective preserves convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transaction costs are modeled by a proper convex penalty on trades, including proportional bid-ask costs and quadratic market impact. Coupling this penalty to a convex portfolio objective preserves convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C(x-x^0)\) is convex in \(x\), so its addition preserves a convex minimization model.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and convexity claim are mathematically plausible and fit the leaf, but no inspectable source supports the portfolio-specific transaction-cost examples and terminology.

children.title: Convex Holding-Cost Models
children.top_down_role: Convex costs associated with maintaining portfolio positions.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Holding-Cost Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex penalties assessed on post-trade portfolio holdings or exposures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For portfolio holdings \(x\in X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), a convex holding-cost model is a proper convex function \(H:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\). Examples include separable borrow or custody costs \(H(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n h_i(x_i)\), where each \(h_i\) is convex, and exposure penalties \(H(x)=\phi(Ax-b)\), where \(A\) is linear and \(\phi\) is convex. The extended value \(+\infty\) may encode forbidden holdings. Adding \(H(x)\) to a convex portfolio minimization objective preserves convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A holding-cost model is a convex penalty on positions or linear exposures. It can encode custody, borrowing, concentration, or forbidden holdings while retaining convexity.
assumptions_latex: Each \(h_i\), or alternatively \(\phi\), is proper and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\) is convex on \(X\), and adding it to a convex minimization objective preserves convexity.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally consistent and fits the holding-cost leaf, but the portfolio-specific examples and modeling interpretation lack an inspectable citation.

children.title: Joint Trading-Friction Regimes
children.top_down_role: Portfolio regimes where trading and holding frictions interact.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic loss of convexity from multiplicative interaction between holding and trade decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\alpha\ne0\), \(J(x,z)=\alpha xz\) is neither convex nor concave on any open rectangle in the joint decision space. Separate convexity of component costs therefore does not validate a multiplicative interaction; the complete coupling must be jointly convex or validly reformulated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplying a holding decision by a trade decision generally destroys joint convexity.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) and \(z\) are independent scalar decision coordinates before affine coupling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: J(x,z)=\alpha xz\text{ is neither convex nor concave on any open rectangle}.
knowledge_statements.title: Bilinear Friction-Coupling Boundary
Joint Trading-Friction Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint convex coupling of transaction and holding frictions in one-period rebalancing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^0\) be the current portfolio, \(x\) the post-trade portfolio, and \(z=x-x^0\). A joint convex friction regime is represented by \(\min_{x\in X}\{F(x)+C(z)+H(x)\}\), possibly subject to affine self-financing constraints. Here \(F\) is the base convex loss, \(C\) is a convex transaction cost, and \(H\) is a convex holding cost. More generally, a jointly convex function \(J(x,z)\) may replace \(C(z)+H(x)\). With convex \(X\) and affine coupling \(z=x-x^0\), the resulting optimization problem is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Trading and holding frictions can be combined additively or through a jointly convex penalty. Affine trade-position coupling keeps the complete rebalancing problem convex.
assumptions_latex: The trade-position and self-financing constraints are affine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The joint objective \(F(x)+C(x-x^0)+H(x)\) and its feasible optimization problem are convex.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation and convexity conditions fit the joint-friction container, but no source supports this portfolio modeling interface.

children.title: Turnover Constraints
children.top_down_role: Limits on aggregate portfolio reallocation.

knowledge_statements.title: Turnover Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex limits on total trading relative to a reference portfolio.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For current weights \(x^0\in\mathbb R^n\), candidate weights \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), and turnover budget \(\tau\ge0\), the standard turnover constraint is \(\sum_{i=1}^n|x_i-x_i^0|\le\tau\), equivalently \(\lVert x-x^0\rVert_1\le\tau\). Weighted turnover uses \(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i|x_i-x_i^0|\le\tau\) with \(w_i\ge0\). Either predicate defines a closed convex feasible set. An epigraph formulation introduces \(u_i\ge0\) satisfying \(-u_i\le x_i-x_i^0\le u_i\) and \(\sum_i w_i u_i\le\tau\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Turnover bounds the weighted absolute change from current holdings. The constraint is convex and has a linear auxiliary-variable formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:\sum_i w_i|x_i-x_i^0|\le\tau\}\) is closed and convex and admits the stated linear formulation.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative turnover weight for asset i.

children.title: Leverage Constraints
children.top_down_role: Limits on gross portfolio exposure or financed positions.

knowledge_statements.title: Leverage Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gross-exposure bounds for portfolios allowing long and short positions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For portfolio weights \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) and gross-leverage limit \(L\ge0\), the standard leverage constraint is \(\lVert x\rVert_1=\sum_{i=1}^n|x_i|\le L\). It defines a closed convex set and is representable linearly by variables \(u_i\ge0\) satisfying \(-u_i\le x_i\le u_i\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^n u_i\le L\). Under the normalization \(\mathbf 1^T x=1\), feasibility requires \(L\ge1\), and the total short exposure equals \((\lVert x\rVert_1-1)/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gross leverage is the sum of absolute portfolio weights. Its bound is convex, has a linear formulation, and directly controls total short exposure under full investment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert x\rVert_1\le L\) is convex and linearly representable; with full investment, short exposure is at most \((L-1)/2\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The gross-leverage formulation and short-exposure identity are consistent and fit a condition container, but no inspectable portfolio source is supplied.

children.title: Shorting Constraints
children.top_down_role: Restrictions governing negative asset positions.

knowledge_statements.title: Shorting Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex restrictions on negative portfolio positions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For portfolio weights \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), the no-shorting condition is \(x_i\ge0\) for every \(i\). Assetwise short limits take the form \(x_i\ge-\ell_i\), where \(\ell_i\ge0\). An aggregate short-exposure limit is \(\sum_{i=1}^n(-x_i)_+\le s\), where \(s\ge0\); it is convex because each positive-part function is convex. Equivalently, introduce \(v_i\ge0\) with \(v_i\ge-x_i\) and impose \(\sum_i v_i\le s\). All three regimes define closed convex feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shorting may be prohibited, bounded asset by asset, or limited in aggregate. Each regime is convex, and aggregate short exposure has a linear auxiliary-variable formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The no-short, assetwise-short, and aggregate-short predicates each define a closed convex feasible set.

notation.meaning: Maximum permitted short position in asset i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The three shorting regimes and their convex formulations are consistent, but the record has no supporting source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Self-Financing Rebalancing and the No-Shorting Constraint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-period portfolio-feasibility conventions, with primary emphasis on restrictions against negative positions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x(0),u\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(x=x(0)+u\). The update is self-financing precisely when \(\mathbf1^\top x=\mathbf1^\top x(0)\), equivalently \(\mathbf1^\top u=0\). Short-selling means allowing some component of \(x\) to be negative; prohibiting short-selling imposes \(x\geq0\), equivalently \(x(0)+u\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transaction vector updates the initial portfolio by addition. Self-financing means that its entries sum to zero. Short-selling allows negative updated positions, whereas a no-short-selling rule requires every updated position to be nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbf1^\top x=\mathbf1^\top x(0)\iff\mathbf1^\top u=0,\qquad\text{and no short-selling requires }x=x(0)+u\geq0.

children.title: Multi-Period Portfolio Planning
children.top_down_role: Portfolio decisions coordinated across a fixed sequence of periods.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-scenario stochastic portfolio planning with nonanticipative trades indexed by information nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal N_t\) be the information nodes at date \(t\) of a finite scenario tree, let \(p_n\ge0\) be the unconditional probability of node \(n\), and let \(\pi(n)\) be its predecessor. Assign a state \(x_n\) to every node and a trade \(z_n\) to every nonterminal node. Impose affine transitions \[x_m=A_mx_{\pi(m)}+B_mz_{\pi(m)}+d_m\] for every nonroot node \(m\), together with convex node constraints. If all stage costs \(F_n(x_n)+C_n(z_n)\) and terminal costs \(F_n^T(x_n)\) are convex, their probability-weighted sum defines a convex deterministic equivalent. Indexing each trade by its information node is equivalent to requiring scenario-indexed trades to agree whenever their scenarios share the same observed history.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite stochastic multi-period portfolio plan is a convex scenario-tree program under affine transitions and convex node models; information-node indexing enforces nonanticipativity.
assumptions_latex: Transitions are affine and node feasible sets are convex.
Stage and terminal costs are proper convex functions on their node domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The deterministic equivalent is convex, and its trade decisions are nonanticipative.
knowledge_statements.title: Scenario-Tree Multi-Period Portfolio Formulation
Multi-Period Portfolio Planning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic convex finite-horizon portfolio planning with affine dynamics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For dates \(t=0,\ldots,T-1\), let holdings obey \(x_{t+1}=A_t x_t+B_t z_t+d_t\), with prescribed \(x_0\), convex state sets \(X_t\), and convex trade sets \(Z_t\). A finite-horizon convex portfolio plan solves \(\min \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}[F_t(x_t)+C_t(z_t)]+F_T(x_T)\) subject to the dynamics, \(x_t\in X_t\), and \(z_t\in Z_t\). If all stage and terminal functions are convex, the complete problem is a convex program in the trajectory \((x_1,\ldots,x_T,z_0,\ldots,z_{T-1})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multi-period plan jointly chooses trades and holdings over a finite horizon. Convex stage costs and constraints with affine portfolio dynamics produce one convex trajectory optimization problem.
assumptions_latex: Every \(F_t\), \(C_t\), and \(F_T\) is proper and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The finite-horizon trajectory problem is a convex optimization problem.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-horizon trajectory representation is mathematically coherent and appropriately classified, but no authoritative multi-period portfolio source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Average Growth Rate of an Iterated Portfolio
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric-mean realized growth over a finite sequence of portfolio decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \{x_k\}_{k=0}^{N}\subset P be portfolio strategies, where N\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}, and let c_0,\ldots,c_N\in\mathbb{R}_+^n be the corresponding growth vectors. The average growth rate after N+1 periods is
\[
\Psi_N:=\left[\prod_{k=0}^{N}\langle c_k,x_k\rangle\right]^{\frac{1}{N+1}}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The average growth rate over N+1 portfolio periods is the geometric mean of the corresponding realized growth factors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Psi_N=\left[\prod_{k=0}^{N}\langle c_k,x_k\rangle\right]^{\frac{1}{N+1}}

children.title: Receding-Horizon Portfolio Control
children.top_down_role: Repeated finite-horizon portfolio decisions under updated information.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Terminal Invariance Certificate for Recursive Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient recursive-feasibility certificate for model-matched receding-horizon portfolio control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(x^+=Ax+Bz+d\) with admissible state-trade pairs \((x,z)\in\mathcal C\), and let each horizon-\(H\) rolling problem require its terminal state to lie in \(X_f\). Suppose that for every \(x\in X_f\) there exists \(z=\kappa_f(x)\) such that \((x,z)\in\mathcal C\) and \(Ax+Bz+d\in X_f\). If the date-\(t\) rolling problem is feasible and its first trade is applied, then the shifted remaining plan followed by \(\kappa_f\) is feasible at date \(t+1\), provided the realized transition and constraints equal those modeled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A controlled-invariant terminal portfolio set and admissible terminal policy certify recursive feasibility under model-matched dynamics and constraints.
assumptions_latex: X_f is controlled invariant under an admissible policy \kappa_f.
The date-t rolling problem is feasible.
The realized transition and admissible set equal the modeled transition and set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Feas}_t\Longrightarrow\operatorname{Feas}_{t+1}.

notation.meaning: Admissible terminal policy preserving the terminal set.

knowledge_statements.title: Terminal Invariance Certificate for Recursive Feasibility
Receding-Horizon Portfolio Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-predictive portfolio control by repeated finite-horizon convex optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a current state \(x_t\), forecast data for dates \(t,\ldots,t+H\), and horizon \(H\ge1\). At date \(t\), solve the convex \(H\)-step portfolio problem \(\min\sum_{k=t}^{t+H-1}[F_{k|t}(x_k)+C_{k|t}(z_k)]+V_{t+H|t}(x_{t+H})\) subject to the forecast affine dynamics and convex constraints. Apply only the first optimizer \(z_t^\star\), observe the next state and updated forecasts, increment \(t\), and repeat. Stop at the prescribed terminal date; output the implemented trade sequence rather than the discarded forecast trades.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly solve a finite-horizon convex portfolio plan, execute only its first trade, then update the state and forecasts. The realized output is the sequence of implemented first-stage trades.
assumptions_latex: Each rolling subproblem has affine dynamics and convex costs and constraints.
An optimizer is selected whenever the rolling problem is feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure outputs the implemented sequence \((z_0^\star,z_1^\star,\ldots)\) generated by repeated first-stage execution.

notation.meaning: At-date-t forecasts of future holding and trading costs.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm correctly describes receding-horizon first-stage execution and fits the algorithm container, but it lacks an inspectable source.

children.title: Horizon-Truncation Effects
children.top_down_role: Consequences of replacing long-horizon structure with a moving finite horizon.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Continuation Value Eliminates Truncation Error
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon truncation whose terminal term is the exact value of the omitted continuation problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J_t(x;u_{t:t+H-1})\) be the cost through date \(t+H-1\), let \(x_{t+H}\) be the resulting state, and let \(V_{t+H}^\star\) be the value of the omitted continuation problem under the same dynamics and admissibility rules. Then \[V_t^\star(x)=\inf_{u_{t:t+H-1}}\left\{J_t(x;u_{t:t+H-1})+V_{t+H}^\star(x_{t+H})\right\}.\] Thus the exact continuation value produces no optimal-value distortion; whenever the relevant infima are attained, an optimal truncated prefix followed by an optimal continuation is globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A truncated problem is exact when its terminal term is the true optimal cost-to-go of the omitted periods.
assumptions_latex: The truncated and continuation problems use identical transition and admissibility rules.
For the optimizer-extension conclusion, the truncated and applicable continuation infima are attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V_t^{(H,V^\star)}(x)=V_t^\star(x).
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Continuation Value Eliminates Truncation Error

knowledge_statements.scope_note: True objective degradation caused solely by uniformly approximating the continuation value on reachable terminal states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q(u)=J(u)+V^\star(x_H(u))\) and \(\widehat Q(u)=J(u)+\widehat V(x_H(u))\) on a common nonempty feasible set \(U\). If \(\sup_{u\in U}|\widehat V(x_H(u))-V^\star(x_H(u))|\le\varepsilon\) and \(\widehat u\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in U}\widehat Q(u)\), then \[0\le Q(\widehat u)-\inf_{u\in U}Q(u)\le2\varepsilon.\] The factor two is best possible under only this uniform-error assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform terminal-value error of at most epsilon limits the true suboptimality of an optimizer of the truncated model to twice epsilon; no smaller universal factor follows from that assumption alone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q(\widehat u)-\inf_{u\in U}Q(u)\le2\varepsilon.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Terminal-Value Error Bound
Horizon-Truncation Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of long-run optimality or feasibility from an inadequately modeled terminal horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the scalar convex control problem \(x_{t+1}=x_t+u_t\), with \(x_0=0\), controls \(u_t\in[0,1]\), zero stage cost, and true terminal cost \((x_2-1)^2\). The two-period optimum chooses controls satisfying \(u_0+u_1=1\) and has value \(0\). A one-period truncation that omits any terminal value assigns every \(u_0\in[0,1]\) the same value \(0\), so the admissible tie choice \(u_0=1\), repeated after replanning, yields \(x_2=2\) and true cost \(1\). Thus convexity alone gives no truncation guarantee without a suitable terminal model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even for convex dynamics and costs, a short horizon with no terminal value can choose actions that are globally suboptimal. Convexity alone does not control truncation error.
assumptions_latex: The truncated controller uses horizon one and terminal value identically zero.
Ties may be resolved by selecting \(u_t=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The truncated policy can incur true cost \(1\) although the full-horizon optimum is \(0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The constructed example is internally consistent and fits a failure-boundary container, but it has neither an external source nor an explicit standard-field rationale or editorial validation.

children.title: Fixed-Fee Portfolio Boundary
children.top_down_role: Loss of convex structure caused by discrete transaction charges.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact mixed-integer formulation for a bounded fixed-fee trade.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under \(|z_i|\le M_i\), an exact formulation is \[z_i=u_i-v_i,\quad 0\le u_i\le M_i y_i,\quad 0\le v_i\le M_i y_i,\quad y_i\in\{0,1\},\] with objective contribution \(f_i y_i+c_i(u_i+v_i)\). Relaxing \(y_i\) to \([0,1]\) is only a convex relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded fixed-fee trade is represented exactly using a binary activation variable and nonnegative buy and sell components.
assumptions_latex: \(f_i>0\), \(c_i\ge0\), and a valid bound \(|z_i|\le M_i\) with \(M_i>0\) is known.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_i\mathbf1_{\{z_i\ne0\}}+c_i|z_i|=\min\{f_i y_i+c_i(u_i+v_i):z_i=u_i-v_i,\ 0\le u_i,v_i\le M_i y_i,\ y_i\in\{0,1\}\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Fixed-Fee Activation Model
Fixed-Fee Portfolio Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed charges for nonzero trades destroy convexity and require discrete modeling or relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a trade \(z\in\mathbb R^n\), a fixed-fee model has cost \(C(z)=\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\mathbf 1_{\{z_i\ne0\}}+c_i|z_i|\), where \(f_i>0\) and \(c_i\ge0\). This cost is nonconvex whenever at least one positive fixed fee can be activated by a nonzero trade. Exact activation modeling uses discrete indicator variables, while a convex replacement is only a relaxation or surrogate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Charging a positive fee whenever an asset is traded creates a discontinuous, nonconvex cost. Exact formulations use discrete activation decisions; convex penalties cannot represent the fixed fee exactly.
assumptions_latex: At least one fixed fee satisfies \(f_i>0\).
A zero trade incurs no fixed fee.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The fixed-fee transaction cost is nonconvex, so an exact generic formulation lies outside continuous convex programming.

notation.meaning: Fixed activation fee for trading asset i.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tight scalar convex relaxation of a fixed activation fee under a symmetric trade bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \([-M,M]\), the convex envelope of \(g(0)=0\) and \(g(z)=f+c|z|\) for \(z\ne0\) is \(\left(c+f/M\right)|z|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite trade bound yields a proportional convex envelope of the fixed fee.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}_{[-M,M]}g(z)=\left(c+\frac fM\right)|z|.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Fixed-Fee Convex Envelope

intermediate_metadata.reason: The locally owned inventory is the seed's fixed-fee nonconvexity boundary and the accepted exact bounded binary activation model. Convex-envelope substitutes are excluded to Convex-Surrogate Limits, while generic binary modeling and ordinary convex transaction costs remain in their respective adjacent scopes.

children.title: Cardinality-Constrained Portfolio Boundary
children.top_down_role: Loss of convex structure caused by limits on the number of active positions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact mixed-integer formulation of bounded portfolio cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If valid bounds \(L_i\le0\le U_i\) are known, then \(\|w\|_0\le k\) is equivalent to the existence of \(y\in\{0,1\}^n\) satisfying \[L_i y_i\le w_i\le U_i y_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,n),\qquad \sum_i y_i\le k.\] Relaxing integrality is not exact in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With valid position bounds, portfolio cardinality has an exact binary activation formulation; its continuous relaxation is generally inexact.
assumptions_latex: Valid finite bounds \(L_i\le0\le U_i\) are known for every position.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|w\|_0\le k\iff\exists y\in\{0,1\}^n:\ L_i y_i\le w_i\le U_i y_i,\ \sum_i y_i\le k.

notation.meaning: Binary activation variable for asset i.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Cardinality Activation Formulation

assumptions_latex: \(w\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and portfolio cardinality counts nonzero positions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{w:\|w\|_0\le k\}\) is nonconvex.

notation.meaning: Number of nonzero coordinates of the portfolio vector.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: cardinality constraints are standard nonconvex portfolio-design constraints
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional portfolio weights with an explicit upper bound on the number of active positions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n>k\ge 1\), define \(S_k=\{w\in\mathbb{R}^n:\|w\|_0\le k\}\). Let \(x=\sum_{i=1}^{k}e_i\) and \(y=\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}e_i+e_{k+1}\). Both \(x\) and \(y\) belong to \(S_k\), whereas \((x+y)/2\) has \(k+1\) nonzero coordinates and does not belong to \(S_k\). Thus a cardinality-constrained feasible portfolio set is generally nonconvex, even before adding return, risk, or budget constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Limiting a portfolio to at most k active assets creates a nonconvex feasible set, so the resulting design problem generally lies outside convex programming.
knowledge_statements.title: Cardinality-Constrained Portfolio Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and nonconvexity claim are mathematically appropriate, but the record has no inspectable citation and includes a proof-style witness argument. A portfolio-specific source with a section, theorem, or page locator is required; the eventual sourced statement should omit proof text.

children.title: Convex-Surrogate Limits
children.top_down_role: Scope limits of convex substitutes for discrete portfolio restrictions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tight scalar convex relaxation of a fixed activation fee under a symmetric trade bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g(0)=0\) and \(g(z)=f+c|z|\) for \(0<|z|\le M\). Then \[\operatorname{conv}_{[-M,M]}g(z)=\left(c+\frac fM\right)|z|.\] This replaces activation by an additional proportional rate and does not preserve exact fixed-fee behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded fixed fee has a proportional convex envelope, but that envelope does not enforce activation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}_{[-M,M]}g(z)=\left(c+\frac fM\right)|z|.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Fixed-Fee Convex Envelope

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tight convex underestimator of cardinality on a symmetric box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \([-M,M]^n\), \[\operatorname{conv}_{[-M,M]^n}(\|w\|_0)=M^{-1}\|w\|_1.\] Thus scaled l1 is the convex envelope of cardinality on this box, but envelope minimization need not produce a cardinality-optimal portfolio.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a uniformly bounded box, scaled l1 is the convex envelope of cardinality but does not ensure discrete optimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}_{[-M,M]^n}(\|w\|_0)=M^{-1}\|w\|_1.

notation.meaning: Convex envelope over the stated box.

knowledge_statements.title: Cardinality Convex Envelope

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex hull of uniformly bounded portfolios with at most k active positions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S_{k,M}=\{w:\|w\|_0\le k,\ \|w\|_\infty\le M\}\), \[\operatorname{conv}(S_{k,M})=\{w:\|w\|_1\le kM,\ \|w\|_\infty\le M\}.\] The right-hand side is the exact convex hull, not the original discrete set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under uniform symmetric position bounds, l1 and infinity-norm constraints describe the exact convex hull but not cardinality feasibility itself.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}(S_{k,M})=\{w:\|w\|_1\le kM,\ \|w\|_\infty\le M\}.

notation.meaning: Uniformly bounded portfolios with at most k nonzeros.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Cardinality Convex Hull

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|w\|_1\le kM\) does not imply \(\|w\|_0\le k\).

notation.meaning: The all-ones vector in n dimensions.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the dense feasibility example directly establishes the limit of the convex l1 surrogate
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limit of the standard bounded \(\ell_1\) relaxation of portfolio cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The convex constraint \(\|w\|_1\le kM\), together with \(\|w\|_\infty\le M\), is necessary for every \(w\in S_{k,M}\) but does not enforce cardinality. Indeed, \(\bar w=(kM/n)\mathbf{1}\) satisfies \(\|\bar w\|_1=kM\) and \(\|\bar w\|_\infty=kM/n\le M\), while \(\|\bar w\|_0=n>k\). Consequently, an optimizer of the convex surrogate can be dense and need not solve the cardinality-constrained portfolio problem without additional exactness conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded l1 relaxation may admit dense portfolios. It is a convex surrogate for cardinality, not a generally exact replacement.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Surrogate Limits

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forecast sensitivity over a fixed convex feasible set with a uniformly strongly convex portfolio objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(w(\mu)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{w\in X}\{r(w)-\mu^{\mathsf T}w\}\). Then the optimizer is unique and, for all \(\mu,\mu'\), \[\|w(\mu')-w(\mu)\|_2\le m^{-1}\|\mu'-\mu\|_2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a fixed convex feasible set and uniform strong convexity, the optimal portfolio is unique and Lipschitz in the return forecast.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(r:X\to\mathbb R\) is lower-semicontinuous and \(m\)-strongly convex for some \(m>0\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w(\mu+\delta)-w(\mu)=\gamma^{-1}\Sigma^{-1}\delta\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact forecast perturbation formula for unconstrained quadratic mean-variance optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(w(\mu)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{w\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{\mu^{\mathsf T}w-(\gamma/2)w^{\mathsf T}\Sigma w\}\). The unique optimizer is \(w(\mu)=\gamma^{-1}\Sigma^{-1}\mu\). Hence, for every forecast perturbation \(\delta\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[w(\mu+\delta)-w(\mu)=\gamma^{-1}\Sigma^{-1}\delta,\] and therefore \(\|w(\mu+\delta)-w(\mu)\|_2\le \|\delta\|_2/(\gamma\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma))\). Small return-forecast errors may thus cause large allocation changes when risk aversion or the smallest covariance eigenvalue is small.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In unconstrained mean-variance optimization, forecast errors are multiplied by the inverse covariance matrix, potentially producing large portfolio changes.
knowledge_statements.title: Return-Forecast Sensitivity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact perturbation identity and norm bound are correct for the explicitly unconstrained, positive-definite mean-variance model, and property fits the leaf. An inspectable source supporting this portfolio-sensitivity formulation is still required.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral robustness boundary for an estimated positive-definite covariance matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Sigma\succ0\) and \(E\in\mathbb S^n\). Weyl's inequality gives \[\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma+E)\ge\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)-\|E\|_2.\] Hence \(\|E\|_2<\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)\) guarantees \(\Sigma+E\succ0\) and \[\|(\Sigma+E)^{-1}\|_2\le\frac1{\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)-\|E\|_2}.\] At the threshold \(\|E\|_2=\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)\), a perturbation aligned with a minimum-eigenvalue eigenvector can make the matrix singular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Covariance errors smaller than the smallest-eigenvalue margin preserve positive definiteness; at the margin, singularity can occur.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed eigenvalue and inverse-norm bounds hold, with a sharp uniform threshold at \(\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Covariance Perturbation Margin

knowledge_statements.scope_note: High-dimensional sampling regime that necessarily produces singular empirical covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(T\ge2\) return observations in \(\mathbb R^n\), the centered sample covariance \[\widehat\Sigma=\frac1{T-1}\sum_{t=1}^T(r_t-\bar r)(r_t-\bar r)^{\mathsf T}\] satisfies \(\operatorname{rank}(\widehat\Sigma)\le\min\{n,T-1\}\). Therefore it is singular whenever \(n\ge T\), and it can also be singular for \(n<T\) when the centered observations lie in a proper subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sample covariance based on no more observations than assets is necessarily singular because centering leaves at most T minus one independent directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}(\widehat\Sigma)\le\min\{n,T-1\}\), so \(n\ge T\) implies singularity.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank Deficiency of Sample Covariance

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularization remedy and its exact spectral effect.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\Sigma\succeq0\) and \(\rho>0\), let \(\Sigma_\rho=\Sigma+\rho I\). Then \[\lambda_i(\Sigma_\rho)=\lambda_i(\Sigma)+\rho,\qquad \kappa_2(\Sigma_\rho)=\frac{\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)+\rho}{\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)+\rho}.\] Thus \(\Sigma_\rho\succ0\), and its condition number is nonincreasing in \(\rho\), strictly decreasing unless \(\Sigma\) is already a scalar multiple of the identity, and tends to one. This changes the risk model by adding \(\rho\|x\|_2^2\); it is not an equivalent rescaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diagonal loading removes singularity and improves the eigenvalue ratio, but it changes the portfolio risk objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Diagonal loading produces the displayed positive-definite spectrum and condition number.
knowledge_statements.title: Diagonal Loading and Spectral Conditioning

assumptions_latex: The portfolio objective has Hessian \(\gamma\Sigma\) with \(\gamma>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa_2(\gamma\Sigma)=\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)/\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)\).

notation.meaning: Smallest eigenvalue of the covariance matrix.
Largest eigenvalue of the covariance matrix.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral failure regime for positive-definite covariance matrices in quadratic portfolio objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The quadratic risk term \((\gamma/2)w^{\mathsf T}\Sigma w\) has Hessian \(\gamma\Sigma\) and spectral condition number \[\kappa_2(\gamma\Sigma)=\kappa_2(\Sigma)=\frac{\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)}{\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)}.\] As \(\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)\downarrow0\), strong convexity vanishes and the inverse norm \(\|\Sigma^{-1}\|_2=1/\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)\) diverges. Consequently, optimizer sensitivity and the numerical difficulty of solving the associated linear systems can become arbitrarily large, despite convexity being retained for every positive \(\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nearly singular covariance matrix preserves convexity but weakens curvature and amplifies both optimizer sensitivity and numerical error.
knowledge_statements.title: Covariance Ill-Conditioning

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The spectral condition-number formulas are correct and failure_boundary fits the local failure-regime container. The broader claim about numerical difficulty and error amplification needs an inspectable source and a clear specification of the numerical problem or algorithm.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed perturbation of a linear objective over an unconstrained quadratic model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\Sigma_\varepsilon=\operatorname{diag}(1,\varepsilon)\), minimizing \(\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_\varepsilon x-b^{\mathsf T}x\) gives \(x^\star=\Sigma_\varepsilon^{-1}b\), so perturbing the second component of \(b\) is amplified by \(1/\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear-term perturbation along a low-curvature eigenvector is amplified by the reciprocal small eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solution-map sensitivity to \(b\) diverges as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|w_{t+1}-w_t\|_2\le \|\mu_{t+1}-\mu_t\|_2/(\gamma\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma))\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Instability of repeated frictionless mean-variance solutions under changing return forecasts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the frictionless unconstrained mean-variance solutions \(w_t=\gamma^{-1}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_t\), successive rebalancing satisfies \[w_{t+1}-w_t=\gamma^{-1}\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_{t+1}-\mu_t).\] Thus \(\|w_{t+1}-w_t\|_2\le \|\mu_{t+1}-\mu_t\|_2/(\gamma\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma))\), while \(\|w_{t+1}-w_t\|_1\le\sqrt n\|w_{t+1}-w_t\|_2\). Repeatedly resolving the frictionless model can therefore generate substantial turnover from small forecast changes, especially when the covariance matrix is ill-conditioned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated frictionless optimization can convert small forecast revisions into large trades, particularly when covariance curvature is weak.
knowledge_statements.title: Rebalancing Instability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The successive-solution identity and norm bounds are correct for a fixed covariance matrix in the stated unconstrained model. The interpretation as rebalancing instability and substantial turnover requires a portfolio-rebalancing source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact no-trade test for unconstrained convex optimization with an l1 trade penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min_x F(x)+\tau\|x-x^0\|_1\), one has \(x^0\in\operatorname*{argmin}_x\{F(x)+\tau\|x-x^0\|_1\}\) if and only if \(\|\nabla F(x^0)\|_\infty\le\tau\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The current portfolio is optimal under a proportional trade penalty exactly when the base-objective gradient lies in the corresponding infinity-norm ball.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is convex and differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^0\in\operatorname*{argmin}_x\{F(x)+\tau\|x-x^0\|_1\}\iff\|\nabla F(x^0)\|_\infty\le\tau.
knowledge_statements.title: Proportional-Cost No-Trade Certificate

assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i:[0,u_i]\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper, closed, and strictly convex.
Strong duality holds, the aggregate inequality is binding at the solution, and a clearing-price bracket is available.
For the bisection assertion, each response is single-valued and continuous and the aggregate response is strictly decreasing on the bracket.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The allocation is recovered from independent price responses \(x_i(\lambda)\), and the clearing price solves \(\sum_i x_i(\lambda)=b\).

notation.meaning: Component response at resource price lambda.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar dual search for a binding single-budget separable allocation problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Lagrange dual function is \[q(\lambda)=-\lambda b+\sum_{i=1}^n\min_{0\le x_i\le u_i}\{f_i(x_i)+\lambda x_i\},\qquad \lambda\ge0.\] Each response \(x_i(\lambda)\) is nonincreasing. A clearing price \(\lambda^\star\) satisfying \(S(\lambda^\star)=b\) recovers the primal optimum componentwise. On a bracket \([\lambda_L,\lambda_U]\) where \(S\) is continuous and strictly decreasing, bisection produces a price interval of width at most \(\varepsilon\) after \(\lceil\log_2((\lambda_U-\lambda_L)/\varepsilon)\rceil\) iterations. For differentiable strictly convex \(f_i\), each response is the box-clipped solution of \(f_i'(x_i)+\lambda=0\), the classical water-filling form. Without strict convexity, flat or set-valued responses can destroy uniqueness of the allocation or clearing price although the KKT certificate remains valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binding single-budget separable allocation reduces to independent price responses and a one-dimensional clearing-price search; differentiable responses give water filling.
knowledge_statements.title: Price Decomposition and Water Filling

assumptions_latex: For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(u_i>0\) and \(f_i:[0,u_i]\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex and lower semicontinuous.
The budget satisfies \(b\ge 0\), the feasible set is nonempty, and a constraint qualification ensuring the KKT conditions holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible point \(x^\star\) is optimal if and only if there is \(\lambda^\star\ge 0\) such that \(0\in\partial f_i(x_i^\star)+\lambda^\star+N_{[0,u_i]}(x_i^\star)\) for every \(i\), together with complementary slackness.

notation.meaning: Convex cost assigned to resource component i.
Multiplier, or shadow price, of the aggregate resource constraint.
Normal cone to the interval at x.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: separable convex allocation and its scalar-price optimality system are standard
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-budget separable convex resource allocation with componentwise box constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[\min_{0\le x_i\le u_i}\ \sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x_i)\quad\text{subject to}\quad\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\le b.\] Under a constraint qualification ensuring the KKT conditions, a feasible point \(x^\star\) is optimal if and only if there exists \(\lambda^\star\ge0\) such that \(0\in\partial f_i(x_i^\star)+\lambda^\star+N_{[0,u_i]}(x_i^\star)\) for every \(i\), \(\lambda^\star(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^\star-b)=0\), and \(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^\star\le b\). For fixed \(\lambda^\star\), the componentwise stationarity conditions are separable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separable convex allocation decomposes into componentwise optimality conditions once the common budget's shadow price is fixed.
knowledge_statements.title: Separable Resource Allocation

assumptions_latex: Each priced block subproblem attains a minimizer.
The resource residuals along the iterates are bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_{0\le j\le k}g(\lambda^j)\to g^\star.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributed price update for coupled-budget allocation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(x_i^k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x_i\in X_i}(f_i(x_i)+(\lambda^k)^{\mathsf T}A_ix_i)\), and update \(\lambda^{k+1}=\Pi_{\mathbb R_+^p}(\lambda^k+\eta_k(\sum_iA_ix_i^k-b))\). The resource residual is a supergradient of the concave dual function. Under the stated boundedness and diminishing-step assumptions, the best dual values converge to the dual optimum. Primal recovery generally requires averaging or another recovery step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Agents optimize independently at current prices, and projected price updates respond to excess shared-resource demand; standard diminishing steps give dual-value convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Projected Price Supergradient Method

assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is proper, closed, and convex, and each \(X_i\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
The primal optimal value is finite.
There is a point in the relevant relative interiors satisfying \(\sum_iA_ix_i<b\) componentwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g(\lambda)=-b^{\mathsf T}\lambda+\sum_i\inf_{x_i\in X_i}\left(f_i(x_i)+\lambda^{\mathsf T}A_ix_i\right),\quad \max_{\lambda\ge0}g(\lambda)=p^\star.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrangian decomposition of separable allocation blocks coupled by shared budgets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min_{x_i\in X_i}\sum_i f_i(x_i)\) subject to \(\sum_iA_ix_i\le b\), the Lagrange dual is \(\max_{\lambda\ge0}g(\lambda)\), where \(g(\lambda)=-b^{\mathsf T}\lambda+\sum_i\inf_{x_i\in X_i}(f_i(x_i)+\lambda^{\mathsf T}A_ix_i)\). A fixed shared-resource price \(\lambda\) therefore separates the blocks. Under the stated relative-interior Slater condition and finite primal value, the primal and dual values agree and a dual optimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing shared budgets separates the allocation blocks, with the common multiplier acting as a resource-price vector.
knowledge_statements.title: Price-Based Dual Decomposition

assumptions_latex: For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^{d_i}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is closed, proper, and convex, and \(X_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_i}\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
For a common integer \(p\ge1\), \(A_i\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times d_i}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^p\), with vector inequalities interpreted componentwise.
The coupled problem has an optimal solution and satisfies a constraint qualification ensuring the KKT conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible point \(x^\star\) is optimal if and only if there exists \(\lambda^\star\in\mathbb{R}_+^p\) satisfying \(0\in\partial f_i(x_i^\star)+A_i^{\mathsf T}\lambda^\star+N_{X_i}(x_i^\star)\) for every \(i\), together with complementary slackness.

notation.meaning: Local resource-consumption matrix for allocation block i.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the formulation and multiplier decomposition are standard convex resource-allocation facts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex block allocation coupled through multiple shared linear resource budgets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[\min_{x_i\in X_i}\ \sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x_i)\quad\text{subject to}\quad\sum_{i=1}^n A_i x_i\le b.\] Under a constraint qualification ensuring the KKT conditions, a feasible point \(x^\star\) is optimal if and only if there exists \(\lambda^\star\in\mathbb{R}_+^p\) such that \(0\in\partial f_i(x_i^\star)+A_i^{\mathsf T}\lambda^\star+N_{X_i}(x_i^\star)\) for every \(i\), and \((\lambda^\star)^{\mathsf T}(\sum_{i=1}^n A_i x_i^\star-b)=0\). The common multiplier \(\lambda^\star\) represents the prices of the coupled resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiple shared budgets couple otherwise separable allocation blocks, and their common multiplier vector represents shared-resource prices.
knowledge_statements.title: Coupled-Budget Allocation

children.title: Proportional-Fair Allocation
children.top_down_role: Allocation templates governed by proportional fairness.

assumptions_latex: \(X=\{x\in X_0:Ax\le c\}\), where \(X_0\) is closed and convex.
Each \(u_i:X_0\to(0,\infty)\) is concave and differentiable, an optimum exists, and Slater's condition holds; each \(a_i>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Optimality is equivalent to a nonnegative capacity-price vector satisfying complementary slackness and log-utility stationarity.

notation.meaning: Normal cone to the residual feasible set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity-price certificate for weighted proportional-fair allocation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasible allocation \(x^\star\) is weighted proportionally fair if and only if there is \(p\ge0\) such that \[0\in-\sum_i\frac{a_i}{u_i(x^\star)}\nabla u_i(x^\star)+A^\top p+N_{X_0}(x^\star),\qquad p_k((Ax^\star)_k-c_k)=0\quad\forall k.\] Thus weighted marginal proportional utility gains are balanced by capacity prices and any normal generated by \(X_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capacity prices certify proportional fairness by balancing weighted marginal proportional gains with binding-resource costs.
knowledge_statements.title: Proportional-Fair Resource-Price Certificate

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is convex, each \(u_i:X\to(0,\infty)\) is concave, and each \(a_i>0\).
For the uniqueness assertion, the attainable utility region \(U=\{(u_1(x),\ldots,u_m(x)):x\in X\}\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Positive participant-wise utility rescaling leaves the optimizer set unchanged; under the stated convexity of \(U\), the optimal utility vector is unique.
review_flags: corrected_builder_assumption: utility-vector uniqueness requires convexity of the attainable utility region, which does not follow merely from concavity of the component utilities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scale invariance and qualified utility-vector uniqueness for weighted proportional fairness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replacing each utility by \(\widetilde u_i=c_i u_i\), with \(c_i>0\), adds the constant \(\sum_i a_i\log c_i\) to the weighted log objective and therefore leaves its optimizer set unchanged. If the attainable utility region \(U\subset\mathbb R_{++}^m\) is convex, strict concavity of \(z\mapsto\sum_i a_i\log z_i\) gives at most one optimal utility vector. Distinct allocations can nevertheless remain optimal when they induce that same vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proportional fairness is invariant to positive utility units and, on a convex attainable utility region, uniquely determines the attained utility vector but not necessarily the allocation.
knowledge_statements.title: Scale Invariance and Utility-Vector Uniqueness

assumptions_latex: Each utility \(u_i:X\to(0,\infty)\) is concave and differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_i a_i(u_i(x)-u_i(x^\star))/u_i(x^\star)\le0\) for every \(x\in X\).

notation.meaning: Positive fairness weight of participant i.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: weighted log-utility and the proportional-fair inequality are the standard definition
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted proportional fairness for positive differentiable concave utilities on a convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \(x^\star\in X\) is weighted proportionally fair when it maximizes \(\sum_{i=1}^m a_i\log u_i(x)\) over \(X\). Equivalently, its first-order optimality condition is \[\sum_{i=1}^m a_i\frac{u_i(x)-u_i(x^\star)}{u_i(x^\star)}\le0\qquad\text{for every }x\in X.\] Thus no feasible change can produce a positive weighted aggregate of participants' proportional utility changes, measured relative to their utilities at \(x^\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proportionally fair allocation maximizes weighted log utility and admits no feasible change with positive aggregate weighted proportional gain.
knowledge_statements.title: Proportional-Fair Allocation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted proportional-fair inequality is appropriate under the stated positivity, concavity, differentiability, and convex-feasibility assumptions, and condition fits the terminal container. The claimed equivalence with weighted log-utility maximization needs an authoritative source with a precise locator.

children.title: Max-Min Fair Allocation
children.top_down_role: Allocation templates prioritizing the least-served participant.

assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is closed and convex, each \(u_i\) is concave and differentiable on a neighborhood of \(X\), and the max-min hypograph problem attains its optimum.
There is a feasible hypograph point \((\bar x,\bar t)\) satisfying \(u_i(\bar x)>\bar t\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible \((x^\star,t^\star)\) is optimal if and only if there is \(\lambda\in\Delta_m\) satisfying complementary slackness and constrained stationarity.

notation.meaning: Convex-analysis normal cone to the feasible set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: KKT certificate for differentiable concave max-min allocation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasible pair \((x^\star,t^\star)\) is max-min optimal if and only if there is \(\lambda\in\Delta_m\) such that \(\lambda_i(u_i(x^\star)-t^\star)=0\) for every \(i\) and \[0\in-\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\nabla u_i(x^\star)+N_X(x^\star).\] Thus positive multiplier weight is confined to participants attaining the minimum utility, and \(x^\star\) maximizes \(\sum_i\lambda_i u_i(x)\) over \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Max-min optimality is certified by simplex weights supported on worst-off participants whose weighted utility gradient satisfies constrained stationarity.
knowledge_statements.title: Active-User Multiplier Certificate

assumptions_latex: The attainable utility set \(U=\{(u_1(x),\ldots,u_m(x)):x\in X\}\) is nonempty and compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An allocation is lexicographically max-min fair exactly when its increasingly sorted utility vector is lexicographically maximal over \(U\).

notation.meaning: Utility vector rearranged in nondecreasing order.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lexicographic refinement of unweighted scalar max-min allocation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An allocation \(x^\star\in X\) is lexicographically max-min fair when \(u^{\uparrow}(x^\star)\) is lexicographically maximal among \(\{u^{\uparrow}(x):x\in X\}\). It is obtained by successively maximizing the smallest utility not fixed by earlier stages and retaining the equalities forced at each stage. The first stage is \(\max_{x\in X}\min_i u_i(x)\); when that stage has multiple optimizers, scalar max-min optimality alone need not determine the lexicographically max-min allocation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lexicographic max-min fairness successively maximizes the worst still-unfixed utility and refines an ambiguous scalar max-min optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Lexicographic Max-Min Refinement

assumptions_latex: Each utility \(u_i:X\to\mathbb{R}\) is concave and upper semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t^\star=\max_{x\in X}\min_i u_i(x)\).

notation.meaning: Guaranteed utility level shared across participants.
Utility of participant i under allocation x.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the hypograph formulation is the standard convex representation of max-min utility
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unweighted max-min fairness represented through a common guaranteed utility level.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The max-min fair value is represented by the convex optimization problem \[\max_{x,t}\ t\quad\text{subject to}\quad x\in X,\qquad u_i(x)\ge t\quad(i=1,\ldots,m).\] Because each superlevel constraint of a concave \(u_i\) is convex, this is a convex program. At every optimum \((x^\star,t^\star)\), \[t^\star=\min_{1\le i\le m}u_i(x^\star)=\max_{x\in X}\min_{1\le i\le m}u_i(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Max-min fairness maximizes the worst participant utility and is a convex program when utilities are concave and the feasible set is convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Max-Min Fair Allocation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The hypograph representation is mathematically appropriate, and representation is the correct content kind. Compactness and upper semicontinuity support attainment, but no inspectable source is supplied for the max-min fairness formulation.

children.title: Fairness-Regime Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Structural differences between proportional and worst-case fairness priorities.

assumptions_latex: The attainable utility set \(U\subset\mathbb R_{++}^m\) is nonempty and compact.
For every \(\alpha>1\), an alpha-fair maximizing utility vector \(u^\alpha\in U\) is selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Every accumulation point of }u^\alpha\text{ as }\alpha\to\infty\text{ maximizes }\min_i u_i\text{ over }U.

notation.meaning: utility vector selected at fairness parameter alpha

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Precise max-min limit of fixed-weight alpha-fair utility vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\alpha>1\), maximizing \(\sum_i a_i u_i^{1-\alpha}/(1-\alpha)\) is equivalent to minimizing \(\sum_i a_i u_i^{-(\alpha-1)}\). If the attainable utility set \(U\) is nonempty and compact in \(\mathbb R_{++}^m\), every accumulation point of alpha-fair maximizing utility vectors as \(\alpha\to\infty\) maximizes \(\min_i u_i\) over \(U\). If that max-min utility vector is unique, the utility vectors converge to it. Convergence of allocation vectors requires additional identifiability. Fixed positive weights affect finite-alpha choices and possible tie selection but do not by themselves produce a weighted max-min leading criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a compact positive utility set, large-alpha solutions approach max-min utility solutions; uniqueness gives utility-vector convergence, while allocation convergence needs further assumptions.
knowledge_statements.title: Large-Alpha Max-Min Limit

assumptions_latex: The scalarization is strictly increasing in every utility coordinate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in X}\Phi(u(x))\Rightarrow x^\star\text{ is Pareto efficient}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Efficiency guarantee shared by finite alpha-fair allocation regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\Phi:\mathbb R_{++}^m\to\mathbb R\) is strictly increasing in every coordinate, every maximizer of \(\Phi(u_1(x),\ldots,u_m(x))\) is Pareto efficient: no feasible allocation can weakly improve every utility and strictly improve at least one. Every finite-alpha weighted alpha-fair objective with positive weights has this property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-weight finite alpha-fair scalarization cannot select an allocation that another feasible allocation improves for all participants, with at least one strict improvement.
knowledge_statements.title: Pareto Efficiency of Alpha-Fair Scalarizations

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha=1\text{ is invariant under }u_i\mapsto c_i u_i;\quad \alpha\ne1\text{ generally is not invariant when the weights remain fixed}.

notation.meaning: positive change in participant i's utility scale

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Participant-specific utility-scale behavior across alpha-fair regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under \(u_i\mapsto c_i u_i\), the alpha-one objective changes by the constant \(\sum_i a_i\log c_i\), so its optimizer is unchanged. For \(\alpha\ne1\), the coefficient of \(u_i^{1-\alpha}/(1-\alpha)\) becomes \(a_i c_i^{1-\alpha}\), so participant-specific rescaling is equivalent to changing the weights and can change the optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proportional fairness is invariant to separate positive changes of utility units; other finite alpha-fair regimes generally absorb those changes into participant weights.
knowledge_statements.title: Utility-Scale Behavior Across Alpha-Fair Regimes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual subgradient allocation for the fixed-route model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Select \(x_r^k\in\arg\max_{t\ge0}\{U_r(t)-(A^{\mathsf T}\lambda^k)_rt\}\) and update \[\lambda^{k+1}=[\lambda^k+\eta_k(Ax^k-c)]_+.\] If \(g^k=c-Ax^k\), then \(g^k\) is a subgradient of the convex dual objective. For any dual optimum \(\lambda^\star\), bounded subgradients \(\|g^k\|\le G\) give \[\min_{0\le j<K}(d(\lambda^j)-d^\star)\le\frac{\|\lambda^0-\lambda^\star\|^2+G^2\sum_{k<K}\eta_k^2}{2\sum_{k<K}\eta_k}.\] Consequently, nonsummable square-summable steps give convergence of best dual values; a constant step chosen for a horizon gives the standard \(O(K^{-1/2})\) best-value bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Links adjust prices according to overload; standard projected-subgradient bounds give dual convergence and a square-root iteration rate with horizon-tuned steps.

u_r^\star,\qquad 
u_r^\star x_r^\star=0,\qquad \lambda_\ell^\star(c_\ell-(Ax^\star)_\ell)=0.\] Thus every positive-rate flow equates marginal utility to the sum of prices on its route.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrangian representation of shared-capacity coupling with separable utilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\max_{x_i\in X_i}\sum_iU_i(x_i)\) subject to \(Ax\le c\), the capacity Lagrangian is \[L(x,\lambda)=c^{\mathsf T}\lambda+\sum_i\bigl(U_i(x_i)-(A^{\mathsf T}\lambda)_ix_i\bigr),\qquad \lambda\ge0.\] Thus fixed prices leave independent activity problems, while all cross-activity information is concentrated in the common resource-price vector. Under a relative-interior constraint qualification, minimizing the resulting convex dual objective recovers the primal value.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural criterion for separation of linear shared-capacity constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Form the bipartite graph with activity vertices \(i\), resource vertices \(\ell\), and an edge \((\ell,i)\) when \(A_{\ell i}>0\). Its connected components determine the maximal independent blocks of \(Ax\le c\): after row and column permutations, the inequalities are block separable exactly along those components. A resource adjacent to activities in two proposed blocks prevents independent feasibility tests for those blocks unless its constraint is coordinated or dualized.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shared-capacity constraints separate precisely along the connected components of their resource-activity incidence graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The connected components of the bipartite incidence graph give the maximal block-separable components of \(Ax\le c\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear coupling of otherwise separate allocations through shared resource constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Allocations are coupled through shared capacities precisely when feasibility requires
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n A_{\ell i}x_i\le c_\ell\quad\text{for every }\ell\in\{1,\ldots,m\},
\]
or, equivalently, \(Ax\le c\). Each individual term \(A_{\ell i}x_i\) is the load contributed by allocation \(i\) to resource \(\ell\). The constraint set \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}_+^n:Ax\le c\}\) is convex and represents the complete shared-capacity coupling condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Several allocations share a resource when their weighted aggregate use must not exceed that resource's capacity; all such inequalities form a convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Shared-Capacity Coupling

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar solution method for parallel-channel water-filling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P>0\), define \(F(\lambda)=\sum_i[w_i/\lambda-n_i/g_i]_+\). It is continuous and strictly decreasing on the region where \(F>0\), satisfies \(F(\lambda)\to\infty\) as \(\lambda\downarrow0\), and vanishes for sufficiently large \(\lambda\). Given a bracket \([\lambda_L,\lambda_U]\) containing the root of \(F(\lambda)=P\), bisection returns an interval of width at most \(\delta\) after \(O(\log((\lambda_U-\lambda_L)/\delta))\) iterations, each using \(O(n)\) arithmetic operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The water level is found by scalar bisection; each iteration scans all channels and halves the price interval.
assumptions_latex: The initial interval brackets the unique root.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bisection finds the water level to interval tolerance \(\delta\) in \(O(n\log((\lambda_U-\lambda_L)/\delta))\) arithmetic work.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between orthogonal power allocation and interference-coupled control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With two links, unit direct and cross gains, unit noise, and \(p_1,p_2\ge0\), the first-link rate is \[r_1(p)=\log\left(1+\frac{p_1}{1+p_2}\right)=\log(1+p_1+p_2)-\log(1+p_2).\] Its Hessian has determinant \[-\frac{1}{(1+p_1+p_2)^2(1+p_2)^2}<0,\] so it is neither jointly convex nor jointly concave. Therefore weighted interference-coupled sum-rate maximization is not generically a convex program.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cross-channel interference can make rates nonconcave in the power vector, so convex rate-region assumptions are substantive.
assumptions_latex: Both powers are unrestricted nonnegative decision variables in the displayed interference model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed rate has an indefinite Hessian and is not jointly concave.
knowledge_statements.title: Interference Destroys Generic Concavity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical convex power allocation over orthogonal channels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(g_i,n_i,w_i>0\) and \(P\ge0\), consider \[\max_{p\ge0,\,\sum_i p_i\le P}\sum_iw_i\log\left(1+\frac{g_ip_i}{n_i}\right).\] The objective is strictly concave, so the optimizer is unique. When \(P>0\), there is a unique positive multiplier \(\lambda\) such that \[p_i^\star=\left[\frac{w_i}{\lambda}-\frac{n_i}{g_i}\right]_+,\qquad \sum_i p_i^\star=P.\] For \(P=0\), the unique optimizer is \(p^star=0\), although a water-level multiplier need not be unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel-channel power allocation has a unique weighted water-filling solution; a common water level exhausts every positive power budget.
assumptions_latex: Channels are orthogonal, so each rate depends only on its own power.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unique optimizer has the displayed weighted water-filling form, with a unique water level when \(P>0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Water-Filling for Parallel Gaussian Channels

At \(\alpha=0\), the utility is linear and uniqueness can fail. For \(\alpha\ge1\), the extended value at zero is \(-\infty\); consequently, a finite optimum requires at least one feasible rate vector with every positively weighted coordinate strictly positive.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order characterization of weighted alpha-fair allocations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R_{++}^n\) be convex. A point \(x^\star\in X\) maximizes \(\sum_iw_iu_\alpha(x_i)\) if and only if \[\sum_iw_i(x_i^\star)^{-\alpha}(x_i-x_i^\star)\le0\qquad\text{for every }x\in X.\] For \(\alpha=1\), this becomes weighted proportional fairness: \(\sum_iw_i(x_i-x_i^\star)/x_i^\star\le0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted \(\alpha\)-fair utilities on strictly positive rates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(t>0\), define the \(\alpha\)-fair utility
\[
u_\alpha(t)=
\begin{cases}
\log t, & \alpha=1,\\
\dfrac{t^{1-\alpha}}{1-\alpha}, & \alpha\ne1.
\end{cases}
\]
Given a feasible rate set \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\), a weighted \(\alpha\)-fair allocation is any maximizer of \(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i u_\alpha(x_i)\) over \(x\in X\). Each \(u_\alpha\) is increasing and concave for \(\alpha\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted alpha-fairness maximizes a concave utility family ranging from throughput emphasis at alpha zero to proportional fairness at alpha one and stronger fairness for larger alpha.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the maximal concurrent-flow problem, define \(\psi(t):=\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{OD}}d_{ij}SP_{ij}(t)\), where \(SP_{ij}(t)\) is the shortest-path value under nonnegative arc weights \(t\). In the regime where the displayed reciprocal normalization is defined, the Lagrange-dual value is \[\psi_\star:=\lambda_\star^{-1}=\max_{t\ge 0}\left\{\psi(t):\langle\bar f,t\rangle=1\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For maximal concurrent flow, the normalized shortest-path dual maximizes the demand-weighted sum of origin–destination shortest-path values over nonnegative arc weights whose capacity-weighted sum is one. The extract equates this value to the reciprocal of the primal flow value, which presupposes that the reciprocal and normalization are defined.
assumptions_latex: \lambda_\star^{-1}\text{ and the constraint }\langle\bar f,t\rangle=1\text{ are well-defined in the stated regime}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \psi_\star=\lambda_\star^{-1}=\max_{\substack{t\ge0\\\langle\bar f,t\rangle=1}}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{OD}}d_{ij}SP_{ij}(t)
