knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:x^TQx\leq0\}\) is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of the general convex-cone guarantee when the quadratic matrix is not positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Positive semidefiniteness is essential for the general convex quadratic design template. With \(Q=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\), the constraint
\[x^TQx\leq0\]
becomes \(x_1^2\leq x_2^2\). Its feasible set is nonconvex: \((1,1)\) and \((1,-1)\) are feasible, while their midpoint \((1,0)\) is infeasible. Hence an indefinite quadratic inequality need not admit the convex rotated-cone representation used for \(Q\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An indefinite quadratic can have a nonconvex sublevel set, so positive semidefiniteness is a sharp assumption for the general convex template.
knowledge_statements.title: Indefinite Quadratic Boundary

children.title: Cone-Representation Choice
children.top_down_role: Routing between norm-based and explicit cone-based design representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Representation Choice
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence criterion for choosing among conic formulations of one engineering design set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a design-feasible set. Two lifted conic formulations \[F_i:=\{x:\exists y_i,\ A_i x+B_i y_i+b_i\in K_i\},\qquad i\in\{1,2\},\] are exact alternative representations precisely when \(F_1=F_2=F\). Either representation preserves the feasible design vectors and every objective depending only on \(x\). Representation choice may nevertheless change lift dimension, cone block structure, sparsity, and numerical conditioning; therefore mathematical equivalence does not imply equal computational behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conic formulations are interchangeable only when their projections equal the same design set, although their computational behavior may differ substantially.
assumptions_latex: The optimization objective depends only on \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_1=F_2=F\) preserves feasible designs and optimal values, but not formulation size or conditioning.
review_flags: A source comparing exact conic lifts and computational representation choices is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projection-equivalence criterion is mathematically sound and principle is the appropriate content kind, but no source is supplied for the formulation-choice and computational-behavior claims. A specific conic-modeling or extended-formulation locator is required.

children.title: Friction-Cone Design
children.top_down_role: Conic design representations for friction-limited interactions.

knowledge_statements.title: Friction-Cone Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order-cone model of isotropic Coulomb friction at a fixed contact.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At contact \(i\), decompose the force as \(f_i=n_i\lambda_i+t_i\), where \(n_i\) is a prescribed unit normal, \(\lambda_i\in\mathbb R\) is the compressive normal magnitude, and \(n_i^Tt_i=0\). The isotropic Coulomb friction condition is \[\lambda_i\geq0,\qquad \|t_i\|_2\leq\mu_i\lambda_i,\] where \(\mu_i\geq0\). This is a Lorentz-cone constraint and hence a convex admissible-force set. It models sticking or non-sliding force admissibility; it does not itself impose contact complementarity or a sliding direction law.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-contact Coulomb friction cone is SOC-representable, but it does not encode separation complementarity or the direction of sliding.
assumptions_latex: \(n_i\) is a fixed unit contact normal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\mu_i\lambda_i,t_i)\in\mathcal Q\) with \(\lambda_i\geq0\) exactly represents the isotropic friction cone.

assumptions_latex: Every \(v_j\) and \(u_j\) lies in the tangent space and has Euclidean norm at most one and exactly one, respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{\mathrm{in}}\subseteq\{(\lambda,t):\|t\|_2\leq\mu\lambda\}\subseteq P_{\mathrm{out}}\).

notation.meaning: chosen tangential generator and test directions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral inner and outer approximations of a fixed-contact isotropic Coulomb cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the circular friction cone \(C=\{(\lambda,t):\lambda\geq0,\ \|t\|_2\leq\mu\lambda\}\), choose tangential vectors \(v_j\) with \(\|v_j\|_2\leq1\). The finite-generator cone
\[P_{\mathrm{in}}=\{(\lambda,t):\lambda\geq0,\ t=\sum_j\beta_jv_j,\ \beta_j\geq0,\ \sum_j\beta_j\leq\mu\lambda\}\]
is an inner approximation of \(C\). If instead \(u_j\) are unit tangential directions, then
\[P_{\mathrm{out}}=\{(\lambda,t):\lambda\geq0,\ u_j^Tt\leq\mu\lambda\ \text{for all }j\}\]
is an outer approximation. Thus an inner friction pyramid may reject admissible forces, whereas an outer polyhedron may accept forces outside the circular cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite generators give a conservative inner friction pyramid, while finitely many supporting inequalities give an outer approximation that may admit excessive tangential force.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Friction-Cone Approximations

assumptions_latex: The contact locations, frames, and maps \(G_i\) are fixed.
Each admissible-force set \(C_i\) is a closed convex cone.
The objective \(\phi\) is convex; to obtain a conic program in standard form, its epigraph must additionally admit a conic representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible set \(\{f:\sum_iG_if_i+w=0,\ f_i\in C_i\}\) is convex and conically represented; minimizing \(\phi\) over it is a convex optimization problem, and it is a conic program when the epigraph of \(\phi\) is conically representable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex equilibrium design over fixed contacts with conic force admissibility.

source_refs.locator: 3.2.2 Contact problems with static friction p. 82

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For prescribed contact locations and frames, let \(G_i\) map contact force \(f_i\) to generalized force and let \(w\) be the applied generalized load. A static contact-force design problem has the form \[\min_{f_1,\ldots,f_N}\ \phi(f_1,\ldots,f_N)\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{i=1}^N G_i f_i+w=0,\qquad f_i\in C_i.\] If \(\phi\) is convex and every \(C_i\) is a closed convex cone, including friction cones, the feasible set is convex and has a conic representation, so the displayed problem is a convex optimization problem. It is a conic program in standard form when the epigraph of \(\phi\) also admits a conic representation; in particular, this holds for a linear objective. The claim presumes that the contact set and contact geometry are fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With fixed contacts, equilibrium and convex force cones define a conically represented convex feasible set. A convex objective gives a convex optimization problem, and the full problem is conic when the objective epigraph is conically representable.
knowledge_statements.title: Contact-Force Design

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2.2 Contact problems with static friction p. 82

assumptions_latex: Each \(C_i\) is a closed convex cone.
The aggregate image cone \(G(C)\), where \(C=\prod_i C_i\), is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nexists f\in C:Gf+w=0\iff\exists y:\ G_i^{\mathsf T}y\in C_i^*\ \forall i,\ w^{\mathsf T}y>0.

notation.meaning: Dual cone of admissible contact forces at contact i.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic alternative for fixed-contact static equilibrium.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\prod_{i=1}^N C_i\) and \(Gf=\sum_iG_if_i\), and suppose the image cone \(G(C)\) is closed. Exactly one of the following holds: \[\exists f\in C:\ Gf+w=0,\] or \[\exists y:\ G_i^{\mathsf T}y\in C_i^*\ \forall i,\qquad w^{\mathsf T}y>0.\] Thus such a vector \(y\) certifies that the prescribed load cannot be balanced by admissible contact forces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separating generalized vector whose contact pullbacks lie in the dual force cones certifies infeasibility of fixed-contact equilibrium.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Separation Certificate for Contact-Force Infeasibility

children.title: Contact-Relaxation Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits of convex contact representations under discrete or nonconvex physical effects.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\lambda=0\) is equivalent to the displayed binary disjunction, and relaxing \(z\) yields \(\operatorname{conv}(S)=\{(g,\lambda)\geq0:g/G+\lambda/L\leq1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact bounded disjunctive formulation and tight convex relaxation of one unilateral gap-force complementarity pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S=\{(g,\lambda):0\leq g\leq G,\ 0\leq\lambda\leq L,\ g\lambda=0\}\), where \(G,L>0\). Complementarity has the exact disjunctive formulation
\[0\leq g\leq Gz,\qquad 0\leq\lambda\leq L(1-z),\qquad z\in\{0,1\}.\]
Replacing \(z\in\{0,1\}\) by \(0\leq z\leq1\) and projecting out \(z\) gives
\[\operatorname{conv}(S)=\{(g,\lambda):g\geq0,\ \lambda\geq0,\ g/G+\lambda/L\leq1\}.\]
The triangular hull is the tightest convex relaxation in the original two variables, but its interior still permits simultaneous positive gap and force.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Valid gap and force bounds give an exact binary contact disjunction; relaxing the binary variable produces the triangular convex hull, whose interior still violates exact complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded Contact Disjunction and Convex Hull
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Contact Disjunction and Convex Hull
Contact-Relaxation Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonconvex boundary introduced by unilateral-contact complementarity and its convex relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a unilateral contact, let \(g_i\geq0\) denote separation and let \(\lambda_i\geq0\) denote compressive normal force. Exact contact status requires \[g_i\lambda_i=0.\] The set \(\{(g_i,\lambda_i):g_i\geq0,\lambda_i\geq0,g_i\lambda_i=0\}\) is nonconvex: it is the union of the two coordinate rays. Dropping complementarity gives the convex relaxation \(g_i\geq0\), \(\lambda_i\geq0\), but admits physically inconsistent simultaneous separation and positive force, such as \((g_i,\lambda_i)=(1,1)\). Thus conic force admissibility alone is not an exact model when contact activation is variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variable unilateral contact introduces nonconvex gap-force complementarity; dropping it is convex but permits force across a positive gap.
assumptions_latex: \(\lambda_i\) is the nonnegative compressive normal force.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_i\lambda_i=0\) is nonconvex, while omitting it yields a strict convex relaxation containing \((1,1)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic stability certificate for a fixed discrete-time linear system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x_{k+1}=Ax_k\), the matrix \(A\) is Schur stable if and only if there exists \(P\in\mathbb S^n\) satisfying \[P\succ0,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}PA-P\prec0.\] Because \(A\) is fixed, the second expression is affine in the decision matrix \(P\) and is an LMI.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A discrete-time linear system is asymptotically stable exactly when it admits a positive-definite quadratic Lyapunov matrix satisfying the discrete-time Lyapunov LMI.
knowledge_statements.title: Discrete-Time Lyapunov Stability LMI

assumptions_latex: Stability means that every eigenvalue of \(A\) has strictly negative real part.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic stability certificate for a fixed continuous-time linear system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\dot x=Ax\), the matrix \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is Hurwitz if and only if there exists \(P\in\mathbb S^n\) such that \(P\succ0\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}P+PA\prec0\). Thus asymptotic stability of a fixed continuous-time linear system has an LMI feasibility certificate in \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous-time linear system is asymptotically stable exactly when it has a positive-definite quadratic Lyapunov matrix satisfying a strict LMI.
knowledge_statements.title: Continuous-Time Lyapunov Stability LMI

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) and \(B\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\) are fixed.
The full-state feedback gain \(K\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) is otherwise unconstrained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists K:\ A+BK\text{ is Hurwitz}\iff\exists(P,Y):\ P\succ0,\ AP+PA^{\mathsf T}+BY+Y^{\mathsf T}B^{\mathsf T}\prec0.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact continuous-time full-state-feedback stabilization LMI with an unconstrained gain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\dot x=Ax+Bu\) and \(u=Kx\), a stabilizing gain exists if and only if there are \(P\in\mathbb S^n\) and \(Y\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) satisfying \[P\succ0,\qquad AP+PA^{\mathsf T}+BY+Y^{\mathsf T}B^{\mathsf T}\prec0.\] Every feasible pair gives \(K=YP^{-1}\). Conversely, a stabilizing \(K\) and a Lyapunov matrix for \(A+BK\) give a feasible pair with \(Y=KP\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unconstrained continuous-time state-feedback stabilization becomes an exact LMI after replacing the controller-Lyapunov product KP by Y.

LMI Control-Design Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine matrix-inequality interface for convex control-analysis and synthesis variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y\in\mathbb R^p\) collect control-design variables after any valid change of variables, and let \(F_j\in\mathbb S^m\) be fixed. The constraint \[F(y):=F_0+\sum_{j=1}^p y_jF_j\preceq0\] is a linear matrix inequality and defines a closed convex feasible set. Multiple such constraints, affine equalities, and a convex objective form a semidefinite control-design problem. This interface applies only after the relevant stability or performance certificate is affine in \(y\); expressions containing products of independently variable controller and Lyapunov matrices are bilinear matrix inequalities, not LMIs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Control conditions form a convex SDP when certificate matrices depend affinely on transformed variables; unresolved controller–Lyapunov products remain nonconvex.
assumptions_latex: Any control-variable substitution used is exact on the stated domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{y:F_0+\sum_jy_jF_j\preceq0\}\) is convex; genuinely bilinear matrix inequalities lie outside this interface.

knowledge_statements.title: Truss Design Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Force-based conic formulation of minimum-compliance truss sizing under one load case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For bars \(i=1,\ldots,m\), let \(a_i\geq0\) be cross-sectional areas, \(q_i\) axial forces, \(\ell_i>0\) lengths, and \(E_i>0\) elastic moduli. Under load \(f\), a compliance epigraph is represented by \[Bq=f,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m\frac{\ell_iq_i^2}{E_ia_i}\leq t,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m\ell_i a_i\leq V.\] Each quadratic-over-linear term is interpreted by its closed perspective and is rotated-cone representable. Consequently, minimizing \(t\) over \((a,q,t)\) is a second-order-cone truss-sizing problem for fixed geometry and a fixed load case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-geometry truss compliance minimization has a force-based SOCP formulation using equilibrium, volume, and quadratic-over-linear bar energies.
assumptions_latex: The truss geometry and equilibrium matrix \(B\) are fixed.
The load \(f\) and volume bound \(V\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min t\) subject to the displayed equilibrium, compliance, and volume constraints is second-order-cone representable.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Force-based SOCP formulation for a finite weighted collection of fixed load cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For fixed load cases \(f^{(k)}\), nonnegative weights \(w_k\), and common bar areas \(a_i\geq0\), introduce forces \(q_i^{(k)}\) and epigraph variables \(s_{ik}\). The constraints
\[Bq^{(k)}=f^{(k)},\qquad \frac{\ell_i(q_i^{(k)})^2}{E_i a_i}\leq s_{ik},\qquad \sum_i\ell_i a_i\leq V\]
use the closed quadratic-over-linear perspective and are second-order-cone representable. Therefore minimizing \(\sum_{k,i}w_ks_{ik}\) gives an SOCP for weighted multiple-load minimum-compliance sizing with fixed geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite weighted multiple-load truss compliance remains an SOCP by sharing bar areas and introducing equilibrium forces and perspective epigraphs for each load case.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Load Truss Compliance Design

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compliance-type truss design model over normalized nonnegative member weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let x_i\in\mathbb{R}^2 for i=1,\ldots,n+p. Let arcs (i_k,j_k), k=1,\ldots,m, satisfy j_k>i_k and i_k\le n, with x_{n+1},\ldots,x_{n+p} fixed, and let f=(f_1,\ldots,f_n)^T\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}. Define d_k=(x_{i_k}-x_{j_k})/\|x_{i_k}-x_{j_k}\|^2 and a_k\in\mathbb{R}^{2n} by blocks a_{k,q}=d_k if q=i_k, a_{k,q}=-d_k if q=j_k\le n, and a_{k,q}=0 otherwise. For \Delta_m=\{t\in\mathbb{R}_+^m:\sum_{k=1}^m t^{(k)}=1\}, set B(t)=\sum_{k=1}^m t^{(k)}a_ka_k^T. The truss topology design value is \psi^*=\inf\{\langle B(t)^{-1}f,f\rangle:t\in\operatorname{rint}\Delta_m\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The truss model assigns each admissible arc a geometry-dependent vector, forms a stiffness-type matrix as a simplex-weighted sum of rank-one matrices, and minimizes the compliance fᵀB(t)⁻¹f over relative-interior design weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \psi^*=\inf_{t\in\operatorname{rint}\Delta_m}\left\langle\left[\sum_{k=1}^m t^{(k)}a_ka_k^T\right]^{-1}f,f\right\rangle

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Max and Minimax Forms of Truss Compliance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent homogeneous representations of the compliance value generated by rank-one stiffness matrices; the ratio is understood on nonzero vectors where its denominator is defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}, let \Delta_m=\{t\in\mathbb{R}_+^m:\sum_{k=1}^m t^{(k)}=1\}, and set B(t)=\sum_{k=1}^m t^{(k)}a_ka_k^T. Assume B(t) is invertible for every t\in\operatorname{rint}\Delta_m, and for f\in\mathbb{R}^{2n} define \psi^*=\inf_{t\in\operatorname{rint}\Delta_m}\langle B(t)^{-1}f,f\rangle. Then \psi^*=\max_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}}\left[2\langle f,x\rangle-\max_{1\le k\le m}\langle a_k,x\rangle^2\right]=\max_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}\setminus\{0\}}\frac{\langle f,x\rangle^2}{\max_{1\le k\le m}\langle a_k,x\rangle^2}. With f^*=\min\{\max_{1\le k\le m}|\langle a_k,x\rangle|:x\in\mathbb{R}^{2n},\ \langle f,x\rangle=1\}, one has \psi^*=(f^*)^{-2}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every relative-interior stiffness matrix is invertible, the minimum compliance equals a concave maximization and a homogeneous quadratic-ratio maximization. It is also the inverse square of the normalized minimum maximum absolute member response.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \psi^*=\max_x\left[2\langle f,x\rangle-\max_k\langle a_k,x\rangle^2\right]=\max_{x\ne0}\frac{\langle f,x\rangle^2}{\max_k\langle a_k,x\rangle^2}=(f^*)^{-2}

knowledge_statements.title: Continuum Structural Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidefinite compliance interface for an affine finite-dimensional stiffness model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\rho\in\mathbb R^p\) be structural design variables and suppose the discretized stiffness is affine, \(K(\rho)=K_0+\sum_{j=1}^p\rho_jK_j\), with \(K(\rho)\succ0\) on the design domain. For a fixed load \(f\), the compliance bound \[f^TK(\rho)^{-1}f\leq t\] is equivalent by the Schur complement to \[\begin{pmatrix}K(\rho)&f\\ f^T&t\end{pmatrix}\succeq0.\] Therefore compliance minimization with convex constraints on \(\rho\), such as box and affine volume constraints, is a semidefinite program under the affine-stiffness model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With affine positive-definite stiffness, a fixed-load compliance bound is an LMI, so convex design restrictions yield an SDP.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^TK(\rho)^{-1}f\leq t\iff\begin{pmatrix}K(\rho)&f\\f^T&t\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\).

source_refs.locator: 4.8 Applications VI: Structural design p. 227

source_witnesses.locator: 4.8 Applications VI: Structural design p. 227

assumptions_latex: \(K(\rho)\) is symmetric, affine in \(\rho\), and positive definite on the design domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_kw_kf_k^TK(\rho)^{-1}f_k\leq t\) has the displayed exact semidefinite epigraph.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidefinite epigraph for weighted compliance under finitely many fixed load cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K(\rho)=K_0+\sum_j\rho_jK_j\succ0\), let fixed loads be \(f_1,\ldots,f_N\), and let \(w_k\geq0\). The weighted compliance bound
\[\sum_{k=1}^N w_k f_k^TK(\rho)^{-1}f_k\leq t\]
has the exact SDP representation
\[\begin{pmatrix}K(\rho)&f_k\\f_k^T&s_k\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\quad(k=1,\ldots,N),\qquad \sum_{k=1}^Nw_ks_k\leq t.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative weighted sum of finitely many fixed-load compliances is represented by one Schur-complement LMI per load and a linear aggregation constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiple Fixed-Load Compliance Interface

assumptions_latex: \(K(\rho)\) is symmetric, affine in \(\rho\), and positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\begin{pmatrix}K(\rho)&f\\f^T&t\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\iff f\in\operatorname{range}K(\rho)\ \text{and}\ t\geq f^TK(\rho)^\dagger f\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized Schur-complement compliance epigraph for singular positive-semidefinite affine stiffness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If the affine stiffness matrix is only positive semidefinite, the block constraint
\[\begin{pmatrix}K(\rho)&f\\f^T&t\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\]
is equivalent to
\[f\in\operatorname{range}K(\rho),\qquad f^TK(\rho)^\dagger f\leq t.\]
Thus the same LMI represents the closed extended-value compliance epigraph: a load outside the stiffness range has infinite compliance and is automatically infeasible. Positive definiteness is sufficient but not necessary for the SDP interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For singular positive-semidefinite stiffness, the compliance LMI remains exact and automatically enforces that the fixed load lies in the stiffness range.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular-Stiffness Compliance Interface

children.title: Structural Convexity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Structural effects that limit direct convex design formulations.

assumptions_latex: The equilibrium operator depends affinely and nontrivially on \(z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B(z)q=f\) is generally bilinear and its feasible set need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bilinearity introduced when truss geometry and member forces are optimized simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a fixed-geometry truss, equilibrium is \(Bq=f\) with constant matrix \(B\). If geometry variables \(z\) enter the direction cosines, equilibrium becomes \(B(z)q=f\). Even when \(B(z)=B_0+\sum_jz_jB_j\) is affine, the terms \(z_jB_jq\) are bilinear in \((z,q)\), so the feasible set need not be convex. For the scalar equation \(zq=1\) with \(z,q>0\), both \((1,1)\) and \((2,1/2)\) are feasible, while their midpoint is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimizing structural geometry jointly with internal forces generally makes equilibrium bilinear and nonconvex, unlike the fixed-geometry truss interface.
knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Geometry Equilibrium Boundary
Structural Convexity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of the affine-stiffness condition can destroy convexity of compliance design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The affine-stiffness hypothesis is a genuine convexity boundary. In a scalar structural model with design \(\rho\in[0,1]\), stiffness \(K(\rho)=1+\rho^2\), and unit load, compliance is \[c(\rho)=\frac{1}{1+\rho^2}.\] Its second derivative is \[c''(\rho)=\frac{6\rho^2-2}{(1+\rho^2)^3},\] which is negative for \(0\leq\rho<1/\sqrt3\). Hence compliance is not convex on the design interval, and the affine-stiffness LMI representation does not apply. Discrete topology restrictions, design-dependent loads, and stability constraints can introduce additional nonconvexities, but are not needed for this counterexample.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonaffine stiffness can make compliance nonconvex; the scalar stiffness 1 plus density squared supplies an explicit counterexample.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c''(\rho)<0\) for \(0\leq\rho<1/\sqrt3\), so \(c(\rho)=1/K(\rho)\) is not convex on \([0,1]\).
review_flags: The explicit counterexample is self-contained, but no supplied locator documents this structural convexity boundary.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The derivative and scalar counterexample are correct, and failure_boundary is the appropriate content kind. Nevertheless, the record has no citation with a specific locator supporting its interpretation as a structural-design convexity boundary; a source is required under the evidence contract.

knowledge_statements.title: Robust Quadratic-Design Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: S-lemma representation for a ball-uncertain quadratic inequality with affine design dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) be a design variable, and let \(Q(x)\in\mathbb S^m\), \(q(x)\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(r(x)\in\mathbb R\) depend affinely on \(x\). Define \(f_x(u):=u^{\mathsf T}Q(x)u+2q(x)^{\mathsf T}u+r(x)\) for \(u\in\mathbb R^m\). The robust constraint \[f_x(u)\le0\quad\text{for every }u\in\mathbb R^m\text{ with }\|u\|_2\le1\] is equivalent to the existence of \(\lambda\ge0\) such that \[\begin{pmatrix}Q(x)-\lambda I_m&q(x)\\q(x)^{\mathsf T}&r(x)+\lambda\end{pmatrix}\preceq0.\] Thus the robust quadratic constraint is semidefinite-representable. If the remaining objective epigraph and constraints also have semidefinite representations, the complete robust design problem can be formulated as a semidefinite program.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic inequality required to hold throughout a Euclidean uncertainty ball has an exact affine semidefinite representation using one nonnegative scalar multiplier. The complete design problem is an SDP when its other components are also semidefinite-representable.
assumptions_latex: \(Q:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb S^m\), \(q:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), and \(r:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) are affine.
The uncertainty set is \(\{u\in\mathbb R^m:\|u\|_2\le1\}\), which has nonempty interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_x(u)\le0\ \forall u\in\mathbb R^m\text{ with }\|u\|_2\le1\iff\exists\lambda\ge0:\begin{pmatrix}Q(x)-\lambda I_m&q(x)\\q(x)^{\mathsf T}&r(x)+\lambda\end{pmatrix}\preceq0.\)

notation.meaning: The uncertain quadratic expression at design x.

No special losslessness theorem is assumed for multiple quadratic premises.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{One strictly feasible quadratic premise permits the lossless S-lemma; multiple premises do not generally do so.}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of exact scalar-multiplier SDP reformulation for robust quadratic design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The lossless scalar-multiplier equivalence used by the S-lemma requires a strict-feasibility condition for one quadratic uncertainty constraint. With several simultaneous quadratic constraints, or without the required interior point, a valid semidefinite multiplier condition remains sufficient but is not generally necessary. Therefore an exact robust counterpart cannot be claimed without an additional losslessness theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The one-multiplier S-lemma is exact for one strictly feasible quadratic premise, but analogous multi-premise SDP conditions are generally only safe relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Single-Constraint Exactness Boundary of the S-Lemma

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact robust quadratic representation over an ellipsoid with nonempty interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_x(u)=u^{\mathsf T}Q(x)u+2q(x)^{\mathsf T}u+r(x)\), with \(Q,q,r\) affine in \(x\), and let \(g(u)=(u-c)^{\mathsf T}W(u-c)-1\), where \(W\succ0\). Then \[f_x(u)\leq0\quad\forall u\text{ satisfying }g(u)\leq0\] if and only if there exists \(\lambda\geq0\) such that \[\begin{pmatrix}Q(x)&q(x)\\q(x)^{\mathsf T}&r(x)\end{pmatrix}-\lambda\begin{pmatrix}W&-Wc\\-c^{\mathsf T}W&c^{\mathsf T}Wc-1\end{pmatrix}\preceq0.\]

children.title: Projection Models
children.top_down_role: Geometric templates centered on projection onto convex sets.

assumptions_latex: The target sets are the displayed \(C\) and \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_C(0)=\varnothing,\qquad P_D(0)=\{-1,1\}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of existence or uniqueness outside the closed-convex projection regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Closedness and convexity play distinct roles. For \(C=(0,\infty)\subset\mathbb R\), \(\inf_{x\in C}|x|=0\) is not attained, so \(P_C(0)\) does not exist. For the closed nonconvex set \(D=\{-1,1\}\), both points minimize \(|x|\) at \(z=0\), so the metric projection is set-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dropping closedness can destroy projection existence, while dropping convexity can destroy uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.title: Closedness and Convexity Boundaries
Projection Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric projection onto a nonempty closed convex set in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), the projection of \(z\in\mathbb R^n\) onto \(C\) is \[P_C(z):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\frac12\|x-z\|_2^2.\] The objective is coercive and strictly convex, so the minimizer exists and is unique. A point \(p\in C\) equals \(P_C(z)\) exactly when \[\langle z-p,x-p\rangle\le0\quad\text{for every }x\in C.\] Thus projection is a convex optimization model with a variational-inequality optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection selects the unique point of a closed convex set nearest to a given point; a single variational inequality characterizes the solution.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
Distance is measured with the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_C(z)\) exists uniquely and \(p=P_C(z)\iff p\in C\) and \(\langle z-p,x-p\rangle\le0\) for all \(x\in C\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional projection definition, uniqueness claim, and variational-inequality characterization are mathematically standard and fit the leaf, but no inspectable citation is supplied.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|P_Cx-P_Cy\|_2^2\le\langle P_Cx-P_Cy,x-y\rangle.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global regularity of Euclidean projection onto a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty closed convex \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and all \(x,y\in\mathbb R^n\), \[\|P_Cx-P_Cy\|_2^2\le\langle P_Cx-P_Cy,x-y\rangle.\] Consequently, \(P_C\) is nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a nonempty closed convex set is firmly nonexpansive and therefore 1-Lipschitz, but this general regularity result is canonically housed outside the application-model leaf.
knowledge_statements.title: Firm Nonexpansiveness of Projection

children.title: Set-Distance Models
children.top_down_role: Geometric templates centered on distances between points or sets.

assumptions_latex: \(C,D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) are nonempty, compact, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dist}(C,D)=\max_{\|u\|_2\le1}\{-\sigma_C(-u)-\sigma_D(u)\}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual representation and lower-bound certificates for compact convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C,D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) are nonempty compact convex sets, then \[\operatorname{dist}(C,D)=\max_{\|u\|_2\le1}\left\{\inf_{x\in C}u^{\mathsf T}x-\sup_{y\in D}u^{\mathsf T}y\right\}=\max_{\|u\|_2\le1}\{-\sigma_C(-u)-\sigma_D(u)\}.\] Every feasible \(u\) gives a certified lower bound on the distance; a maximizing \(u\) together with a nearest pair gives matching primal and dual values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For compact convex sets, distance has a unit-ball support-function dual; any feasible dual direction certifies a distance lower bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Support-Function Distance Dual

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dist}(C,D)=\operatorname{dist}(0,C-D),\qquad C\cap D\ne\varnothing\iff0\in C-D.

notation.meaning: Minkowski difference of C and D.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent origin-to-set formulation of distance between two sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty \(C,D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), define \(C-D=\{x-y:x\in C,y\in D\}\). Then \[\operatorname{dist}(C,D)=\inf_{z\in C-D}\|z\|_2=\operatorname{dist}(0,C-D).\] Moreover, \(C\cap D\ne\varnothing\) if and only if \(0\in C-D\). Zero distance implies intersection when \(C-D\) is closed, but not in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set distance is the distance from the origin to the Minkowski difference; intersection is equivalent to the difference containing zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Minkowski-Difference Representation
Set-Distance Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-program representation of distance between two convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty sets \(C,D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), their Euclidean distance is \[\operatorname{dist}(C,D):=\inf_{x\in C,\,y\in D}\|x-y\|_2.\] If \(C\) and \(D\) are convex, this is a convex optimization problem in \((x,y)\). If both sets are closed and at least one is compact, the infimum is attained. Introducing \(t\in\mathbb R\) gives the second-order-cone representation \[\min t\quad\text{subject to }x\in C,\ y\in D,\ \|x-y\|_2\le t.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance between convex sets is the optimal value of a joint convex problem and has a direct second-order-cone epigraph formulation.
assumptions_latex: For attainment, both sets are closed and at least one is compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(C,D)=\min\{t:x\in C,\ y\in D,\ \|x-y\|_2\le t\}\) under the attainment assumptions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The convex distance model, attainment condition, and epigraph formulation are plausible and appropriately classified as a representation, but they have no cited source with a locator.

children.title: Feasibility–Separation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes distinguishing intersecting, separated, or approximately feasible sets.

assumptions_latex: The displayed uniform separation inequalities hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\cap D=\varnothing,\qquad\operatorname{dist}(C,D)\ge(\beta-\alpha)/\|a\|_2.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate interpretation of a positive-margin affine separator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If sets \(C,D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) admit \(a\ne0\) and \(\alpha<\beta\) satisfying \(a^{\mathsf T}c\le\alpha<\beta\le a^{\mathsf T}d\) for every \(c\in C,d\in D\), then \(C\cap D=\varnothing\) and \[\operatorname{dist}(C,D)\ge\frac{\beta-\alpha}{\|a\|_2}>0.\] Thus \((a,\alpha,\beta)\) is a quantitative infeasibility certificate for the intersection system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strict affine separator certifies empty intersection and supplies an explicit positive lower bound on set distance.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Separation Feasibility Alternative

assumptions_latex: \(C\) and \(D\) are the displayed subsets of \(\mathbb R^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\cap D=\varnothing\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{dist}(C,D)=0.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of positive-distance separation and nearest-pair attainment without compactness or a substitute coercivity condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb R^2\), let \[C=\{(x,y):y\ge e^x\},\qquad D=\{(x,0):x\in\mathbb R\}.\] Both sets are nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(C\cap D=\varnothing\). Nevertheless, \(\operatorname{dist}(C,D)=0\), since the distance from \((x,e^x)\in C\) to \((x,0)\in D\) tends to zero as \(x\to-\infty\). Thus no nearest pair or positive-margin separator exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two disjoint closed convex sets can have zero distance when neither is compact, so infeasibility alone does not ensure a positive separation margin.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Disjoint Closed Sets at Zero Distance
knowledge_statements.title: Disjoint Closed Sets at Zero Distance
Feasibility–Separation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intersection-versus-strict-separation alternative derived from nearest points of convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C,D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty closed convex sets, with at least one compact. Exactly one of the following regimes holds: \(C\cap D\ne\varnothing\), in which case \(\operatorname{dist}(C,D)=0\); or \(C\cap D=\varnothing\), in which case nearest points \(c^*\in C\), \(d^*\in D\) exist and \(\delta:=\|d^*-c^*\|_2>0\). In the latter regime, with \(a=d^*-c^*\), \[\sup_{c\in C}a^{\mathsf T}c\le a^{\mathsf T}c^*<a^{\mathsf T}d^*\le\inf_{d\in D}a^{\mathsf T}d,\] so an affine hyperplane strictly separates the sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two closed convex sets, one compact, either intersect or have positive distance and a strict separating hyperplane determined by nearest points.
assumptions_latex: \(C,D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) are nonempty, closed, and convex.
At least one of \(C\) and \(D\) is compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\cap D\ne\varnothing\), or there exist \(a\ne0\) and \(\alpha<\beta\) with \(a^{\mathsf T}c\le\alpha<\beta\le a^{\mathsf T}d\) for all \(c\in C,d\in D\).

notation.meaning: A nearest pair from the two sets.
Normal vector of the separating hyperplane.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The intersection-versus-strict-separation theorem is correct under the stated finite-dimensional compactness assumption, but the theorem and nearest-point construction require an authoritative citation.

children.title: Extremal-Ellipsoid Models
children.top_down_role: Geometric templates for enclosing or inscribed extremal ellipsoids.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contact characterization of the Euclidean ball as a maximum-volume inscribed ellipsoid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a convex body with \(B_2^n\subseteq K\). The unit ball is a maximum-volume ellipsoid in \(K\) if and only if there are \(u_j\in\partial K\cap\mathbb S^{n-1}\) and \(c_j>0\) such that \[\sum_jc_ju_j=0,\qquad\sum_jc_ju_ju_j^{\mathsf T}=I_n.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inscribed unit ball is extremal exactly when weighted contact points balance their first and second moments.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is compact, convex, and has nonempty interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The contact equations are necessary and sufficient for extremality of the unit ball.
review_flags: The nonsymmetric-body form includes the first-moment equation.
knowledge_statements.title: John Contact Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of a positive-volume enclosing optimum without affine spanning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a finite point set lies in a proper affine subspace of \(\mathbb R^n\), full-dimensional enclosing ellipsoids can be compressed arbitrarily in directions orthogonal to that affine hull while retaining all points. Their volumes therefore approach zero, and no positive-definite minimum-volume enclosing ellipsoid is attained in the ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without affine spanning, the ambient minimum-volume enclosing-ellipsoid problem degenerates.
assumptions_latex: The points' affine hull has dimension strictly below \(n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Affine spanning is essential for an attained positive-volume ambient enclosing ellipsoid.
knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Dimensional Enclosing-Ellipsoid Degeneracy

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Log-determinant formulation for an ellipsoid inscribed in a polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\}\) be bounded with nonempty interior and let \(E(c,B)=\{c+Bu:\|u\|_2\le1\}\), where \(B\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\). Then \(E(c,B)\subseteq P\) is equivalent to \[a_i^{\mathsf T}c+\|Ba_i\|_2\le b_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),\] and a maximum-volume inscribed ellipsoid solves \[\max_{c,B\succ0}\log\det B\quad\text{s.t. the displayed inequalities}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum-volume ellipsoid inside a bounded full-dimensional polyhedron has a convex log-determinant formulation.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is bounded and has nonempty interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An optimizer defines a maximum-volume inscribed ellipsoid.

notation.meaning: ellipsoid with center and shape map

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Volume Inscribed Ellipsoid Program

assumptions_latex: \(K\) is compact, convex, and has nonempty interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed contact equations are necessary and sufficient for \(B_2^n\) to be the minimum-volume ellipsoid containing \(K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contact characterization of the Euclidean unit ball as a minimum-volume enclosing ellipsoid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq B_2^n\) be a convex body. The unit ball is a minimum-volume ellipsoid containing \(K\) if and only if there exist contact points \(u_j\in K\cap\mathbb S^{n-1}\) and weights \(c_j>0\) such that \[\sum_j c_j u_j=0,\qquad\sum_j c_j u_j u_j^{\mathsf T}=I_n.\] Taking traces gives \(\sum_jc_j=n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An enclosing unit ball is minimum-volume exactly when weighted contact points balance their first and second moments.
knowledge_statements.title: Löwner Contact Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attained and unique Löwner ellipsoid for an affinely spanning finite set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z_1,\ldots,z_N\in\mathbb R^n\) affinely span \(\mathbb R^n\). For \(A\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^n\), define \(E(A,b)=\{z:\|Az+b\|_2\le1\}\). Since \[\operatorname{vol}(E(A,b))=\operatorname{vol}(B_2^n)(\det A)^{-1},\] the minimum-volume enclosing ellipsoid is obtained from \[\max_{A\succ0,\ b}\ \log\det A\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\|Az_i+b\|_2\le1\quad(i=1,\ldots,N).\] The problem attains its optimum, and the resulting geometric ellipsoid is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affinely spanning points have a unique minimum-volume enclosing ellipsoid, obtained by maximizing log determinant in the inverse-shape parametrization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed convex optimization problem attains an optimum whose ellipsoid is the unique minimum-volume ellipsoid containing all points.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Point Minimum-Volume Enclosing Ellipsoid
Extremal-Ellipsoid Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-volume enclosing ellipsoid model for finitely many points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given points \(z_1,\ldots,z_N\in\mathbb R^n\) whose affine hull is \(\mathbb R^n\), represent an ellipsoid as \[E(A,b):=\{z:\|Az+b\|_2\le1\},\qquad A\in\mathbb S_{++}^n.\] Its volume is proportional to \((\det A)^{-1}\). Hence the unique minimum-volume ellipsoid containing all points is obtained from the convex program \[\operatorname*{maximize}_{A\in\mathbb S_{++}^n,\,b\in\mathbb R^n}\ \log\det A\quad\text{subject to }\|Az_i+b\|_2\le1,\quad i=1,\ldots,N.\] The objective is concave and each containment constraint is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum-volume ellipsoid enclosing finitely many full-dimensional points is computed by maximizing log determinant under convex norm constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((A^*,b^*)\) maximizes \(\log\det A\) subject to \(\|Az_i+b\|_2\le1\), and \(E(A^*,b^*)\) is the minimum-volume enclosing ellipsoid.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The log-determinant formulation fits the extremal-ellipsoid leaf, but neither the formulation nor the asserted uniqueness is supported by a citation with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality certificate for a Euclidean minimum enclosing ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasible Euclidean ball \(B(c,r)\) enclosing \(z_1,�ldots,z_N\) is minimum-radius if and only if there are active indices \(I\subseteq\{j:\|z_j-c\|_2=r\}\) and \(\alpha_j\ge0\) such that \[\sum_{j\in I}\alpha_j=1,\qquad\sum_{j\in I}\alpha_j(z_j-c)=0.\] A certificate with at most \(n+1\) active points exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Euclidean enclosing ball is optimal exactly when its center lies in the convex hull of active boundary points.
assumptions_latex: The candidate ball contains every supplied point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The contact equations certify global minimum radius.
knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Enclosing-Ball Contact Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonempty interior does not ensure a finite largest inscribed ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The halfspace \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:x_1\ge0\}\) is a full-dimensional polyhedron. For every \(r>0\), the Euclidean ball centered at \(re_1\) with radius \(r\) lies in \(P\). Hence its inradius is \(+\infty\) and no largest finite-radius ball exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full-dimensional unbounded polyhedron can contain balls of arbitrarily large radius.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonempty interior alone is insufficient for finite attained inradius.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Inradius Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex circumcenter model for finitely many sites under a norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(z_1,\ldots,z_N\in\mathbb R^n\), \[\min_{c,r}r\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\|z_j-c\|\le r\quad(j=1,\ldots,N)\] is equivalent to minimizing \(c\mapsto\max_j\|z_j-c\|\). For \(N\ge1\), an optimum exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-set circumcenter minimizes the largest norm distance to the supplied points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The program is convex, attains its minimum, and returns the least enclosing norm-ball radius.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimum Enclosing-Ball Center

assumptions_latex: \(\|\cdot\|_*\) is the dual norm of the placement norm.
The displayed primal has a finite optimal value.
Invoking equality through strong duality additionally requires an applicable qualification, such as strict feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and equality \(r=b^{\mathsf T}y\) certify a globally largest inscribed norm ball.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual upper bound and optimality certificate for a largest inscribed norm ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), set \(d_i=\|a_i\|_*\), and consider \[\max_{c,\,r\ge0}r\quad\text{s.t.}\quad a_i^{\mathsf T}c+d_ir\le b_i.\] Its Lagrange dual is \[\min_{y\ge0}b^{\mathsf T}y\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_i y_i a_i=0,\qquad\sum_i y_i d_i\ge1.\] Every dual-feasible \(y\) gives \(r\le b^{\mathsf T}y\) for every primal-feasible \((c,r)\). Equal attained values certify optimality; under an applicable qualification and finite primal optimum, strong duality supplies such equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Balanced nonnegative facet weights bound the inradius and certify a Chebyshev center when their value equals the candidate radius.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Chebyshev-Center Dual Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Largest inscribed norm ball under sufficient existence assumptions and exact facet margins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\) be a compact polyhedron with nonempty interior, and let \(\|\cdot\|_*\) be dual to \(\|\cdot\|\). Then \(c+r\{u:\|u\|\le1\}\subseteq P\) if and only if \[a_i^{\mathsf T}c+r\|a_i\|_*\le b_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,m).\] Consequently a largest inscribed norm ball is obtained from \[\max_{c\in\mathbb R^n,\ r\ge0}r\quad\text{s.t.}\quad a_i^{\mathsf T}c+r\|a_i\|_*\le b_i,\] and an optimizer exists with finite positive radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a compact full-dimensional polyhedron, norm-ball containment is exactly a system of dual-norm facet margins, and maximizing the radius attains a finite inball.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a compact polyhedron with nonempty interior.
\(\|\cdot\|\) is a norm with dual norm \(\|\cdot\|_*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed convex program attains the finite positive inradius of \(P\), and its feasible pairs are exactly the contained norm balls.
knowledge_statements.title: Attained Polyhedral Norm-Incenter Formulation
Convex Centering Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chebyshev-center formulation for a polyhedron under an arbitrary norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), and let \(\|\cdot\|\) have dual norm \(\|\cdot\|_*\). A largest norm ball \(\{c+u:\|u\|\le r\}\) contained in \(P\) is obtained from \[\operatorname*{maximize}_{c\in\mathbb R^n,\,r\ge0}r\quad\text{subject to }a_i^{\mathsf T}c+r\|a_i\|_*\le b_i,\quad i=1,\ldots,m.\] These inequalities are equivalent to containment because \(\sup_{\|u\|\le r}a_i^{\mathsf T}u=r\|a_i\|_*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The largest norm ball inside a polyhedron is found by maximizing its radius subject to one affine margin constraint per facet.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty polyhedron with nonempty interior.
\(\|\cdot\|_*\) is the dual of the chosen placement norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((c^*,r^*)\) solves the displayed convex program if and only if the ball centered at \(c^*\) with radius \(r^*\) is a largest such ball contained in \(P\).

notation.meaning: Center of the inscribed norm ball.
Radius of the inscribed norm ball.

children.title: Enclosure–Centering Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Structural relations between extremal enclosure and center selection.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why unrestricted translated ellipsoids do not obey the simple centered polarity correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(E=c+rB_2^n\) with \(c\ne0\), \(r>0\), and \(0\in\operatorname{int}E\), \[E^\circ=\{y:\langle c,y\rangle+r\|y\|_2\le1\}.\] In dimensions \(n\ge2\), this polar is generally not an ellipsoid. Thus polarity does not map unrestricted translated ellipsoid optimization directly to the same translated-ellipsoid family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of a translated ball is generally not an ellipsoid, so the simple extremal correspondence requires a fixed origin and origin-centered candidates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The origin-centered restriction is essential for the elementary ellipsoid-to-ellipsoid polarity equivalence.
knowledge_statements.title: Translation Boundary for Polar Ellipsoids

assumptions_latex: \(K\) is compact, convex, and has nonempty interior.
\(E\) is a maximum-volume ellipsoid contained in \(K\).
The \(\sqrt n\) variant additionally assumes that \(K\) is centrally symmetric about the center of \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The extremal inscribed ellipsoid approximates \(K\) from both sides within factor \(n\), or \(\sqrt n\) in the centrally symmetric case.

notation.meaning: homothety of the ellipsoid by factor \(\alpha\) about its center

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative enclosure loss when an extremal inscribed ellipsoid is reused as an outer approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a convex body and let \(E\) be its maximum-volume inscribed ellipsoid, with homotheties taken about the center of \(E\). Then \[E\subseteq K\subseteq nE.\] If \(K\) is centrally symmetric about that center, then the sharper inclusion \[E\subseteq K\subseteq\sqrt n\,E\] holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximum-volume inscribed ellipsoid also gives a dimension-dependent outer enclosure, with a sharper factor for centrally symmetric bodies.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: John Enclosure Bounds from an Inscribed Extremal Ellipsoid
knowledge_statements.title: John Enclosure Bounds from an Inscribed Extremal Ellipsoid

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correct boundary of the simple reciprocal-volume polarity correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=c+rB_2^n\) with \(\|c\|_2<r\). Its polar is the ellipsoid \[E^\circ=\{y:y^{\mathsf T}(r^2I-cc^{\mathsf T})y+2c^{\mathsf T}y\le1\}.\] Although polarity therefore preserves the ellipsoid family, \[\operatorname{vol}(E)\operatorname{vol}(E^\circ)=\operatorname{vol}(B_2^n)^2\left(1-\frac{\|c\|_2^2}{r^2}\right)^{-(n+1)/2},\] which depends on the translation and equals the centered constant only when \(c=0\). Thus unrestricted translated extremal problems are not converted by the centered constant-volume-product argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarity preserves translated ellipsoids containing the origin, but their volume product varies with translation, so the simple centered extremal equivalence does not extend unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Origin centering is essential to the constant-volume-product argument, not to preservation of the ellipsoid family itself.
knowledge_statements.title: Translated-Ellipsoid Volume-Product Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact conversion between origin-centered inscribed and enclosing extremal-ellipsoid problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) be compact and convex with \(0\in\operatorname{int}K\). For \(Q\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\), write \(E_Q=Q^{1/2}B_2^n\). Then \(E_Q^\circ=E_{Q^{-1}}\), \[E_Q\subseteq K\iff K^\circ\subseteq E_{Q^{-1}},\] and \[\operatorname{vol}(E_Q)\operatorname{vol}(E_Q^\circ)=\operatorname{vol}(B_2^n)^2.\] Hence \(E_Q\) maximizes volume among origin-centered ellipsoids contained in \(K\) if and only if \(E_{Q^{-1}}\) minimizes volume among origin-centered ellipsoids containing \(K^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarity reverses containment, inverts the shape matrix, and gives a constant volume product for origin-centered ellipsoids, exchanging centered maximum-inscribed and minimum-enclosing problems.
assumptions_latex: All candidate ellipsoids are centered at the origin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: E_Q\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{\substack{E\subseteq K\\E\text{ origin-centered ellipsoid}}}\operatorname{vol}(E)\iff E_{Q^{-1}}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\substack{G\supseteq K^\circ\\G\text{ origin-centered ellipsoid}}}\operatorname{vol}(G).
knowledge_statements.title: Centered Extremal-Ellipsoid Polarity Equivalence
Enclosure–Centering Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polarity duality between origin-centered enclosing and inscribed ellipsoids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a compact convex set with \(0\in\operatorname{int}K\), and restrict attention to origin-centered ellipsoids. For \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), define \(S^\circ:=\{y:\sup_{x\in S}y^{\mathsf T}x\le1\}\). Polarity reverses containment: \(E\subseteq K\) if and only if \(K^\circ\subseteq E^\circ\). Moreover, for every origin-centered ellipsoid \(E\), \(\operatorname{vol}(E)\operatorname{vol}(E^\circ)=\operatorname{vol}(B_2^n)^2\). Therefore \(E\) is a maximum-volume origin-centered ellipsoid contained in \(K\) if and only if \(E^\circ\) is a minimum-volume origin-centered ellipsoid containing \(K^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For origin-centered ellipsoids, polarity converts maximum-volume inscribed problems into minimum-volume enclosing problems while reversing containment.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) is compact and convex with \(0\in\operatorname{int}K\).
All candidate ellipsoids are centered at the origin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{F\subseteq K}\operatorname{vol}(F)\iff E^\circ\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{G\supseteq K^\circ}\operatorname{vol}(G)\), over origin-centered ellipsoids.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The origin-centered polarity duality and volume-product statement are mathematically plausible and fit the duality leaf, but no authoritative locator supports them.

children.title: Continuous Facility Location
children.top_down_role: Convex location templates with continuously selectable facility positions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subgradient certificate for unconstrained weighted Euclidean facility location.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=\sum_iw_i\|x-a_i\|_2\), \(x^*\) minimizes \(F\) if and only if \[0\in\sum_{i:a_i\ne x^*}w_i\frac{x^*-a_i}{\|x^*-a_i\|_2}+\sum_{i:a_i=x^*}w_iB_2^n.\] If no positive-weight site equals \(x^*\), this reduces to equality of the first sum with zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted geometric median is certified by balanced unit directions, with unit-ball subgradients at coincident sites.
assumptions_latex: \(w_i\ge0\) and at least one weight is positive.
The location is unconstrained in \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inclusion is necessary and sufficient for global optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Geometric-Median Optimality Test

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order-cone representation of weighted Euclidean single-facility location.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(w_i\ge0\), \[\min_{x\in C}\sum_iw_i\|x-a_i\|_2\] is equivalent to \[\min_{x,t}\sum_iw_it_i\quad\text{s.t.}\quad(t_i,x-a_i)\in\mathcal Q_{n+1},\quad x\in C,\] where \(\mathcal Q_{n+1}=\{(t,u):\|u\|_2\le t\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted Euclidean facility location has one second-order-cone distance epigraph per demand point.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) has an exact conic representation if a complete SOCP is required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The formulations have equal values and the same optimal location variables whenever an optimum exists.
knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Facility-Location SOCP

assumptions_latex: The location variable ranges over \(\mathbb R^n\).
Every retained weight is strictly positive.
The uniqueness conclusion assumes that the retained sites are not contained in one affine line.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Noncollinearity implies a unique Euclidean geometric median; collinearity does not guarantee uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict-convexity criterion for the unconstrained weighted Euclidean single-facility problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m w_i\|x-a_i\|_2\), where every retained weight satisfies \(w_i>0\). If the positive-weight sites are not all contained in one affine line, then \(F\) is strictly convex and has a unique minimizer. Collinearity permits nonuniqueness: for two distinct sites with equal positive weights, every point on their joining segment is optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Noncollinear positive-weight Euclidean demand sites give a unique geometric median, while collinear data can have a segment of minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniqueness of a Noncollinear Euclidean Geometric Median
knowledge_statements.title: Uniqueness of a Noncollinear Euclidean Geometric Median

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specialized iteration for the unconstrained weighted Euclidean single-facility problem, including demand-site handling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For distinct sites \(a_i\) with weights \(w_i>0\), define, when \(x
otin\{a_i\}\), \[T(x)= rac{\sum_i w_i a_i/\|x-a_i\|_2}{\sum_i w_i/\|x-a_i\|_2}.\] The classical Weiszfeld iteration is \(x^{k+1}=T(x^k)\). At a site \(a_j\), set \[R_j=\sum_{i
e j}w_i rac{a_i-a_j}{\|a_i-a_j\|_2}.\] If \(\|R_j\|_2\le w_j\), then \(a_j\) is optimal. Otherwise let \[T_j= rac{\sum_{i
e j}w_i a_i/\|a_j-a_i\|_2}{\sum_{i
e j}w_i/\|a_j-a_i\|_2},\qquad \eta_j= rac{w_j}{\|R_j\|_2},\] and use the vertex-safe update \(x^+=\eta_j a_j+(1-\eta_j)T_j\). Coincident sites are first merged by adding their weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weiszfeld iteration repeatedly forms an inverse-distance weighted average; at a demand site, an optimality test either stops or a modified convex-combination step avoids division by zero.
assumptions_latex: The problem is unconstrained and uses the Euclidean norm.
All retained weights are strictly positive.
Coincident sites are aggregated before applying the displayed formulas.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed rule is well-defined away from sites and supplies a valid site-safe continuation whenever a reached site fails the geometric-median optimality test.
review_flags: The update is specific to unconstrained Euclidean geometric medians; constrained and non-Euclidean variants require different steps.
knowledge_statements.title: Classical and Vertex-Safe Weiszfeld Updates

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conditional Convergence of Classical Weiszfeld Iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence and singular-site boundary for the classical unconstrained Euclidean iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the positive-weight sites are not all collinear. If \(x^0\notin\{a_i\}\) and no classical Weiszfeld iterate reaches a site, then the sequence \(x^{k+1}=T(x^k)\) converges to the unique minimizer of \(F(x)=\sum_iw_i\|x-a_i\|_2\). If an iterate reaches a nonoptimal site, the classical formula is undefined and this conclusion cannot be invoked without a vertex-safe modification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For noncollinear Euclidean data, classical Weiszfeld iterates converge to the unique geometric median provided they never hit a demand site; hitting a nonoptimal site is the algorithm's singular boundary.
assumptions_latex: Every retained weight is strictly positive.
The positive-weight sites are not contained in one affine line.
The initial point and every classical iterate avoid the demand sites.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^k\to x^*,\qquad x^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\sum_iw_i\|x-a_i\|_2.
review_flags: A source locator is desirable for the named algorithm's convergence theorem.
The statement deliberately does not claim convergence of every modified Weiszfeld variant.
knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Convergence of Classical Weiszfeld Iteration

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity and attainment of weighted continuous facility location on a closed region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R^n\), \(w_i\ge0\), \(W=\sum_iw_i>0\), let \(\|\cdot\|\) be any norm, and let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and closed. Then \[F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m w_i\|x-a_i\|\] is finite, continuous, and convex, and satisfies \[F(x)\ge W\|x\|-\sum_iw_i\|a_i\|.\] Thus \(F\) is coercive and \(\min_{x\in C}F(x)\) attains its minimum. If \(C\) is convex, this is a convex optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive total demand weight makes the arbitrary-norm distance objective coercive, so it attains an optimum on every nonempty closed region and is a convex program when that region is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\sum_iw_i\|x-a_i\|\ne\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.title: Coercive Arbitrary-Norm Single-Facility Model
Continuous Facility Location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted single-facility location over a continuous convex feasible region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given demand points \(a_1,ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R^n\), weights \(w_i\ge0\), a norm \(\|\cdot\|\), and a nonempty closed convex region \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), the continuous single-facility location model is \[\operatorname*{minimize}_{x\in C}\ \sum_{i=1}^m w_i\|x-a_i\|.\] Its objective is convex. If \(C\) is compact, or if \(\sum_iw_i>0\) and \(C\) is unbounded but closed, an optimal location exists because the objective is respectively continuous on a compact set or coercive along unbounded feasible sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous facility location chooses any point in a convex region minimizing the weighted sum of norm distances to demand points.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in C}\sum_{i=1}^m w_i\|x-a_i\|\) is a convex optimization model and attains its minimum under the stated assumptions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Average individual-expense bound for continuous location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded consequence of the preceding smoothed continuous-location guarantee; the extract does not independently specify the algorithm producing \(\hat x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the preceding continuous-location algorithmic setup,
\[
f(\hat{x})-f^*\leq \frac{2P\bar r}{\sqrt{N(N+1)}}.
\]
If \(P>0\), \(\bar f=f/P\), and \(\bar f^*=f^*/P\), then
\[
\bar f(\hat{x})-\bar f^*\leq \frac{2\bar r}{\sqrt{N(N+1)}}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the preceding algorithmic setup, the total location-objective error is bounded by 2P times the radius divided by the square root of N(N+1). Normalizing the objective by the positive quantity P yields the corresponding average individual-expense bound.
assumptions_latex: \text{The preceding smoothed continuous-location guarantee applies to }\hat x\text{ and }N
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(\hat{x})-f^*\leq \frac{2P\bar r}{\sqrt{N(N+1)}}\quad\text{and}\quad \bar f(\hat{x})-\bar f^*\leq \frac{2\bar r}{\sqrt{N(N+1)}}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the Euclidean facility-location model and the quadratic prox geometry selected for its radius-bounded feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given city locations \(c_j\in\mathbb R^n\) and population weights \(m_j\), \(j=1,\ldots,p\), define
\[
f^*=\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\left\{\sum_{j=1}^p m_j\|x-c_j\|_2:\ \|x\|_2\leq\bar r\right\}.
\]
For the prox-function \(d_1(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|_2^2\), the associated parameter on this ball is
\[
D_1=\tfrac12\bar r^2.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A service center is chosen inside the Euclidean ball of radius r-bar to minimize the population-weighted sum of Euclidean distances to the cities. With the squared Euclidean prox-function, the associated prox parameter is one half of r-bar squared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^*=\min_{\|x\|_2\leq\bar r}\sum_{j=1}^p m_j\|x-c_j\|_2,\qquad D_1=\frac12\bar r^2

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted Euclidean single-facility location model with the facility restricted to a centered Euclidean ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let p\in\mathbb{N}, m_j>0, and c_j\in\mathbb{R}^n for j=1,\ldots,p. With the Euclidean norm, define f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^p m_j\|x-c_j\|_2. Given \bar r>0, the constrained location problem is f^*=\min\{f(x):x\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ \|x\|_2\le\bar r\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given positively weighted demand points in Euclidean space and a positive radius, the constrained continuous location problem minimizes the weighted sum of distances from a facility to the demand points while requiring the facility to lie in the centered ball of that radius.

children.title: Convex Placement Models
children.top_down_role: Spatial placement templates retaining convex feasible structure.

assumptions_latex: Each displacement map \(x\mapsto A_ix-a_i\) is affine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The simultaneous placement set \(S\) is convex.

notation.meaning: set of placements satisfying all service requirements

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Placement as an intersection of convex service regions around prescribed sites.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and, for each site \(a_i\), let \(g_i:\mathbb R^{q_i}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex, let \(A_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^{q_i}\) be linear, and let \(\rho_i\in\mathbb R\). Then \[S=C\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x:g_i(A_ix-a_i)\le\rho_i\}\] is convex. Thus simultaneous convex service requirements define a convex feasibility problem; when \(g_i(u)=\|u\|\), the service regions are affine preimages of norm balls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersecting a convex placement region with convex service regions around prescribed sites preserves convex feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Service-Region Placement Feasibility

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proper Convex Placement Objective and Epigraph Lift
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General affine-displacement placement template with explicit domain and zero-weight conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, let \(f_0:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(\phi_i:\mathbb R^{q_i}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex functions, let \(A_i\) be linear, and let \(w_i>0\) for retained terms. Define \[F(x)=f_0(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m w_i\phi_i(A_ix-a_i)+\delta_C(x).\] If some \(\bar x\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}f_0\) satisfies \(A_i\bar x-a_i\in\operatorname{dom}\phi_i\) for every \(i\), then \(F\) is proper and convex. Minimizing \(F\) is equivalent to \[\min_{x,t}\ f_0(x)+\sum_iw_it_i\quad\text{s.t.}\quad x\in C,\quad \phi_i(A_ix-a_i)\le t_i.\] Terms assigned zero weight are omitted before extended-real evaluation, avoiding \(0\cdot(+\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex base cost plus positive-weight convex penalties of affine displacements gives a proper convex placement objective when their domains meet, and epigraph variables give an equivalent lift.
assumptions_latex: \(f_0\) and every retained \(\phi_i\) are proper convex functions.
Every retained weight is strictly positive.
A common finite feasible placement \(\bar x\) exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is proper and convex, and the original and lifted problems have the same feasible }x\text{-projections, values, and minimizers}.

notation.meaning: convex indicator of the placement region

knowledge_statements.title: Proper Convex Placement Objective and Epigraph Lift
Convex Placement Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General convex template for placing an object relative to sites and convex restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex. For sites \(a_i\in\mathbb R^n\), affine maps \(A_i\), nonnegative weights \(w_i\), and proper convex penalties \(\phi_i\), a convex placement model has the form \[\operatorname*{minimize}_{x\in C}\ f(x):=f_0(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m w_i\phi_i(A_ix-a_i),\] where \(f_0\) is convex. The objective is convex by affine composition and nonnegative summation. Epigraph variables \(t_i\) give the equivalent formulation \[\min f_0(x)+\sum_iw_it_i\quad\text{subject to }x\in C,\ \phi_i(A_ix-a_i)\le t_i.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex placement minimizes a convex base cost plus weighted convex penalties of affine displacement from prescribed sites.
assumptions_latex: \(f_0\) and every \(\phi_i\) are proper convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=f_0(x)+\sum_iw_i\phi_i(A_ix-a_i)\) is convex, and its epigraph formulation is equivalent whenever the problem has finite feasible value.

children.title: Discrete-Site Boundary
children.top_down_role: Loss of direct convexity when placement is restricted to discrete candidate sites.

assumptions_latex: Every value \(f(s_i)\) can be evaluated and compared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(s_{i^*})=\min_{s\in S}f(s),\qquad \text{time}=O(mT_f).

notation.meaning: Uniform upper bound on the cost of evaluating the objective at one site.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact solution of an explicitly listed finite-site location problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{s_1,\ldots,s_m\}\) be an explicitly listed nonempty set and let \(f:S\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\). Evaluating \(f(s_i)\) for every site and returning any \(s_{i^*}\) with \(i^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{1\le i\le m}f(s_i)\) solves \(\min_{s\in S}f(s)\) exactly. The inequalities \(f(s_{i^*})\le f(s_i)\) for all \(i\) form a complete optimality certificate. If one evaluation costs at most \(T_f\), exhaustive solution takes \(O(mT_f)\) time and \(O(1)\) additional words when sites are streamed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explicitly listed finite-site problem is solved exactly by evaluating every site; comparison with every candidate certifies global optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Site Enumeration and Certificate
Discrete-Site Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of convexity when a facility must be selected from a finite site set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Convexity of a placement objective does not make discrete-site selection a convex program. For example, let the admissible sites be \(S=\{-1,1\}\subset\mathbb R\) and let \(f(x)=x^2\). The discrete problem satisfies \[\min_{x\in S}f(x)=1.\] Replacing \(S\) by its convex hull gives \[\min_{x\in[-1,1]}f(x)=0,\] attained at \(x=0\notin S\). Thus convex-hull relaxation can have a strict integrality gap, and continuous convex placement methods alone do not solve the discrete-site model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting a convex placement problem to finitely many sites destroys convex feasibility; convex-hull relaxation can return an infeasible point with a strict gap.
assumptions_latex: The admissible location set is the finite set \(S=\{-1,1\}\).
The placement loss is the convex function \(f(x)=x^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in S}x^2=1>0=\min_{x\in\operatorname{conv}S}x^2\).

notation.meaning: Finite set of admissible facility sites.
Convex-hull relaxation of the site set.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit example correctly demonstrates a strict convex-hull relaxation gap and the failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but the broader discrete-site boundary claim has no cited evidence.

assumptions_latex: Blocks are required not to overlap.
Relative horizontal or vertical precedence is not fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal F_{\mathrm{nonoverlap}}\text{ is generally nonconvex}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between a fixed-precedence convex interface and combinatorial floor planning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For two axis-aligned rectangles \(i\) and \(j\), nonoverlap requires the disjunction \[x_i+w_i\le x_j\ \lor\ x_j+w_j\le x_i\ \lor\ y_i+h_i\le y_j\ \lor\ y_j+h_j\le y_i.\] If no branch is fixed, the feasible set is generally a union of convex sets and need not be convex. For two unit intervals on a line, placements \((x_i,x_j)=(0,1)\) and \((1,0)\) are feasible, while their midpoint \((1/2,1/2)\) overlaps and is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unfixed rectangle nonoverlap is disjunctive and generally nonconvex; fixing precedence exposes the convex interface.
knowledge_statements.title: Unfixed Nonoverlap Disjunction

assumptions_latex: All nonoverlap precedence choices are fixed data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: w_ih_i\ge A_i\iff (w_i,h_i,\sqrt{2A_i})\in\mathcal Q_r^3.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact conic representation of positive rectangular-block area constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A_i>0\), the constraint \(w_i\ge0,\ h_i\ge0,\ w_ih_i\ge A_i\) is equivalent to \[(w_i,h_i,\sqrt{2A_i})\in\mathcal Q_r^3:=\{(u,v,z):u\ge0,\ v\ge0,\ 2uv\ge z^2\}.\] Hence, after relative ordering is fixed, the block-area, containment, and precedence constraints form an SOCP-representable feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each positive rectangle-area lower bound has an exact rotated-second-order-cone representation, so fixed-order floor planning is conic-representable.
knowledge_statements.title: Rotated-Cone Area Interface
Floor-Planning Convex Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex floor-planning model under fixed horizontal-or-vertical relative ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For rectangular blocks \(i=1,\ldots,N\), choose lower-left coordinates \((x_i,y_i)\), positive dimensions \((w_i,h_i)\), and floor dimensions \((W,H)\). Given areas \(A_i>0\) and a fixed nonoverlap ordering, impose \[w_ih_i\ge A_i,\quad 0\le x_i,\quad x_i+w_i\le W,\quad 0\le y_i,\quad y_i+h_i\le H,\] together with either \(x_i+w_i\le x_j\) or \(y_i+h_i\le y_j\) for every ordered pair. The feasible set is convex because \(w_ih_i\ge A_i\) is equivalent to \(\log w_i+\log h_i\ge\log A_i\). Minimizing any convex nondecreasing function of \((W,H)\) is therefore a convex floor-planning interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With relative block ordering fixed, variable rectangle dimensions, area requirements, containment, and a convex floor-size objective form a convex program.
assumptions_latex: A horizontal or vertical precedence relation is fixed for each pair requiring nonoverlap.
The floor-size objective is convex and coordinatewise nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed floor-planning feasible set is convex, so minimizing a convex nondecreasing function of \((W,H)\) is a convex optimization problem.

notation.meaning: Positive width and height of block i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: With one precedence choice fixed for each relevant pair, the displayed positive-dimension area constraints and linear ordering constraints define a convex feasible set. The model nevertheless lacks a source supporting this exact fixed-ordering interface.
