children.title: Objective Template Scope
children.top_down_role: Reusable objective structures retained within the chapter.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective Template Scope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-valued convex objective assembled from a base term, affine-composed penalties, and feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\in\mathbb N\), let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(f_0:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) and \(\phi_i:\mathbb R^{p_i}\to\mathbb R\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), be finite continuous convex functions. For each \(i\), let \(A_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^{p_i}\) be linear, let \(b_i\in\mathbb R^{p_i}\), and let \(\lambda_i\ge0\). An objective template in this scope is \[F(x):=f_0(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\phi_i(A_ix+b_i)+\delta_C(x),\] where \(\delta_C(x)=0\) for \(x\in C\) and \(\delta_C(x)=+\infty\) otherwise. Then \(F\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex, and minimizing \(F\) over \(\mathbb R^n\) is equivalent to minimizing \(f_0(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\phi_i(A_ix+b_i)\) over \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective scope consists of a finite continuous convex base cost, nonnegative affine-composed convex penalties, and feasibility encoded by the indicator of a nonempty closed convex set. The resulting extended-valued objective is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex.
assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb N\) and \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(f_0:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) and \(\phi_i:\mathbb R^{p_i}\to\mathbb R\) are finite continuous convex functions.
\(A_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^{p_i}\) is linear, \(b_i\in\mathbb R^{p_i}\), and \(\lambda_i\ge0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=f_0+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\bigl(\phi_i\circ(A_i\,\cdot+b_i)\bigr)+\delta_C\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex.

notation.meaning: Convex indicator of the feasible set C.
Linear map and translation vector defining the ith affine argument.

children.title: Loss Template Scope
children.top_down_role: Reusable loss families retained within the chapter.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite aggregation rules for reusable extended-valued loss templates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\ell_j:Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), \(j=1,\ldots,m\), be proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions with \(\bigcap_j\operatorname{dom}\ell_j\neq\varnothing\), and let \(\lambda_j>0\). Then \(\max_j\ell_j\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex, while \(\sum_j\lambda_j\ell_j\) is proper and convex. The weighted sum is also lower-semicontinuous, and hence a loss template of the same class, whenever all \(\ell_j\) are finite and continuous on \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite maxima preserve proper closed convex losses under common-domain compatibility. Positive weighted sums are proper and convex, and remain closed under an explicit continuity qualification.
assumptions_latex: Each \(\ell_j\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex.
For the weighted-sum closedness conclusion, every \(\ell_j\) is finite and continuous on \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_j\ell_j\) is a proper lower-semicontinuous convex loss; \(\sum_j\lambda_j\ell_j\) is proper and convex and is continuous under the stated additional hypothesis.

notation.meaning: Effective domain of the jth loss.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Loss Aggregation Closure
Loss Template Scope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines convex losses admissible in an objective template.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space and let \(\overline{\mathbb R}=\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\). A loss template is a proper, lower-semicontinuous convex function \(\ell:Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), possibly parameterized by observed data. For an affine prediction map \(p(x)=Ax+b\), the instantiated loss \(x\mapsto \ell(p(x))\) is a proper convex objective term whenever its effective domain \(\{x:p(x)\in\operatorname{dom}\ell\}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A loss template is a proper closed convex function; composing it with an affine prediction map yields a convex objective term when the resulting domain is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\mapsto\ell(Ax+b)\) is proper and convex.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The affine-composition claim is standard, but no source is cited. The domain of x and the compatible domains of A and b are also not introduced explicitly.

children.title: Objective–Loss Composition Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits on combining application objectives with reusable loss templates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar failure of convexity when outer monotonicity is absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g(x)=x^2-1\) and \(\ell(t)=t^2\). Both are convex on \(\mathbb R\), but \((\ell\circ g)(x)=(x^2-1)^2\) is not convex; its second derivative at zero is \(-4\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity of the outer and inner functions alone does not ensure convexity of their composition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell\) and \(g\) are convex, but \(\ell\circ g\) is not convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex-with-Convex Composition Failure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise curvature and monotonicity conditions sufficient for convex loss composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, let \(g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m):C\to\mathbb R^m\), and let \(\ell:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) be convex. Partition the coordinates as \(I_+\cup I_-\). If \(\ell\) is nondecreasing in each coordinate in \(I_+\), nonincreasing in each coordinate in \(I_-\), each \(g_i\) is convex for \(i\in I_+\), and each \(g_i\) is concave for \(i\in I_-\), then \(\ell\circ g\) is convex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex outer loss may combine convex increasing coordinates and concave decreasing coordinates in one inner map.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell\) is finite convex and has the stated global coordinatewise monotonicities.
Each inner coordinate has the matching curvature.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\mapsto\ell(g(x))\) is convex on \(C\).

notation.meaning: Coordinates on which the outer loss is nondecreasing.
Coordinates on which the outer loss is nonincreasing.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Monotonicity Composition Rule
Objective–Loss Composition Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies when a convex loss preserves convexity under composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, let \(g:C\to\mathbb R^m\), and let \(\ell:\mathbb R^m\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be convex. Convexity of \(\ell\circ g\) is guaranteed if \(g\) is affine. More generally, it is guaranteed componentwise when every \(g_i\) is convex and \(\ell\) is nondecreasing in each argument on \(g(C)\). Without such affine or monotonicity-compatible curvature conditions, convexity of both \(\ell\) and the components of \(g\) does not by itself imply convexity of \(\ell\circ g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex loss safely composes with an affine map, or with convex components under coordinatewise monotonicity; otherwise convexity need not be preserved.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell\) is convex on a convex set containing \(g(C)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated affine or monotone-composition conditions imply convexity of \(\ell\circ g\); absent them, no general guarantee holds.

notation.meaning: the ith component of the inner map
extended real line without negative infinity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The affine case and failure boundary are standard, but the nonlinear composition condition requires monotonicity on an appropriate domain containing the relevant inner values, not merely an unqualified assertion on g(C). An authoritative composition-rule source is required.

children.title: Regularizer Template Scope
children.top_down_role: Reusable convex regularization structures retained within the chapter.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}(\lambda R)=\operatorname{dom}R\) for \(\lambda>0\), while \(\lambda=0\) requires an explicit modeling convention.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safe treatment of a disabled extended-valued regularizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\lambda>0\), scaling a proper extended-valued convex regularizer preserves its effective domain. At \(\lambda=0\), \(0\cdot(+\infty)\) has no convention-independent optimization meaning. The model must explicitly remove the disabled term or retain the intended hard restriction separately, for example through \(\delta_{\operatorname{dom}R}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive scaling preserves an extended-valued regularizer's domain; zero weight requires an explicit choice between removing the term and retaining its hard restriction.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Weight Extended-Value Boundary
Regularizer Template Scope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines proper convex penalties used to encode structural preference.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a finite-dimensional real vector space \(X\), a regularizer template is a proper, lower-semicontinuous convex function \(R:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\). For \(\lambda\ge 0\), it contributes the term \(\lambda R(x)\) to a convex objective. Extended values may encode hard structural restrictions through \(R(x)=+\infty\); for \(\lambda=0\), the product is interpreted as the zero function only when no such restriction is intended.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regularizer template is a proper closed convex penalty, optionally extended-valued, scaled by a nonnegative weight in a convex objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\mapsto\lambda R(x)\) is convex under the stated convention.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The regularizer definition is plausible, but the treatment of zero times an extended-valued function is convention-dependent and no authoritative source is supplied.

children.title: Low-Complexity Template Scope
children.top_down_role: Reusable templates promoting sparse, low-rank, or otherwise parsimonious structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{Ax=b}\|x\|_1\) contains both one-sparse and dense points.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates convex promotion of low complexity from unconditional exact recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A=[1\;1]\) and \(b=1\), every \(x=(t,1-t)\) with \(0\le t\le1\) minimizes \(\|x\|_1\) subject to \(Ax=b\). Thus the solution set contains the dense point \((1/2,1/2)\) although one-sparse feasible points exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex surrogate can have dense minimizers even when sparse feasible solutions exist, so exact recovery requires additional assumptions.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Surrogate Exactness Boundary

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\) is compact, centrally symmetric, and spans \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_{\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)}\) is a norm and \(\|z\|_{\mathcal A}^*=\max_{a\in\mathcal A}\langle z,a\rangle\).

notation.meaning: gauge of the atomic convex hull

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm criterion and polar representation for an atomic low-complexity template.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\mathcal A\subset X\) is compact, centrally symmetric, and spanning, then \(\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)\) is the unit ball of the atomic norm \(\|x\|_{\mathcal A}=\gamma_{\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)}(x)\), whose dual norm is \(\|z\|_{\mathcal A}^*=\max_{a\in\mathcal A}\langle z,a\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact symmetric spanning atomic family generates a norm whose dual is the largest pairing with an atom.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Atomic Norm Criterion and Dual Norm
knowledge_statements.title: Atomic Norm Criterion and Dual Norm

assumptions_latex: The ambient vector and matrix spaces are finite-dimensional.
Rank-one atoms use unit Euclidean norms for both factors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_{\operatorname{conv}\{\pm e_i\}}(x)=\|x\|_1\) and \(\gamma_{\operatorname{conv}\{uv^{\mathsf T}:\|u\|_2=\|v\|_2=1\}}(X)=\|X\|_*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixes the normalization and symmetry conventions for the canonical sparse and low-rank atomic gauges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For vectors, the gauge generated by the signed coordinate atoms \(\mathcal A_1=\{\pm e_i\}\) is \(\|x\|_1\). For real matrices, the gauge generated by \(\mathcal A_*=\{uv^{\mathsf T}:\|u\|_2=\|v\|_2=1\}\) is the nuclear norm; this atom family is centrally symmetric because changing the sign of either factor changes the sign of the atom.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Signed unit coordinate atoms generate the l1 norm, while unit-factor rank-one matrix atoms generate the nuclear norm.
knowledge_statements.title: Normalized Atomic Examples
Low-Complexity Template Scope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies convex surrogates for sparse, low-rank, or atomic structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be finite-dimensional and let \(\mathcal A\subset X\) be a compact set of elementary atoms whose convex hull contains the origin. The associated low-complexity template is the gauge \[\gamma_{\mathcal A}(x)=\inf\{t\ge 0:x\in t\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)\}.\] It is convex and positively homogeneous on its effective domain. Choosing signed coordinate atoms gives the \(\ell_1\)-norm, while choosing unit-norm rank-one matrix atoms gives the nuclear norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Low-complexity templates are convex atomic gauges; standard choices recover sparsity-promoting l1 norms and rank-promoting nuclear norms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_{\mathcal A}\) is a convex, positively homogeneous extended-real-valued function.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The gauge construction is mathematically plausible, but the nuclear-norm example must specify the rank-one atom normalization and symmetry/sign convention. No source supports the construction or examples.

children.title: Structural-Prior Interface
children.top_down_role: Handoff between generic convex penalties and application-specific structural meaning.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convexity of \(R_Q\) does not determine which coordinate system carries the intended sparsity prior.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates convex optimization compatibility from validity of an intended structural interpretation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Convexity of \(R\) does not imply that \(R\) measures the intended structure. For an orthogonal matrix \(Q\), \(R_Q(x)=\|Qx\|_1\) promotes sparsity in the \(Q\)-coordinate system, which generally differs from sparsity of \(x\) in the original coordinates. The structural class, representation, and calibration must therefore be declared independently of convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex penalty is computationally compatible but is not automatically a valid structural prior; even l1 sparsity depends on the declared coordinates.
knowledge_statements.title: Prior-Validity Boundary
Structural-Prior Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Connects a structural model to a convex regularizer and admissible parameter domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq X\) denote a modeled structural class and let \(R:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be a convex regularizer. A valid structural-prior interface specifies a convex admissible set \(C\subseteq\operatorname{dom}R\), a weight \(\lambda\ge0\), and a calibration rule such that structurally simpler points receive no larger intended penalty. Concretely, for a declared complexity preorder \(\preceq_S\), compatibility requires \[x\preceq_S y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad R(x)\le R(y)\] whenever \(x,y\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A structural prior is interfaced through a convex domain, regularizer, weight, and calibration whose penalty order agrees with the declared complexity order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\preceq_S y\) implies \(R(x)\le R(y)\) for \(x,y\in C\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The preorder-based compatibility condition is a proposed interface convention rather than a standard consequence of convex regularization. Its calibration semantics require an authoritative source or explicit project convention.

children.title: Constraint Template Scope
children.top_down_role: Reusable convex constraint structures retained within the chapter.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Template Scope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines convex inequality and affine equality templates, including indexed families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex. A convex constraint template consists of inequalities \(f_i(x)\le0\), where each \(f_i:C\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is convex, together with affine equalities \(Ax=b\). An indexed robust family \(f(x,u)\le0\) is within scope when, for every fixed \(u\) in its uncertainty set, the map \(x\mapsto f(x,u)\) is convex. The resulting feasible set is convex, including for infinite index sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex constraint templates use convex inequalities and affine equalities; pointwise convex uncertain families also define convex feasible sets.
assumptions_latex: Each inequality function is convex in the decision variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x\in C:f_i(x)\le0\ \forall i,\ Ax=b\}\) is convex.

source_refs.locator: 2.3 Tractability of Robust Counterpart p. 40

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3 Tractability of Robust Counterpart p. 40

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar examples delimiting admissible convex inequalities and equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=x^2-1\), the sublevel set \(\{x:f(x)\le0\}=[-1,1]\) is convex, whereas \(\{x:f(x)\ge0\}=(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)\) and \(\{x:f(x)=0\}=\{-1,1\}\) are nonconvex. Thus convexity of \(f\) does not generally validate a reversed inequality or nonlinear equality; affine equalities always define convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reversing a convex inequality or imposing a nonlinear convex equality can destroy feasible-set convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convexity of \(f\) alone does not make \(f(x)\ge0\) or \(f(x)=0\) a convex constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Orientation and Equality Boundary

children.title: Robust-Counterpart Scope
children.top_down_role: Reusable robust reformulation interfaces retained within the chapter.

knowledge_statements.title: Robust-Counterpart Scope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the exact worst-case reformulation of an uncertain scalar constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be a nonempty uncertainty set and suppose \(x\mapsto f(x,u)\) is convex for every \(u\in U\). The robust counterpart of the uncertain constraint \(f(x,u)\le0\) for all \(u\in U\) is the deterministic constraint \[\phi(x):=\sup_{u\in U}f(x,u)\le0.\] The function \(\phi\) is convex as a pointwise supremum of convex functions. This representation is exact, although a finite conic reformulation exists only for suitable structures of \(f\) and \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An uncertain constraint is exactly its worst-case supremum constraint; this is convex in the decision but not necessarily tractably representable.
assumptions_latex: For every \(u\in U\), the map \(x\mapsto f(x,u)\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x,u)\le0\ \forall u\in U\) is equivalent to \(\sup_{u\in U}f(x,u)\le0\), and the supremum is convex in \(x\).

source_refs.locator: 2.3 Tractability of Robust Counterpart p. 40
6.2 Robust Counterpart of uncertain conic problem: tractability p. 190

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3 Tractability of Robust Counterpart p. 40

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effects of enlarging the scenario family and imposing realization-wise closed convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty \(U_1\subseteq U_2\), define \(\phi_i(x)=\sup_{u\in U_i}f(x,u)\) and \(F_i=\{x:\phi_i(x)\le0\}\). Then \(\phi_1\le\phi_2\) pointwise and \(F_2\subseteq F_1\). If every \(f(\cdot,u)\) is lower-semicontinuous and convex, then each \(\phi_i\) is lower-semicontinuous and convex, possibly extended-valued, and each \(F_i\) is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enlarging the uncertainty set raises the worst-case function and shrinks robust feasibility; closed convex scenario constraints yield a closed convex robust feasible set.
assumptions_latex: For closedness, every realization-wise function is lower-semicontinuous and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi_1\le\phi_2\), \(F_2\subseteq F_1\), and under the regularity hypothesis each \(F_i\) is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Uncertainty-Set Monotonicity and Closedness

children.title: Uncertainty-Set Boundary
children.top_down_role: Handoff between generic robust templates and domain-specific uncertainty semantics.

assumptions_latex: For every fixed \(u\), \(x\mapsto f(x,u)\) is affine and hence convex.
The uncertainty set is allowed to depend on \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\mapsto\sup_{u\in U(x)}f(x,u)\) need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary for the convexity guarantee based on an exogenous index set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Decision dependence invalidates the pointwise-supremum convexity argument. For example, on \(\mathbb R\), let \(U(x)=\{x^2\}\) and \(f(x,u)=ux\). Each fixed-\(u\) function is affine in \(x\), but \(\sup_{u\in U(x)}f(x,u)=x^3\), which is not convex on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even realization-wise affine constraints can produce a nonconvex worst-case function when the uncertainty set depends on the decision.
knowledge_statements.title: Decision-Dependent Uncertainty Counterexample

assumptions_latex: \(u\mapsto f(x,u)\) is upper semicontinuous on \(U\) for the fixed decision \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{u\in U}f(x,u)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes universal robust feasibility from existence of a maximizing scenario.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(U\) is nonempty and compact and \(u\mapsto f(x,u)\) is upper semicontinuous, then the worst-case supremum is attained. Without compactness or a substitute such as upper-level compactness, a finite supremum need not be attained; for example, \(\sup_{u\in(0,1)}u=1\) has no maximizing scenario.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compactness and upper semicontinuity guarantee a worst-case realization; robust feasibility can remain meaningful without such a realization.
knowledge_statements.title: Worst-Case Attainment Boundary

assumptions_latex: Suprema are interpreted in the extended real line.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi_1(x)\le \phi_2(x)\) and \(\{x:\phi_2(x)\le0\}\subseteq\{x:\phi_1(x)\le0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order property induced by enlarging an exogenous uncertainty set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U_1\subseteq U_2\) and \(\phi_i(x)=\sup_{u\in U_i}f(x,u)\). Then \(\phi_1(x)\le\phi_2(x)\) for every \(x\), so robust feasibility for \(U_2\) implies robust feasibility for \(U_1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enlarging an uncertainty set can only increase the worst-case value and shrink the robust feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Uncertainty-Set Monotonicity
Uncertainty-Set Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates exogenous robust uncertainty from decision-dependent or probabilistic specifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the standard robust template, the uncertainty set \(U\) is nonempty, specified independently of the decision \(x\), and quantified universally. If \(U=U(x)\), then \(\sup_{u\in U(x)}f(x,u)\) need not be convex even when each fixed-\(u\) function is convex. If uncertainty is instead specified by a probability law and a violation level, the model is a chance constraint rather than an exact robust constraint unless an explicit safe robust approximation is declared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Standard robust uncertainty is nonempty, exogenous, and universally quantified; decision-dependent sets may destroy convexity, while probabilistic requirements define chance constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(x\mapsto f(x,u)\) is convex for each fixed \(u\).
The standard case uses a nonempty set \(U\) independent of \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exogenous universal uncertainty yields a convex worst-case function; decision dependence or probabilistic semantics lies outside that guarantee.

children.title: Representation Template Scope
children.top_down_role: Reusable model representations retained within the chapter.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonclosed Projection of a Closed Conic Slice
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of closedness preservation under lifted conic projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q_r^3=\{(a,b,c):a\ge0,\ b\ge0,\ 2ab\ge c^2\}\), the closed rotated second-order cone. The affine slice \(S=\{(x,y):(x,y,\sqrt2)\in Q_r^3\}=\{(x,y):x\ge0,\ y\ge0,\ xy\ge1\}\) is closed and convex, but its projection onto the \(x\)-coordinate is \((0,\infty)\), which is not closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection of an affine slice of a closed convex cone can be convex but nonclosed.
assumptions_latex: \(Q_r^3\) is the displayed closed rotated second-order cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A lifted conic representation over a closed cone does not by itself imply that the represented projection is closed.

notation.meaning: Closed affine conic slice before projection.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Projection of a Closed Conic Slice

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary constructions preserving exact lifted conic representability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(C_j=\{x:\exists y_j,\ M_jx+N_jy_j+q_j\in K_j\}\), \(j=1,\ldots,m\), are exact representations. Then \(\bigcap_jC_j\) has the exact product-cone representation \((M_jx+N_jy_j+q_j)_{j=1}^m\in\prod_jK_j\). For an affine map \(T(z)=Pz+r\), the inverse image \(T^{-1}(C_j)\) is represented exactly by substituting \(x=Pz+r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite intersections and affine inverse images preserve exact lifted conic representability.
assumptions_latex: Each \(K_j\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcap_jC_j\) and every affine inverse image \(T^{-1}(C_j)\) have exact lifted conic representations.

notation.meaning: Affine inverse image of a represented set.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure of Exact Conic Representations
Representation Template Scope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines exact lifted conic representations of convex sets and functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^q\) be a closed convex cone. A set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) has a conic representation when there exist matrices \(A,B\) and a vector \(c\) such that \[x\in C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists y\in\mathbb R^p:\ Ax+By+c\in K.\] A convex function \(f\) has a representation template when its epigraph admits such a representation. The template is exact only when both implications hold after projection over the auxiliary variable \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A representation template expresses a convex set, or a function epigraph, exactly as the projection of affine conic constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Membership in \(C\) is equivalent to feasibility of the lifted conic system.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lifted conic representation is standard and the representation content kind fits, but no source or inspectable locator is provided.

children.title: Certificate Template Scope
children.top_down_role: Reusable certificate structures retained within the chapter.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite recession witness for unboundedness of a feasible canonical conic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\), if \(x_0\) is feasible and \(d\in K\) satisfies \(Ad=0\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\), then \(x_0+td\) is feasible for every \(t\ge0\), the primal value is \(-\infty\), and the associated dual cannot be feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point and a negative-cost conic recession direction certify primal unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}=-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.title: Conic Improving-Ray Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite strict-separation witness sufficient for infeasibility of a canonical conic system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), where \(K\) is a convex cone and \(K^*=\{s:\langle s,x\rangle\ge0\ \forall x\in K\}\), any \(y\) satisfying \(A^{\mathsf T}y\in K^*\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\) certifies infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual-cone multiplier whose value on the right-hand side is negative certifies that the primal conic equations have no feasible point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Conic Primal-Infeasibility Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Incomplete Conic Alternatives at Nonclosed Images
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on universal availability of strict finite infeasibility certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The multiplier condition \(A^{\mathsf T}y\in K^*\), \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\) is sufficient for infeasibility, but need not exist for every infeasible conic system. In particular, if \(A(K)\) is not closed and \(b\in\operatorname{cl}A(K)\setminus A(K)\), then \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), is infeasible while no linear functional can strictly separate \(b\) from \(A(K)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonclosed conic images can produce infeasible systems with no strict Farkas-type multiplier certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conic system is infeasible, but a strict-separation certificate of the displayed form need not exist.

notation.meaning: Linear image of the cone under A.

knowledge_statements.title: Incomplete Conic Alternatives at Nonclosed Images
Certificate Template Scope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies primal-dual data that certify feasibility and optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the conic pair \[\inf_x\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\in K\},\qquad \sup_y\{b^{\mathsf T}y:c-A^{\mathsf T}y\in K^*\}.\] A certificate template consists of \((x,y,s)\) satisfying \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), \(s=c-A^{\mathsf T}y\in K^*\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}x-b^{\mathsf T}y=0\). These finite checks certify primal and dual feasibility and, by weak duality, global optimality of \(x\) and \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matching feasible primal and dual conic points with zero objective gap form a finite, directly checkable global-optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed feasibility conditions and zero gap certify global primal-dual optimality.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The primal-dual feasibility and zero-gap conditions correctly describe an optimality certificate under the stated dual-cone convention, but the nontrivial conic-duality claim lacks a source.

children.title: Solver-Readable Evidence Interface
children.top_down_role: Handoff from model structure to solver-consumable optimality or feasibility evidence.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient conditions for transferring an exact canonical certificate to the modeled problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a canonical conic reformulation be exact, and let \(R\) recover a modeled point \(x=R(z)\) from each canonical feasible point \(z\). If recovery preserves modeled feasibility and \(f(R(z))=c^{\mathsf T}z+\kappa\) for a fixed \(\kappa\), then a canonical primal-dual feasible pair with zero canonical gap recovers a globally optimal modeled point. Transferable evidence must therefore record the canonical variables and enough recovery and objective-correspondence metadata to verify these conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact feasibility recovery and objective preservation transfer a zero-gap canonical certificate to the original model.
assumptions_latex: The canonical reformulation is exact after projection.
\(R\) maps canonical feasible points to modeled feasible points.
The modeled and canonical objectives agree up to a fixed offset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A zero-gap canonical optimality certificate yields a globally optimal recovered modeled point.

notation.meaning: Fixed objective offset introduced by canonicalization.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Preserving Evidence Recovery

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of scale-independent interpretation for an unnormalized absolute residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\alpha>0\), consider \(\min_x x\) subject to \(\alpha x=0\), whose unique feasible point is \(x^*=0\). For an absolute tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), the point \(x_\alpha=\varepsilon/\alpha\) satisfies \(|\alpha x_\alpha|=\varepsilon\), but its modeled objective error is \(\varepsilon/\alpha\), which is unbounded as \(\alpha\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed absolute canonical residual may permit arbitrarily large modeled error after constraint rescaling.
assumptions_latex: Feasibility is judged only through \(|\alpha x|\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An unnormalized absolute residual does not uniformly control modeled objective error.

notation.meaning: Residual-qualified candidate for the scaled canonical equation.

knowledge_statements.title: Raw Residual Scaling Failure
Solver-Readable Evidence Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines machine-checkable evidence tied to the canonical conic model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For canonical conic data \((A,b,c,K)\), solver-readable evidence is a tuple of numeric primal-dual variables, cone-membership claims, residuals, and an objective gap, all expressed in the canonical coordinates. Given tolerances \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm p},\varepsilon_{\mathrm d},\varepsilon_{\,g}\ge0\), an approximate optimality certificate must satisfy \[\|Ax-b\|\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm p},\quad \operatorname{dist}(x,K)\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm p},\quad \operatorname{dist}(c-A^{\mathsf T}y,K^*)\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm d},\quad |c^{\mathsf T}x-b^{\mathsf T}y|\le\varepsilon_{g}.\] The interface must retain the inverse map from canonical variables to modeled variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solver-readable evidence contains canonical primal-dual values, cone and residual checks, a bounded gap, and a map back to model variables.
assumptions_latex: Canonicalization retains an inverse recovery map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The tuple is mechanically checkable against the canonical conic data at the declared tolerances.

notation.meaning: distance from z to cone K

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual tuple is mechanically checkable, but its interpretation as an approximate optimality certificate depends on norms, scaling, and solver conventions. The statement also alternates between epsilon_{\,g} and epsilon_g.

knowledge_statements.title: Canonicalization Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transforms a verified convex model into an equivalent solver-supported conic form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a convex model assembled from atoms with known graph representations. Introduce an epigraph variable for each nonlinear objective atom and auxiliary variables for each represented subexpression; replace every atom by its exact affine-conic graph constraints; collect the result as \[\min_z\ d^{\mathsf T}z\quad\text{subject to}\quad Hz+h\in K.\] Store maps from original variables to components of \(z\) and from conic solutions back to model variables. Output the conic data and these maps; reject the input if an atom lacks a verified compatible representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Canonicalization recursively replaces supported convex atoms by exact conic graph forms, emits one conic program, and records solution-recovery maps.
assumptions_latex: Every nonlinear atom has an exact compatible graph representation.
The model satisfies the required convex composition rules.
The target cone product \(K\) is supported by the selected solver.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output conic program has the same optimal value and recoverable model solutions as the input model.

children.title: Conic Solver Routing
children.top_down_role: Routing standardized cone representations toward compatible solver families.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Solver Routing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility rule for routing a canonical conic program to a solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the canonical problem be 
\[\min_x\ c^{\mathsf T}x\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax+s=b,\qquad s\in K=K_1\times\cdots\times K_q.\]
A solver \(S\) is an admissible route exactly when it supports every cone factor \(K_i\), the required numerical precision, and the supplied data representation. Among admissible solvers, routing may select
\[S^\star\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{S}\widehat C(S;A,b,c,K),\]
where \(\widehat C\) is a declared resource-cost estimate. If no solver is admissible, the interface must return unsupported or invoke an explicit equivalent reformulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Route a conic model only to solvers supporting every cone, precision requirement, and data representation; otherwise reformulate explicitly or report unsupported.
assumptions_latex: Canonicalization preserves the original problem's solution correspondence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S^\star\) is selected only from solvers compatible with \((A,b,c,K)\).

notation.meaning: cone factors in the canonical product cone

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the solver-compatibility routing predicate.

assumptions_latex: \(K_i\) is a cone factor of the canonical model.
The candidate solver does not natively support \(K_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An exact route requires a projection-exact replacement; otherwise a different problem is solved.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-reformulation boundary rather than a complete solver-routing condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a solver does not support a cone factor \(K_i\), an outer approximation relaxes feasibility and an inner approximation restricts feasibility unless an exact projected reformulation is established.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unsupported cone cannot be silently replaced by an inner or outer approximation without changing the problem.

children.title: Representation-Dependent Routing
children.top_down_role: Solver-selection regimes determined by the resulting canonical representation.

assumptions_latex: The compared representations are exact and possess valid recovery maps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Mathematical equivalence does not imply representation-independent runtime, memory use, or numerical behavior.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits what follows computationally from equivalence of canonical forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exact equivalence preserves the modeled optimal value and recovered solutions but does not order computational cost. Cone dimensions, barrier parameters, KKT-system sparsity, coefficient scaling, and available native primitives may change under lifting or reformulation. Equivalence or a nominal cone-family label alone therefore does not determine the preferred route.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent formulations can have very different numerical costs, so equivalence or a cone label alone does not determine the best route.
knowledge_statements.title: No Representation-Invariant Cost Ordering
Representation-Dependent Routing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Routing among equivalent canonical representations using compatibility and estimated cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\) be a convex problem and let \(R(P)\) be a finite set of canonical representations having the same optimal value and a specified recovery map for primal solutions. For each representation \(r\in R(P)\) and solver \(S\), let \(\chi(r,S)\in\{0,1\}\) indicate solver compatibility. Representation-dependent routing selects
\[(r^\star,S^\star)\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{r,S:\,\chi(r,S)=1}\widehat C(r,S).\]
Thus equivalent formulations need not receive the same route: cone dimensions, sparsity, conditioning, and available solver primitives may change \(\widehat C\).

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Solver Routing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order smooth routing for convex objectives with Lipschitz gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the problem \(\min_{x\in Q} f(x)\), the smooth first-order route is admissible when \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is closed and convex, \(f\) is convex and differentiable on a neighborhood of \(Q\), and a finite constant \(L>0\) satisfies
\[\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in Q.\]
The solver interface must therefore expose gradient evaluations and, for constrained methods, a projection or another declared smooth constrained oracle for \(Q\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dimension Does Not Determine Resource Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension-only failure boundary for resource-aware routing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(n\), \(A_n=I_n\) and a generic dense matrix \(B_n\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) have identical dimensions. Under conventional explicit representations, \(A_n\) uses \(\Theta(n)\) stored entries and its matrix-vector product costs \(\Theta(n)\), whereas \(B_n\) uses \(\Theta(n^2)\) entries and its product costs \(\Theta(n^2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diagonal and dense matrices can have identical dimensions but linear versus quadratic storage and product cost, so dimension alone cannot select a large-scale route.
assumptions_latex: Arithmetic and storage use conventional explicit sparse or dense representations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Model dimensions alone do not determine storage or matrix-vector cost and are not a sufficient large-scale routing predicate.

notation.meaning: generic dense instance of the same dimension

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension Does Not Determine Resource Cost
Large-Scale Solver Routing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resource-feasible routing based on operator access and per-iteration costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a problem instance have dimension \(n\), data size \(N\), memory budget \(M\), and candidate solvers \(S\). A large-scale route is admissible only if its declared storage \(m_S(n,N)\le M\) and every required oracle is available. Routing selects an admissible solver using an estimate of total work
\[W_S(\varepsilon)=k_S(\varepsilon)\,c_S(n,N),\]
where \(c_S\) estimates per-iteration work and \(k_S(\varepsilon)\) estimates iterations needed for the declared accuracy \(\varepsilon\). Dimension alone is not a sufficient routing predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Large-scale routing admits only methods fitting memory and available oracles, then compares estimated total work at the requested accuracy rather than dimension alone.
assumptions_latex: A target accuracy \(\varepsilon>0\) and memory budget \(M>0\) are declared.
Each candidate solver provides compatible resource estimates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected solver satisfies \(m_S(n,N)\le M\) and minimizes the declared estimate \(W_S(\varepsilon)\) among admissible routes.

notation.meaning: estimated total work to requested accuracy

children.title: Decomposition Solver Routing
children.top_down_role: Routing choices driven by separability or distributed model structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic structural certificate for multiplier-mediated block decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[\inf_{x_i\in X_i}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^p f_i(x_i):\sum_{i=1}^p A_i x_i=b\right\},\]
the partial Lagrangian is
\[L(x,\lambda)=-\langle\lambda,b\rangle+\sum_{i=1}^p\bigl(f_i(x_i)+\langle A_i^{\mathsf T}\lambda,x_i\rangle\bigr).\]
Hence
\[g(\lambda)=-\langle\lambda,b\rangle+\sum_{i=1}^p g_i(\lambda),\qquad g_i(\lambda)=\inf_{x_i\in X_i}\bigl(f_i(x_i)+\langle A_i^{\mathsf T}\lambda,x_i\rangle\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing the sole linear coupling equation makes dual-function evaluation split exactly into independent block infima for each fixed multiplier.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i:\mathbb R^{n_i}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex.
Each \(X_i\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_i}\) is nonempty and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For each fixed \(\lambda\), evaluation of \(g(\lambda)\) separates into independent block infima; this algebraic identity does not require strong duality.
knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Lagrangian Separability Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separability exposed by local copies and a shared consensus variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For proper closed convex \(f_i\), consider \[\min_{x_1,\ldots,x_p,z}\sum_i f_i(x_i)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad x_i=z.\] Its augmented Lagrangian is \[L_\rho=\sum_i\left(f_i(x_i)+\langle y_i,x_i-z\rangle+\frac\rho2\|x_i-z\|_2^2\right).\] For fixed \((z,y_1,\ldots,y_p)\), minimization over the \(x_i\) separates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local copies tied to a consensus variable expose independent augmented-Lagrangian block subproblems.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The formulation supports block-parallel local updates when every displayed block subproblem is callable.

One exact iteration is executable without undeclared cross-block access if and only if, for every reachable \(z\): each \(S_i(z)\) is callable using block-local data and the communicated part of \(z\); the \(R_i\) have declared compatible codomains and can be assembled into the required residual or consensus statistic; and that statistic suffices to evaluate \(U\). Algebraic separation alone is not an implementability certificate.

children.title: Coupling-Structure Thresholds
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes determining whether decomposition remains useful.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of unweighted coupling density as a universal decomposition threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an unweighted block-coupling graph \(G=(V,E)\) containing an edge \(\{i,j\}\), and let \(\rho=2|E|/[p(p-1)]\). For every \(d\ge1\), assign \(d\)-dimensional variables to blocks \(i,j\) and a dense \(d\times d\) coupling operator to that edge. The graph and \(\rho\) remain fixed, while the edge data and a direct matrix-vector product require \(\Theta(d^2)\) storage and arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed coupling graph can carry arbitrarily large dense block operators, so edge density alone cannot bound resources or define a universal decomposition threshold.
assumptions_latex: \(p\ge2\) and \(G=(V,E)\) is an unweighted block-coupling graph.
At least one coupling edge is present and may carry dense operators of increasing block dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No function of \(\rho=2|E|/[p(p-1)]\) alone gives an instance-independent bound on coupling storage or direct product cost.

notation.meaning: endpoint block dimension in the construction

knowledge_statements.title: No Universal Density-Only Threshold
Coupling-Structure Thresholds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit threshold rule for choosing monolithic or decomposed execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(p\) blocks, let \(E\subseteq\{\{i,j\}:i\ne j\}\) contain pairs coupled by a constraint or objective term, and define the coupling density
\[\rho=\frac{2|E|}{p(p-1)}\quad\text{for }p\ge2.\]
Given a declared threshold \(\tau\in[0,1]\), graph-based decomposition is enabled only when \(\rho\le\tau\) and every resulting block fits the local resource limit. The threshold \(\tau\) is an implementation policy calibrated to cost estimates, not a universal mathematical constant; it must therefore be recorded with the route.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enable graph-based decomposition only below a declared coupling-density threshold and when every block fits local resources; the threshold is policy, not a universal constant.
assumptions_latex: The coupling graph and resource limit are defined before routing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Decomposition is enabled only if \(\rho\le\tau\) and all induced blocks meet the declared resource constraint.

children.title: Sparsity Interface
children.top_down_role: Routing based on sparse model structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation-size and matrix-vector cost for conventional sparse formats.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q=\operatorname{nnz}(A)\) for \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\). A coordinate representation uses \(\Theta(q)\) value-and-index words; compressed sparse row uses \(\Theta(m+q)\), and compressed sparse column uses \(\Theta(n+q)\). Each format evaluates \(Ax\) or \(A^{\mathsf T}y\) using \(\Theta(q)\) stored-entry contributions and \(O(m+n+q)\) total work including output initialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conventional sparse formats store and multiply using resources proportional to the stored nonzeros plus format-dependent row, column, and output arrays.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has \(q\) explicitly stored entries.
Indices and scalar values occupy constant-size machine words.
Duplicate coordinates, if permitted, are combined consistently when defining the represented operator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Sparse storage is \(\Theta(q)\), \(\Theta(m+q)\), or \(\Theta(n+q)\) for coordinate, row-compressed, or column-compressed formats respectively, and either operator product costs \(O(m+n+q)\).

notation.meaning: number of stored entries of the sparse representation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sparse model data need not produce equally sparse direct factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The positive-definite sparse matrix \[A=\begin{bmatrix}4&1&1&0\\1&4&0&1\\1&0&4&1\\0&1&1&4\end{bmatrix}\] has \(A_{23}=0\), but eliminating the first variable creates the Schur-complement entry \(S_{23}=-1/4\). Thus factor sparsity depends on ordering and the filled graph, not only on \(\operatorname{nnz}(A)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Elimination can create factor nonzeros absent from sparse input data.
assumptions_latex: A sparse direct factorization is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Input nonzero count alone does not certify factor memory or factorization complexity.

notation.meaning: Schur complement after eliminating the first variable

assumptions_latex: Every entry outside \(\Omega\) is identically zero.
Parameter updates may change values only at positions in \(\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Gamma\) is a value-independent structural superset of \(\operatorname{supp}(A^{\mathsf T}A)\).

notation.meaning: structural pattern of the rectangular matrix

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural sparsity propagation from a rectangular operator to its normal matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\times\{1,\ldots,n\}\) be a structural pattern for \(A\). Define \(\Gamma\) by \((j,k)\in\Gamma\) if and only if some row \(i\) has both \((i,j)\in\Omega\) and \((i,k)\in\Omega\). Every numerical realization supported on \(\Omega\) satisfies \[\operatorname{supp}(A^{\mathsf T}A)\subseteq\Gamma.\] The inclusion may be strict because of cancellation, so \(\Gamma\), rather than a current numerical support, is the safe symbolic pattern under value updates preserving \(\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The column-intersection pattern safely contains the normal matrix's support, although cancellation can make a particular realization sparser.
knowledge_statements.title: Symbolic Normal-Matrix Pattern

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional certificate that indexed sparse data reproduce both declared operator directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widetilde A\) be represented by indexed data \((\Omega,(v_{ij})_{(i,j)\in\Omega})\), with entries outside \(\Omega\) interpreted as zero, and let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) be the intended operator. Then \(\widetilde A=A\) if and only if \(\widetilde A e_j=Ae_j\) for every standard basis vector \(e_j\). Equivalently, \(\widetilde A^{\mathsf T}u_i=A^{\mathsf T}u_i\) for every standard basis vector \(u_i\). Checking both families also verifies that supplied forward and transpose routines represent the same sparse data. A parameter update is structurally admissible only when it changes values at positions in the declared permitted pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sparse data are lossless exactly when their basis-vector products reproduce the intended matrix; checking both directions also detects an inconsistent transpose routine.
assumptions_latex: The sparse format has deterministic semantics for duplicate coordinates.
Entries outside the declared pattern are interpreted as zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The basis tests are necessary and sufficient for equality of the represented and intended operators, and bidirectional success certifies transpose consistency.

notation.meaning: operator induced by the sparse data

review_flags: The exhaustive test is a correctness certificate, not a scalable testing method.
knowledge_statements.title: Bidirectional Sparse-Operator Losslessness Test
Sparsity Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lossless sparse representation of solver data and structural nonzeros.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a matrix \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), a sparsity interface supplies an index set \(\Omega\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\times\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and values \((A_{ij})_{(i,j)\in\Omega}\) such that
\[A_{ij}=0\qquad\text{for every }(i,j)\notin\Omega.\]
The sparse representation and the dense matrix must define identical products \(Ax\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}y\) for all conforming vectors. Structural zeros and entries permitted to vary numerically must be distinguished so symbolic factorization or chordal structure is not invalidated by later parameter updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sparsity interface stores indexed nonzeros losslessly, reproduces matrix and transpose products, and distinguishes structural zeros from parameter-dependent entries.
assumptions_latex: The declared pattern contains every entry permitted to be nonzero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sparse data represent the same linear operator \(A\) and adjoint \(A^{\mathsf T}\) as the dense data.

children.title: Matrix-Free Interface
children.top_down_role: Routing based on operator access without explicit matrix storage.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic finite-dimensional validation of a declared matrix-free adjoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) and \(\mathcal B:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n\) be linear. Then \(\mathcal B=\mathcal A^*\) if and only if
\[\langle\mathcal A e_j,u_i\rangle=\langle e_j,\mathcal B u_i\rangle\qquad(1\le i\le m,\ 1\le j\le n),\]
where \((e_j)\) and \((u_i)\) are the standard bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finite-dimensional linear routines, the adjoint identity on every pair of standard basis vectors is necessary and sufficient for exact adjoint consistency.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\) and \(\mathcal B\) are linear routines between finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
The standard bases are available for deterministic validation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All \(mn\) identities hold exactly if and only if \(\mathcal B=\mathcal A^*\); one failure rejects the declared adjoint.
review_flags: The exhaustive test is a correctness certificate, not a scalable validation algorithm.
knowledge_statements.title: Adjoint-Consistency Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of exact-gradient calculations under an inconsistent declared adjoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F(x)=	frac12\|Ax-b\|_2^2\), \(
abla F(x)=A^{\mathsf T}(Ax-b)\). If a supplied linear routine \(B
e A^{\mathsf T}\) is substituted, then \(B(Ax-b)\) need not equal \(
abla F(x)\), so guarantees requiring exact gradients or the true adjoint do not apply unless an inexact-oracle analysis covers the error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inconsistent adjoint invalidates exact-gradient and exact-adjoint guarantees.
assumptions_latex: \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) and \(B:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n\) are linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact-adjoint convergence results are inapplicable without a suitable error analysis.
knowledge_statements.title: Adjoint-Mismatch Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition of forward and adjoint calls without forming a Gram matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given exact routines for \(x\mapsto Ax\) and \(y\mapsto A^{\mathsf T}y\), the product \(A^{\mathsf T}Ax\) is evaluated as \(A^{\mathsf T}(Ax)\) without materializing \(A\) or \(A^{\mathsf T}A\). Likewise, \((A^{\mathsf T}A+\lambda I)x\) uses one forward call, one adjoint call, and a scaled vector addition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward and adjoint products compose to evaluate normal operators without forming the matrix or Gram matrix.
assumptions_latex: The routines are exact linear maps with compatible dimensions.
The adjoint routine is consistent with the forward routine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The operator cost is \(O(C_A+C_{A^*}+n)\), excluding oracle-internal workspace.
knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Free Normal-Operator Evaluation

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\) and \(\mathcal B\) are fixed linear maps between finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
The test vectors are independent and have distributions absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure.
The probability-one statement is interpreted in exact arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nonzero discrepancy rejects adjoint consistency; zero or near-zero floating-point discrepancies are not deterministic certificates without a scale-aware error analysis.
review_flags: Floating-point use requires a scale-aware tolerance and does not retain the exact-arithmetic certificate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalable probabilistic detection of an inconsistent matrix-free adjoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given linear routines \(\mathcal A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) and \(\mathcal B:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n\), draw independent absolutely continuous random vectors \(x\) and \(y\) and compute \[d=\langle\mathcal A x,y\rangle-\langle x,\mathcal B y\rangle.\] If \(\mathcal B=\mathcal A^*\), then \(d=0\) for every draw. In exact arithmetic, if \(\mathcal B\ne\mathcal A^*\), then \(\Pr(d=0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A random inner-product test detects any fixed incorrect linear adjoint with probability one in exact arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Adjoint Test

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Method-dependent test for whether operator access suffices without matrix materialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an algorithm require a subset \(\mathcal R\subseteq\{x\mapsto Ax,\ y\mapsto A^{\mathsf T}y\}\), with declared dimensions \((m,n)\). A matrix-free implementation is admissible if every action in \(\mathcal R\) is supplied by a callable routine that does not materialize \(A\), all dimensions agree, and, when both directions are required, \(\langle\mathcal A x,y\rangle=\langle x,\mathcal A^*y\rangle\) for all \(x,y\). Supplying only \(Ax\) is insufficient for an algorithm that also uses gradients, normal products, or \(A^{\mathsf T}y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matrix-free access is sufficient exactly when it supplies every operator direction used by the selected algorithm, with compatible dimensions and a true adjoint when required.
assumptions_latex: The selected algorithm's required linear operations are known.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The routines form a valid matrix-free handoff precisely under operation-completeness, dimension, nonmaterialization, and required-adjoint conditions.

notation.meaning: operator actions required by the selected algorithm

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Free Algorithm Admissibility
Matrix-Free Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operator-oracle interface that avoids explicit matrix materialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A matrix-free interface for a linear map \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) consists of callable oracles
\[\mathcal A(x)=Ax,\qquad \mathcal A^*(y)=A^{\mathsf T}y,\]
plus the dimensions \((m,n)\). Neither oracle may require the caller to materialize \(A\). If a selected algorithm uses only one direction, only that oracle is mandatory; algorithms requiring gradients, normal products, or primal-dual updates must receive both directions or equivalent routines. The declared adjoint must satisfy \(\langle\mathcal A(x),y\rangle=\langle x,\mathcal A^*(y)\rangle\) for all \(x,y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix-free interface provides operator and required adjoint products without materializing the matrix, with dimensions and an exact adjoint-consistency contract.
assumptions_latex: The spaces use the Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracles implement \(A\) and its adjoint without exposing an explicit matrix.

children.title: Scaling Interface
children.top_down_role: Handoff of numerical scaling considerations to solver configuration.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Primal-Dual Recovery Under Conic Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete coordinate and dual recovery contract for an invertible conic scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[\min c^{\mathsf T}x\quad\text{subject to }Ax+s=b,\ s\in K,\]
with dual
\[\max -b^{\mathsf T}y\quad\text{subject to }c+A^{\mathsf T}y=0,\ y\in K^*.\]
For invertible \(D,E\), set \(x=E\hat x\), \(\hat s=Ds\), \(\hat A=DAE\), \(\hat b=Db\), \(\hat c=E^{\mathsf T}c\), and \(\hat K=DK\). Then
\[\hat A\hat x+\hat s=\hat b,\quad \hat s\in\hat K,\quad \hat y\in\hat K^*=D^{-\mathsf T}K^*,\quad \hat c+\hat A^{\mathsf T}\hat y=0.\]
Recovery is
\[x=E\hat x,\qquad s=D^{-1}\hat s,\qquad y=D^{\mathsf T}\hat y,\]
and
\[\hat c^{\mathsf T}\hat x=c^{\mathsf T}x,
\qquad-\hat b^{\mathsf T}\hat y=-b^{\mathsf T}y.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invertible conic scaling must record its coordinate maps; the stated inverse primal maps and transpose dual map preserve feasibility and both objective values exactly.
assumptions_latex: The transformed cone \(DK\) is represented exactly.
Dual cones use the Euclidean pairing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The scaled and original primal-dual systems correspond bijectively, with exact primal, dual, and objective recovery.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Primal-Dual Recovery Under Conic Scaling
Scaling Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invertible diagonal scaling with exact primal and dual recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the conic system \(Ax+s=b\), \(s\in K\), choose invertible diagonal matrices \(D\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) and \(E\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) with positive diagonals and set \(x=E\hat x\), \(s=D^{-1}\hat s\). The scaled system is
\[(DAE)\hat x+\hat s=Db,
\qquad \hat s\in DK.\]
The interface must return \(D,E\), transform the objective consistently, and recover original primal and dual variables by the corresponding inverse transformations. Scaling is valid only when these maps preserve feasibility and objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scaling interface applies recorded invertible diagonal transformations, transforms cones and objectives consistently, and provides exact recovery of original primal and dual variables.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) and \(E\) are diagonal with strictly positive entries.
The transformed cone \(DK\) is supported or represented exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The original and scaled systems correspond bijectively under \(x=E\hat x\) and \(s=D^{-1}\hat s\).
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports this precise conic scaling convention.
Dual-variable recovery convention requires source review.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the Scaling Interface leaf and the displayed primal scaling is algebraically consistent, but no source supports the convention. The record also requires dual recovery without stating the corresponding dual-variable transformation.

children.title: Warm-Start Interface
children.top_down_role: Handoff of prior solution information to repeated solver calls.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Performance boundary for an admissible solver initialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Admissibility of a warm-start state does not imply fewer iterations or lower running time. Absent a solver-specific comparison theorem, either initialization may be faster.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid warm start has no solver-independent speedup guarantee.
assumptions_latex: The supplied state belongs to the selected solver's admissible initialization domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{warm}}\leq T_{\mathrm{cold}}\text{ does not follow from admissibility alone.}

notation.meaning: Work or running time under warm and default initialization.

knowledge_statements.title: No Universal Warm-Start Speedup

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Warm Starts Preserve the Canonical Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic separation of initialization state from canonical problem data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed canonical problem data P, supplying an accepted initialization w^0 changes the algorithmic initial state but not the feasible set, objective, optimal value, or solution set. Ordinary termination certificates therefore retain their usual meaning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A warm start changes initialization, not the mathematical problem or its final certificates.
assumptions_latex: The canonical problem data are unchanged.
The solver accepts w^0 and uses its ordinary termination tests.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{val}(P)\text{ and }\operatorname*{argmin}P\text{ are independent of }w^0.
knowledge_statements.title: Warm Starts Preserve the Canonical Problem
Warm-Start Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity contract for reusing approximate primal-dual solver state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a parameterized problem \(P(\theta)	o P(\theta')\), a warm-start state may contain a primal point \(x^0\), dual point \(y^0\), slack \(s^0\), and solver-specific state \(z^0\). The route may reuse a component only if its dimensions and cone domains match the new canonical representation and the selected solver accepts it. If strict interiority is required, the interface must ensure \(s^0\in\operatorname{int}K\) and the analogous dual condition. Invalid components are discarded or repaired explicitly; they are never silently reinterpreted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reuse prior solver state only when dimensions, cone domains, representation, and solver requirements remain compatible; otherwise explicitly repair or discard invalid components.
assumptions_latex: Both instances use identified canonical variables and constraints.
The selected solver declares its admissible initialization domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Only warm-start components valid for \(P(\theta')\) and the selected solver may initialize the new solve.

notation.meaning: slack cone in the new canonical problem

knowledge_statements.title: Data-Generation Handoff
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility condition connecting generated observations to the uncertainty model used by a convex template.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D:\Omega\to\mathcal D\) be observed data on a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,Q)\), let \(c:\mathcal D\to\mathcal C\) be measurable, and let \(\mathfrak M\) be the set of data-generating laws admitted by a convex template \(T\). The data-generation handoff is valid precisely when \(D\) is measurable, \(Q\in\mathfrak M\), and the instantiated coefficients belong to the template domain almost surely: \[D\text{ is measurable},\qquad c\text{ is measurable},\qquad Q\in\mathfrak M,\qquad Q\{c(D)\in\operatorname{dom}T\}=1.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generated data validly enter the template when the data and coefficient-extraction map are measurable, their law is admitted, and the resulting coefficients lie in the template domain almost surely.
assumptions_latex: \(D:\Omega\to\mathcal D\) is defined on a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,Q)\).
\(c:\mathcal D\to\mathcal C\) is the specified measurable coefficient-extraction map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\) and \(c\) are measurable, \(Q\in\mathfrak M\), and \(Q\{c(D)\in\operatorname{dom}T\}=1\).

notation.meaning: Convex optimization template with a prescribed coefficient domain.
Admissible class of data-generating probability laws.

children.title: Assumption Handoff
children.top_down_role: Transfer of application-specific modeling assumptions to domain theory.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit verification interface for premises required by an external guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a_j(c,\mathfrak M)\) be the translated predicates required for a guarantee \(G\). For each j, fix a verifier \(V_j\) satisfying \[V_j(w;c,\mathfrak M)=\mathrm{true}\ \Longrightarrow\ a_j(c,\mathfrak M)=\mathrm{true}.\] A handoff certificate is a tuple \((w_1,\ldots,w_k)\) for which every verifier returns true. It supports invoking \(G\) only if the listed predicates are complete premises for \(G\); the certificate does not establish unlisted domain assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An assumption handoff consists of witnesses checked by sound, explicitly declared verifiers for every premise of the claimed guarantee.
assumptions_latex: The guarantee G lists predicates \(a_1,\ldots,a_k\) as complete required premises.
Each verifier \(V_j\) has the stated soundness implication.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Acceptance by every \(V_j\) certifies all listed predicates and supports applying G within its declared scope.

notation.meaning: Declared sound verifier for predicate j.

knowledge_statements.title: Verified Assumption Handoff
Assumption Handoff
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate transferring domain assumptions into explicit predicates on template data and uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_1,\ldots,A_k\) be the domain assumptions required for a guarantee \(G\), and let \(a_j(c,\mathfrak M)\) be their formal translations for template coefficients \(c\) and uncertainty model \(\mathfrak M\). An assumption-handoff certificate is a tuple \((w_1,\ldots,w_k)\) such that each \(w_j\) is independently checkable and verifies \(a_j(c,\mathfrak M)\). The certificate supports invoking \(G\) only when \[\bigwedge_{j=1}^{k}a_j(c,\mathfrak M)=\mathrm{true}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid handoff supplies checkable witnesses for every domain assumption translated into the template; the associated guarantee is invoked only when all translated predicates hold.
assumptions_latex: Each \(A_j\) has a specified translation \(a_j(c,\mathfrak M)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigwedge_{j=1}^{k}a_j(c,\mathfrak M)=\mathrm{true}\) certifies applicability of \(G\) to the instantiated model.

notation.meaning: A domain-level assumption required by a claimed guarantee.
Formal template-level predicate translating the domain assumption.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standing hypotheses for the subsequent LMI-based stability analysis, followed by their specialization to the stability-radius problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume
\[
\exists(x,u)\quad Px+Qu+r\succeq0,\qquad A_0[x]\succ0,
\]
\[
\forall i\quad b_i\ne0\quad\text{and}\quad \forall x\in\mathcal X\; a_i[x]\ne0,
\qquad \rho_*<+\infty.
\]
For the problem of computing \(\rho[A^*,D]\), the nondegeneracy condition is automatic; LMI feasibility becomes
\[
\exists X\succeq I\quad (A^*)^TX+XA^*\prec-I,
\]
which expresses stability of \(A^*\), and the finiteness condition becomes \(\rho[A^*,D]<+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assume that the displayed LMI system is feasible, every b_i is nonzero, every a_i[x] is nonzero for every x in the uncertainty set, and the optimal radius rho_* is finite. For computation of the stability radius rho[A*,D], nondegeneracy is automatic, feasibility means that some X at least I satisfies the strict Lyapunov inequality for A*, and finiteness means that rho[A*,D] is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{These conditions are the standing hypotheses; for }\rho[A^*,D],\ I.1\iff\exists X\succeq I:\ (A^*)^TX+XA^*\prec-I,\quad I.3\iff\rho[A^*,D]<+\infty.

knowledge_statements.title: Misspecification Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates computational validity of a convex instance from validity of claims tied to its data model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\) be the actual data-generating law and \(\mathfrak M\) the law class under which a guarantee \(G(T,D)\) was established. If \(Q\notin\mathfrak M\), or if a required translated predicate \(a_j(c(D),\mathfrak M)\) is false, then the guarantee is outside its stated scope. The instantiated optimization problem may remain convex and solvable, but convexity alone does not imply \(G(T,D)\) under this misspecification.

At least one of \(Q\notin\mathfrak M\) or \(a_j(c(D),\mathfrak M)=\mathrm{false}\) holds.
