children.title: Parameter Semantics
children.top_down_role: Covers the domain meaning assigned to template parameters.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Application-facing metadata that assigns domain meaning to admissible template parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a template \(T(x;\theta)\) with admissible parameter domain \(\Theta\), a parameter-semantics declaration consists of a map \(s:\Theta\to\mathcal S\) together with component metadata sufficient for its intended use, such as the represented domain quantity, units, scale, indexing, and sign convention. These declarations annotate the numerical parameter; they do not alter the mathematical parameter \(\theta\) or follow from convexity of T.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parameter semantics declares what admissible numerical parameters mean, including any units, scale, indexing, or sign conventions needed by the application.
assumptions_latex: \(T(x;\theta)\) has a declared admissible parameter domain \(\Theta\).
\(\mathcal S\) is the chosen interpretation space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s:\Theta\to\mathcal S\) and its declared metadata assign application meaning without redefining \(\theta\).
knowledge_statements.title: Declared Parameter Semantics
Parameter Semantics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal meaning assigned to parameters appearing in an application-facing convex template.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex template \(T(x;\theta)\) with parameter space \(\Theta\), parameter semantics is a declared map \(s:\Theta\to\mathcal S\) into a domain interpretation space. A valid declaration specifies, for every component \(\theta_i\), its admissible set \(\Theta_i\), units or scale when applicable, and the domain object \(s_i(\theta_i)\) represented by its value. The optimization parameter is therefore the pair \((\theta,s(\theta))\), not the numerical value \(\theta\) alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parameter semantics maps each admissible numerical parameter to its intended domain object, including units, scale, and component meaning where applicable.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal S\) is a specified space of domain interpretations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s:\Theta\to\mathcal S\) assigns the declared domain meaning to every admissible parameter value.

notation.meaning: Numerical parameter vector supplied to the convex template.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf, but the proposed semantic-map formalism and the assertion that an optimization parameter is a pair (theta,s(theta)) are local conventions without cited authoritative support.

children.title: Interpretation Handoff
children.top_down_role: Covers transfer from parameterized template output to domain-facing interpretation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Non-tautological admissibility and consistency condition for transferring a domain object into template parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(e:\mathcal Z\to\bar\Theta\) encode domain objects into an ambient parameter space, let \(\Theta\subseteq\bar\Theta\) be the admissible template domain, let \(s:\Theta\to\mathcal S\) be the declared parameter semantics, and let \(r:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal S\) be the domain interpretation. The handoff is valid at z exactly when \[e(z)\in\Theta\quad\text{and}\quad s(e(z))=r(z).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A handoff is valid when the encoded value is admissible and its declared template meaning agrees with the domain-side interpretation.
assumptions_latex: \(e:\mathcal Z\to\bar\Theta\), \(\Theta\subseteq\bar\Theta\), \(s:\Theta\to\mathcal S\), and \(r:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal S\) are declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The handoff is valid at z if and only if \(e(z)\in\Theta\) and \(s(e(z))=r(z)\).

notation.meaning: Encoding into the ambient parameter space.
Admissible parameter domain within the ambient space.

knowledge_statements.title: Semantic-Commutation Handoff
Interpretation Handoff
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency condition between domain quantities and the parameters instantiated in a convex template.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z\in\mathcal Z\) be a domain object, \(e:\mathcal Z\to\Theta\) an encoding map, and \(s:\Theta\to\mathcal S\) the declared parameter-semantics map. Given a domain interpretation \(r:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal S\), the interpretation handoff is valid at \(z\) exactly when the encoded parameter is admissible and the two interpretations agree: \[e(z)\in\Theta,\qquad s(e(z))=r(z).\] This condition concerns meaning; it is independent of whether solving \(T(x;e(z))\) is numerically successful.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A domain object is handed off consistently when its encoded parameter is admissible and the declared parameter meaning equals the domain interpretation.
assumptions_latex: \(e:\mathcal Z\to\Theta\) and \(r:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal S\) are specified.
\(s:\Theta\to\mathcal S\) is the declared semantic map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e(z)\in\Theta\) and \(s(e(z))=r(z)\).

notation.meaning: Encoding from domain objects to template parameters.

children.title: Semantic Ambiguity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Covers cases where parameter meaning does not support a unique domain interpretation.

assumptions_latex: \(N:\Theta\to\mathcal I\) assigns each admissible parameter value its complete numerical optimization instance.
There exist \(\theta_1,\theta_2\in\Theta\) with distinct domain meanings but \(N(\theta_1)=N(\theta_2)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N(\theta_1)=N(\theta_2)\implies q(N(\theta_1))=q(N(\theta_2))\text{ for every instance-determined }q,\text{ so the intended meaning is not identifiable from the numerical instance alone.}

notation.meaning: Map from admissible parameter values to complete numerical instances.
Any output, statistic, or certificate determined solely by a numerical instance.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic nonidentifiability caused by distinct domain meanings lying in one fiber of the numerical-instance map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N:\Theta\to\mathcal I\) map each admissible parameter value to the complete numerical optimization instance it generates. Two parameters are numerically observationally equivalent when \(N(\theta_1)=N(\theta_2)\). If observationally equivalent parameters have distinct domain meanings, then every output, statistic, or certificate \(q(N(\theta))\) determined solely by the numerical instance is identical for them. Hence the numerical instance, whether or not its optimum is attained, cannot identify the intended meaning without additional semantic information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When two different domain meanings generate exactly the same numerical instance, nothing computed solely from that instance can identify which meaning was intended; optimizer existence is irrelevant.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Numerical Observational Equivalence and Semantic Nonidentifiability
knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Observational Equivalence and Semantic Nonidentifiability
Semantic Ambiguity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of optimization output to determine a unique domain interpretation of its parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s_1,s_2:\Theta\to\mathcal S\) be two admissible semantic maps for the same numerical template \(T(x;\theta)\). If there exists \(\theta\in\Theta\) such that \(s_1(\theta)\ne s_2(\theta)\), while both interpretations instantiate the identical objective and feasible set, then every optimizer \(x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_x T(x;\theta)\) is compatible with both meanings. Consequently, the optimization instance and its solution cannot identify which domain interpretation is intended without additional semantic information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When distinct domain meanings produce the same numerical problem, neither the optimizer nor its solution can select the intended meaning without external semantic information.
assumptions_latex: Both semantic maps yield the same numerical objective and feasible set at \(\theta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\) does not identify whether \(s_1(\theta)\) or \(s_2(\theta)\) is the intended interpretation.

notation.meaning: An optimizer of the numerical instance.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary idea is plausible, but no source is supplied and the conclusion presupposes an optimizer although nonemptiness of the argmin is not assumed.

children.title: Empirical Validation
children.top_down_role: Covers evidence used to assess template behavior against observed application data.

assumptions_latex: A nominal fixed-candidate confidence statement is applied to a decision selected after inspecting the same validation observations.
No simultaneous or selection-adjusted guarantee covering the selection rule is supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P\{R(\widehat x)\le U_m(\widehat x)\}\ge1-\delta\) does not follow from pointwise coverage for fixed \(x\).

notation.meaning: Decision selected using the validation sample.
Nominal sample-dependent upper bound for a candidate's population risk.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of a fixed-candidate holdout guarantee after unadjusted adaptive reuse of the same validation sample.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an upper bound \(U_m(x)\) has coverage \(\mathbb P\{R(x)\le U_m(x)\}\ge1-\delta\) for each candidate \(x\) fixed independently of the validation sample. If \(\widehat x\) is instead selected after inspecting that same sample, the pointwise statement alone does not imply \(\mathbb P\{R(\widehat x)\le U_m(\widehat x)\}\ge1-\delta\). Valid coverage then requires fresh validation data or an inference guarantee simultaneous over the selection rule's candidate class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A confidence bound valid for a fixed candidate need not retain its nominal coverage when the candidate is chosen by repeatedly inspecting the same validation data.
knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Validation-Reuse Boundary

assumptions_latex: The deployment or target risk is evaluated under a possibly different law \(P_{\mathrm{tar}}\).
No assumption or bound relates \(P_{\mathrm{tar}}\) to \(P_{\mathrm{val}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R_{P_{\mathrm{val}}}(x)\le\tau\ \not\Rightarrow\ R_{P_{\mathrm{tar}}}(x)\le\tau.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributional scope of an empirical validation certificate, distinguished from operational readiness under a changed environment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A holdout confidence bound based on observations from \(P_{\mathrm{val}}\) controls \(R_{P_{\mathrm{val}}}(x)=\mathbb E_{P_{\mathrm{val}}}[\ell(x,Z)]\). Without an assumption or independently verified bound relating a target law \(P_{\mathrm{tar}}\) to \(P_{\mathrm{val}}\), it entails no corresponding threshold guarantee for \(R_{P_{\mathrm{tar}}}(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A validation certificate controls risk under the validation distribution; without a justified link between distributions, it does not control risk under a different deployment distribution.
knowledge_statements.title: Validation-Distribution Scope Boundary
Empirical Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Holdout-sample criterion for validating a deployed decision against a prespecified application metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^\star\) be produced without using an independent validation sample \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m\), let \(\ell(x,Z)\in[0,1]\), and define \(\widehat R_m(x)=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m\ell(x,Z_i)\). For \(0<\delta<1\), Hoeffding's inequality gives \[\mathbb P\!\left\{R(x^\star)\le \widehat R_m(x^\star)+\sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{2m}}\right\}\ge1-\delta,\] where \(R(x)=\mathbb E[\ell(x,Z)]\). For a prespecified tolerance \(\tau\), the decision passes this validation rule when \[\widehat R_m(x^\star)+\sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{2m}}\le\tau.\] A passing result therefore supplies a \(1-\delta\) upper-confidence certificate at threshold \(\tau\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decision passes when its independent holdout loss plus a Hoeffding upper-confidence margin is at most the prescribed tolerance; the resulting bound has coverage at least one minus delta.
assumptions_latex: \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m\) are independent and identically distributed and independent of \(x^\star\).
\(0<\delta<1\), and \(\tau\) is prescribed independently of the validation sample.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P\{R(x^\star)\le \widehat R_m(x^\star)+\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/(2m)}\}\ge1-\delta\); if the displayed validation rule passes, its upper bound is at most \(\tau\).

notation.meaning: Population risk under the validation distribution.

children.title: Deployment Handoff
children.top_down_role: Covers transfer of a validated template into an operational setting.

assumptions_latex: The environment class \(\mathcal E\), index set \(J\), constraints \(g_j\), performance metric \(R\), and threshold \(\tau\) are declared before handoff.
Each reported upper bound is independently checkable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_j(x^\star,e)\le0\text{ for all }(j,e)\in J\times\mathcal E,\quad R(x^\star,e)\le\tau\text{ for all }e\in\mathcal E.\)

notation.meaning: Declared class of covered deployment environments.
Declared index set for operational constraints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical form and interpretation of a checkable handoff certificate, without prescribing an application-specific method for computing its bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a deployment-environment class \(\mathcal E\), an operational-constraint index set \(J\), constraints \(g_j(x,e)\le0\), and a required performance bound \(R(x,e)\le\tau\). A deployment-handoff certificate for \(x^\star\) may consist of independently checkable bounds \(u_j\) and \(u_R\) such that \[\sup_{e\in\mathcal E}g_j(x^\star,e)\le u_j\le0\quad(j\in J),\qquad \sup_{e\in\mathcal E}R(x^\star,e)\le u_R\le\tau.\] These inequalities certify the declared requirements throughout \(\mathcal E\), but make no assertion about undeclared environments or requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deployment handoff can certify all declared constraints and the performance threshold by checkable uniform upper bounds over the declared environment class; it says nothing outside that declaration.
knowledge_statements.title: Declaration-Relative Deployment Handoff Certificate
Deployment Handoff
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Checkable certificate connecting a validated optimizer to specified operational constraints and performance requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^\star\) be a validated optimizer, \(\mathcal E\) the declared deployment environment class, \(g_j(x,e)\le0\) the operational constraints, and \(R_e(x)\le\tau\) the required performance condition. A deployment-handoff certificate consists of verifiable bounds \(u_j\) and \(u_R\) satisfying \[\sup_{e\in\mathcal E}g_j(x^\star,e)\le u_j\le0\quad\text{for every }j,\qquad \sup_{e\in\mathcal E}R_e(x^\star)\le u_R\le\tau.\] The certificate applies only to the declared class \(\mathcal E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deployment handoff requires verifiable uniform bounds showing that the validated decision satisfies every operational constraint and performance threshold throughout the declared environment class.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal E\), the operational constraints, and the performance threshold are fixed before certification.
The bounds \(u_j\) and \(u_R\) are independently checkable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_j(x^\star,e)\le0\) and \(R_e(x^\star)\le\tau\) for every \(e\in\mathcal E\) and every \(j\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind fits the handoff leaf, but the uniform robustness formulation is uncited and domain-dependent. The range of the operational-constraint index j is also not introduced.

children.title: Deployment Readiness Boundary
children.top_down_role: Covers gaps that prevent empirical results from supporting operational use.

knowledge_statements.title: Deployment Readiness Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary beyond which validation or certification no longer entails safe operational use.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a deployment certificate establishes \(g_j(x^\star,e)\le0\) and \(R_e(x^\star)\le\tau\) only for environments \(e\in\mathcal E\). If the actual environment satisfies \(e_{\mathrm{act}}\notin\mathcal E\), the certificate entails neither \(g_j(x^\star,e_{\mathrm{act}})\le0\) nor \(R_{e_{\mathrm{act}}}(x^\star)\le\tau\). If instead \(e_{\mathrm{act}}\in\mathcal E\) but an actual operational constraint \(\widetilde g_j\) differs from the certified constraint \(g_j\), the certificate does not entail \(\widetilde g_j(x^\star,e_{\mathrm{act}})\le0\), although its certified performance conclusion may remain applicable. In either case, any readiness claim requiring all actual constraints and the stated performance threshold is not established. Convex optimality of \(x^\star\) does not remove this boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An out-of-class environment invalidates both certified feasibility and performance entailments. A changed operational constraint invalidates the corresponding feasibility entailment, though an otherwise applicable performance bound may remain. Either gap prevents a full readiness conclusion.
assumptions_latex: A certificate is restricted to \(e\in\mathcal E\), constraints \(g_j\), and performance functions \(R_e\).
Either \(e_{\mathrm{act}}\notin\mathcal E\), or \(e_{\mathrm{act}}\in\mathcal E\) and \(\widetilde g_j\ne g_j\) for some \(j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The certificate does not entail all actual deployment requirements at \(e_{\mathrm{act}}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary between properties of an encoded convex problem and validation of its external application model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let external domain theory select \(\theta\), \(C(\theta)\), \(f(\cdot;\theta)\), and an interpretation map \(s\). A certificate that \[x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C(\theta)}f(x;\theta)\] establishes optimality only relative to those encoded data. It does not, without separate premises, establish correctness of the domain theory, validity of \(\theta\), adequacy of \(C\) or \(f\), or correctness of \(s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimization can certify the encoded problem, but it cannot by itself validate the external theory, data, or interpretation that produced that problem.
assumptions_latex: The objective, feasible set, parameters, and interpretation are supplied externally.
\(x^\star\) is certified optimal for the encoded problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimality conclusion is conditional on the external modeling premises and does not validate them.
knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Scope of Optimization Conclusions
External Domain-Theory Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits what convex-programming results can establish about an externally supplied application model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a domain theory select parameters \(\theta\), feasible set \(C(\theta)\), objective \(f(\cdot;\theta)\), and interpretation map \(s\). Convex programming can establish properties such as feasibility or optimality of \(x^\star\) relative to the encoded problem \[x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C(\theta)}f(x;\theta).\] This conclusion alone establishes neither correctness of the domain theory, validity of \(\theta\), adequacy of \(C(\theta)\) and \(f\), nor correctness of \(s\); those are external premises requiring domain-specific evidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex optimization certifies properties of the encoded problem, not the correctness of the domain theory, parameters, objective, constraints, or interpretation that produced it.
assumptions_latex: \(x^\star\) is an optimizer of the encoded problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Optimality of \(x^\star\) is conditional on the externally supplied model and does not validate that model.

notation.meaning: Feasible set supplied by the application model.
External interpretation of model parameters and outputs.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 Data uncertainty in Linear Optimization p. 27

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1 Data uncertainty in Linear Optimization p. 27

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits the topic and is logically sound, but the cited section on data uncertainty in linear optimization does not inspectably support the broader claims about objectives, feasible sets, parameters, interpretations, and external domain theory.

children.title: Learning Domain Handoff
children.top_down_role: Covers transfer of convex templates into learning-oriented problem settings.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment condition for the convex learning handoff.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F(w)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(w;a_i,b_i)+\lambda r(w)+\delta_{\mathcal W}(w). If F is proper, lower semicontinuous, and level-bounded on \mathbb R^d, then F attains its minimum. In particular, attainment follows when \mathcal W is nonempty compact and the finite objective is lower semicontinuous on \mathcal W.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper lower-semicontinuous, level-bounded empirical objective has a minimizer; compact feasible sets give a common sufficient case.
assumptions_latex: F is proper and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{w\in\mathbb R^d}F(w)\neq\varnothing.

notation.meaning: Extended-value indicator of the hypothesis-parameter set.

knowledge_statements.title: Existence of an Empirical-Risk Minimizer
Learning Domain Handoff
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Empirical-risk representation of a supervised learning task as a convex optimization template.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=((a_i,b_i))_{i=1}^n\) be training data, \(\mathcal W\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) a nonempty convex hypothesis-parameter set, \(\ell(w;a,b)\) convex in \(w\), and \(r\) a convex regularizer. The learning task is handed to convex programming through the representation \[\widehat w\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{w\in\mathcal W}\left\{\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(w;a_i,b_i)+\lambda r(w)\right\},\qquad \lambda\ge0.\] The learned predictor is the domain-specified map \(h_{\widehat w}\), not merely the vector \(\widehat w\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A learning task becomes a convex template by minimizing regularized empirical loss over a convex parameter set, then interpreting the optimizer as a predictor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed empirical-risk problem is convex, and its optimizer parametrizes the learned predictor \(h_{\widehat w}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind and convex ERM formulation fit the leaf, but no locator is supplied. Convexity and nonemptiness of W alone also do not ensure that the displayed argmin contains an optimizer.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed boundary between empirical optimization and population guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exact minimization of convex empirical risk does not by itself imply a population-risk, consistency, calibration, fairness, robustness, or out-of-sample guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solving convex empirical risk alone does not certify statistical generalization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat w\in\operatorname*{argmin}F_S\centernot\implies R(\widehat w)-\inf_wR(w)\leq\varepsilon\text{ without statistical assumptions.}
review_flags: The claim is mathematically sound but primarily belongs to the Learning-to-Statistics Interface because it relates empirical optimization to population interpretation.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimization Does Not Imply Generalization

intermediate_metadata.reason: The leaf owns convex regularized empirical-risk handoff, predictor interpretation, and sufficient conditions for minimizer existence. The proposed generalization boundary was deferred to Learning-to-Statistics; statistical modeling, duality, certificates, and particular algorithms were excluded.

children.title: Statistical Domain Handoff
children.top_down_role: Covers transfer of convex templates into statistical modeling settings.

knowledge_statements.title: Statistical Domain Handoff
knowledge_statements.scope_note: M-estimation representation linking a sample convex program to a population statistical target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n\) be observations, let \(\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be a nonempty convex parameter set, and let \(m(\theta;z)\) be convex in \(\theta\). The statistical handoff represents the estimator and its population target as \[\widehat\theta_n\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta\in\Theta}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n m(\theta;Z_i),\qquad \theta_\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb E_Q[m(\theta;Z)].\] Convex optimization computes \(\widehat\theta_n\); claims relating it to \(\theta_\star\) additionally require statistical assumptions on \(Q\), identifiability, and sampling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex M-estimator minimizes a sample criterion, while its population target minimizes expected criterion loss; connecting the two requires separate statistical assumptions.
assumptions_latex: The displayed expectations are finite where required, and both displayed argmin sets are nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\theta_n\) is obtained by convex optimization, whereas inference about \(\theta_\star\) is conditional on additional statistical assumptions.

children.title: Learning-to-Statistics Interface
children.top_down_role: Covers shared template roles across learning-oriented and statistical uses.

assumptions_latex: The observations \((a_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n\) are conditionally independent under a parameter \(\theta\in\Theta\), where \(\Theta\) is convex.
Each loss \(\ell_i(\theta)=-\log p_\theta(y_i\mid a_i)\) and the regularizer \(R:\Theta\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper convex functions.
The density proportional to \(\exp(-n\lambda R(\theta))\) is normalizable for \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta\in\Theta}\left\{\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell_i(\theta)+\lambda R(\theta)\right\}=\operatorname*{argmax}_{\theta\in\Theta}p(\theta\mid (a_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n).\]

notation.meaning: Model parameter and its convex domain.
Negative conditional log-likelihood for observation i.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sample regularized likelihood interpreted as Bayesian maximum a posteriori estimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For data \((a_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n\), define the regularized empirical-risk estimator by \[\widehat\theta\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta\in\Theta}\left\{\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell_i(\theta)+\lambda R(\theta)\right\}.\] If \(\ell_i(\theta)=-\log p_\theta(y_i\mid a_i)\) and the prior satisfies \(\pi(\theta)\propto\exp(-n\lambda R(\theta))\), then the displayed objective equals the negative log-posterior up to an additive constant. Consequently, its minimizers are precisely the maximum a posteriori estimators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regularized empirical likelihood becomes maximum a posteriori estimation when the prior’s negative log-density equals the scaled regularizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Learning-to-Statistics Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The MAP correspondence is mathematically coherent and fits the interface container, but the record supplies no inspectable source for the likelihood-prior scaling or conclusion.

children.title: Inverse-Problem Domain Handoff
children.top_down_role: Covers transfer of convex templates into inverse-problem settings.

assumptions_latex: \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear, \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty closed convex, and \(\phi,R\) are proper closed convex functions.
No coercivity, strict convexity, injectivity, or statistical identifiability assumption is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Convexity alone does not imply attainment, uniqueness, or stable recovery of the underlying object.}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes convex representability of an inverse problem from existence, uniqueness, and recovery guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the convex inverse formulation \[\inf_{x\in C}\{\phi(Ax-b)+\lambda R(x)\},\] convexity of the objective and feasible set does not by itself ensure that the infimum is attained, that a minimizer is unique, or that a minimizer stably recovers an underlying object. Attainment needs an additional compactness, coercivity, or level-boundedness condition; uniqueness needs suitable strict convexity or identifiability; recovery guarantees need further assumptions on the forward map, noise, and model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex inverse formulation can still be unattained, nonunique, or statistically unstable unless additional existence, identifiability, and recovery assumptions hold.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Versus Solvability and Recovery

assumptions_latex: The forward map \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear and the observation is \(b\in\mathbb R^m\).
The functions \(\phi\) and \(R\) are proper closed convex, the set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty closed convex, and \(\lambda\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\widehat x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\{\phi(Ax-b)+\lambda R(x)\}\] is a convex-programming formulation of the inverse problem.

notation.meaning: Data-fidelity function, regularizer, and feasible set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional linear inverse problems with convex fidelity, prior penalty, and constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An inverse problem with forward operator \(A\), data \(b\), admissible set \(C\), data-fidelity function \(\phi\), and regularizer \(R\) is handed to convex programming as \[\widehat x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\{\phi(Ax-b)+\lambda R(x)\}.\] The objective is convex because affine precomposition preserves convexity and nonnegative weighted sums of convex functions are convex. Thus the domain quantities determine a convex objective and feasible set without changing the physical interpretation of \(A\widehat x\) as predicted data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear inverse problem becomes a convex program by combining convex data mismatch, convex regularization, and convex admissibility constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Inverse-Problem Domain Handoff

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional convex inverse-problem representation is standard and locally appropriate, but no citation supports the formulation.

children.title: Imaging Domain Handoff
children.top_down_role: Covers transfer of convex templates into imaging settings.

assumptions_latex: The image is represented by \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), the acquisition model is \(b=Ax+\varepsilon\), and \(A\) is linear.
The bound vector satisfies \(u\in\mathbb R_+^n\), the discrete gradient \(D\) is linear, and \(\lambda\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\widehat x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{0\leq x\leq u}\left\{\frac12\|Ax-b\|_2^2+\lambda\|Dx\|_1\right\}\] is a convex imaging reconstruction.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear imaging with Gaussian data fidelity, total variation, and intensity bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a linear imaging system \(b=Ax+\varepsilon\), bounded-intensity total-variation reconstruction is the template \[\widehat x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{0\leq x\leq u}\left\{\frac12\|Ax-b\|_2^2+\lambda\|Dx\|_1\right\}.\] The quadratic data term, the \(\ell_1\)-norm of the discrete gradient, and the box \(\{x:0\leq x\leq u\}\) are convex. The optimizer is therefore an image-domain estimate whose forward projection \(A\widehat x\) can be compared directly with the acquired measurements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vectorized linear imaging with total variation and intensity bounds is directly expressible as a convex reconstruction problem.
knowledge_statements.title: Imaging Domain Handoff

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded total-variation imaging model is mathematically consistent and appropriately classified as a representation, but it has no supporting citation.

children.title: Reconstruction-to-Imaging Interface
children.top_down_role: Covers the shared template boundary between reconstruction structure and imaging interpretation.

assumptions_latex: \(\phi:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(R:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper convex functions.
\(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and convex, and \(\lambda\geq0\).
The joint effective domain of \(x\mapsto\phi(Ax-b)+\lambda R(x)+\delta_C(x)\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(z)=\phi(z-b),\ K=A,\ G(x)=\lambda R(x)+\delta_C(x)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \inf_x\{F(Kx)+G(x)\}=\inf_{x\in C}\{\phi(Ax-b)+\lambda R(x)\},

notation.meaning: Convex indicator of the admissible image set.
Generic composite-template functions and linear operator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convexity conditions for mapping a generic composite reconstruction template into imaging semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The substitutions \(K=A\), \(F(z)=\phi(z-b)\), and \(G(x)=\lambda R(x)+\delta_C(x)\) produce the imaging objective \[F(Kx)+G(x)=\phi(Ax-b)+\lambda R(x)+\delta_C(x).\] This is a proper convex composite objective when \(A\) is linear, \(\phi\) and \(R\) are proper convex, \(C\) is nonempty convex, \(\lambda\geq0\), and the joint effective domain is nonempty. Without these conditions, the semantic substitution alone does not establish convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reconstruction-to-imaging substitution is convex only when the acquisition map is linear and the fidelity, image penalty, and admissible set have the required convexity and domain compatibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity Conditions for the Imaging Substitution
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Conditions for the Imaging Substitution

assumptions_latex: The imaging forward model \(A\), observed image data \(b\), and admissible image set \(C\) are specified.
The noise model induces a convex negative log-likelihood \(\phi\), and the image model induces a convex penalty \(R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\min_{x\in C}\phi(Ax-b)+\lambda R(x)\] is the reconstruction template instantiated by the imaging model.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identification of imaging semantics with a generic convex reconstruction template.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The reconstruction-to-imaging interface makes the substitutions \(K=A\), \(y=b\), \(F(z)=\phi(z-b)\), and \(G(x)=\lambda R(x)+\delta_C(x)\) in the composite template \(\min_x F(Kx)+G(x)\), where \(\delta_C\) is the convex indicator of \(C\). Hence \[\min_x F(Kx)+G(x)=\min_{x\in C}\{\phi(Ax-b)+\lambda R(x)\}.\] The forward model, noise law, image prior, and physical bounds determine the operator, fidelity, regularizer, and feasible set, respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The generic composite reconstruction template becomes an imaging problem by mapping acquisition, noise, image structure, and physical bounds to its four components.
knowledge_statements.title: Reconstruction-to-Imaging Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied, and the assumptions do not explicitly state that A is linear or that C is convex, although both are required for the claimed convex composite representation.

children.title: Allocation Domain Handoff
children.top_down_role: Covers transfer of convex templates into resource-allocation settings.

assumptions_latex: The allocation vector is \(x\in\mathbb R_+^n\), available resources are \(c\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(B\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\).
Each utility \(u_i:\mathbb R_+\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\) is concave, and the feasible allocation set \(\{x\geq0:Bx\leq c\}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\max_{x\geq0,\,Bx\leq c}\sum_{i=1}^n u_i(x_i)= -\min_{x\geq0,\,Bx\leq c}\sum_{i=1}^n[-u_i(x_i)]\] is a convex optimization handoff.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separable concave utility maximization under linear resource capacities.

source_refs.locator: 1. Basic Concepts of Convex Analysis p. 1

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A divisible-resource allocation problem with concave utilities is \[\max_{x\geq0,\,Bx\leq c}\sum_{i=1}^n u_i(x_i).\] Its convex minimization form is obtained by negating the objective: \[\min_{x\geq0,\,Bx\leq c}\sum_{i=1}^n[-u_i(x_i)].\] Because each \(-u_i\) is convex and the resource and nonnegativity constraints are affine, this is a convex program. Its optimizer allocates resources while respecting every capacity represented by \(Bx\leq c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Concave utility maximization with linear capacities is handed to a convex solver by minimizing negative total utility over feasible allocations.
knowledge_statements.title: Allocation Domain Handoff

source_witnesses.locator: 1. Basic Concepts of Convex Analysis p. 1

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shadow-price interpretation for separable concave allocation.

For \max\{\sum_i u_i(x_i):x\geq0,\ Bx\leq c\}, suppose the utilities are closed concave and differentiable at a feasible x^\star, and a Slater point exists. Then x^\star is optimal if and only if there are p^\star,
u^\star\geq0 satisfying u_i'(x_i^\star)=(B^	op p^\star)_i-
u_i^\star,\ p_j^\star((Bx^\star)_j-c_j)=0, and 
u_i^\star x_i^\star=0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under Slater regularity, feasibility, stationarity, and complementary slackness characterize an optimum, with capacity multipliers interpreted as resource prices.
assumptions_latex: Each u_i is proper closed concave and differentiable at x_i^\star.
There exists \bar x>0 with B\bar x<c.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^\star\text{ is optimal if and only if the stated KKT conditions hold.}
knowledge_statements.title: Resource Prices and Allocation Optimality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the direct convex allocation handoff.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The formulation \min\{-\sum_i u_i(x_i):x\geq0,\ Bx\leq c\} is convex when total utility is concave on a convex feasible set. Nonconcave utility, integer indivisibility, or a nonconvex coupling constraint generally invalidates this direct convex representation, although a relaxation may remain convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonconcave utilities, indivisible allocations, or nonconvex coupling constraints invalidate the direct convex handoff.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Utility concavity and feasible-set convexity are required for the stated convex representation.}
knowledge_statements.title: Allocation Convexity Boundary

children.title: Network Domain Handoff
children.top_down_role: Covers transfer of convex templates into network-oriented settings.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Network interpretation of optimality for separable convex-cost capacitated flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f^\star satisfy Nf^\star=d and 0\leq f^\star\leq c. Under a relative-interior constraint qualification, f^\star minimizes \sum_e\varphi_e(f_e) if and only if there are node potentials \pi, bound multipliers \alpha,\beta\geq0, and g_e\in\partial\varphi_e(f_e^\star) such that g+N^\top\pi-\alpha+\beta=0,\ \alpha_e f_e^\star=0, and \beta_e(c_e-f_e^\star)=0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible convex-cost flow is optimal exactly when edge marginal costs balance node-potential differences and active capacity multipliers.
assumptions_latex: A relative-interior feasible flow exists for the effective edge-cost domains and affine constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^\star\text{ is optimal if and only if the stated network KKT system holds.}
review_flags: Signs correspond to the Lagrangian convention \pi^\top(Nf-d)-\alpha^\top f+\beta^\top(f-c).
knowledge_statements.title: Node-Potential Optimality Certificate

assumptions_latex: A directed network has node-edge incidence matrix \(N\), demand vector \(d\), and capacities \(c\in\mathbb R_+^E\).
Each edge cost \(\varphi_e:[0,c_e]\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper convex, and \(\{f:Nf=d,\ 0\leq f\leq c\}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\widehat f\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{Nf=d,\,0\leq f\leq c}\sum_{e\in E}\varphi_e(f_e)\] is a convex network-flow formulation.

notation.meaning: Node-edge incidence matrix and net demands.
Capacity and convex cost of edge e.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-commodity capacitated flow with separable convex edge costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A capacitated network problem is handed to convex programming as \[\widehat f\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{Nf=d,\,0\leq f\leq c}\sum_{e\in E}\varphi_e(f_e).\] The equality \(Nf=d\) enforces flow conservation and prescribed net supply or demand, while the componentwise inequalities impose edge capacities. Since the objective is a sum of convex edge costs and all constraints are affine, the feasible problem is convex. The optimizer \(\widehat f\) is therefore a domain-valid network flow minimizing total routing cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex edge costs, flow conservation, and capacity bounds produce a convex network-flow problem whose optimizer is directly interpretable as routed flow.
knowledge_statements.title: Network Domain Handoff

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The single-commodity separable convex-cost flow formulation is precise and fits the handoff container, but no inspectable network-optimization source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed generic Farkas certificate for the bounded balance system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For Nf=d and 0\leq f\leq c, infeasibility is certified by y and u,v\geq0 satisfying N^\top y-u+v=0 and d^\top y+c^\top v<0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Farkas multiplier can certify incompatibility of balance and capacity constraints.
assumptions_latex: N,d, and finite c\geq0 are given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{f:Nf=d,\ 0\leq f\leq c\}=\varnothing\iff\exists(y,u,v):u,v\geq0,\ N^\top y-u+v=0,\ d^\top y+c^\top v<0.
review_flags: This is the generic Farkas alternative for affine bounds, not a primarily network-owned statement; a cut-form network theorem would be local.
knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Balance Feasibility Certificate

intermediate_metadata.reason: The leaf owns the separable convex-cost flow handoff and its node-potential/capacity-price optimality interpretation. The proposed generic Farkas alternative was deferred to general duality; specialized circulation, cut, algorithmic, allocation, and finance results were excluded.

children.title: Finance Domain Handoff
children.top_down_role: Covers transfer of convex templates into financial decision settings.

assumptions_latex: The portfolio return vector has mean \(\mu\in\mathbb R^n\) and covariance matrix \(\Sigma\in\mathbb S_+^n\).
The admissible portfolio set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty closed convex and includes the budget constraint \(\mathbf1^\top w=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\widehat w\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{w\in C,\,\mathbf1^\top w=1}\left\{\frac\gamma2w^\top\Sigma w-\mu^\top w\right\}\] is a convex quadratic portfolio model.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional mean-variance portfolio selection with convex trading restrictions.

source_refs.locator: 2.3 Analysis with symmetric matrices p. 16

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Mean-variance portfolio selection is handed to convex programming as \[\widehat w\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{w\in C,\,\mathbf1^\top w=1}\left\{\frac\gamma2w^\top\Sigma w-\mu^\top w\right\}.\] The quadratic risk term is convex because \(\Sigma\succeq0\), expected return contributes a linear term, and the budget equation is affine. Any convex trading restrictions, such as long-only bounds, may be included in \(C\). The optimizer balances variance against expected return at the specified risk aversion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mean-variance portfolio choice is a convex quadratic program when covariance is positive semidefinite and trading restrictions form a convex set.
knowledge_statements.title: Finance Domain Handoff

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3 Analysis with symmetric matrices p. 16

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Curvature and feasible-set boundary for the direct mean-variance handoff.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function w\mapsto w^\top\Sigma w is convex on \mathbb R^n if and only if (\Sigma+\Sigma^\top)/2\succeq0. On a restricted portfolio domain, negative curvature along a feasible line segment destroys convexity. Nonconvex trading restrictions likewise invalidate the direct convex-QP handoff.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive-semidefinite risk curvature along feasible directions and convex trading restrictions are required for the direct convex formulation.
assumptions_latex: Only the symmetric part of \Sigma contributes to w^\top\Sigma w.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: w^\top\Sigma w\text{ is convex on }\mathbb R^n\iff(\Sigma+\Sigma^\top)/2\succeq0.
knowledge_statements.title: Mean-Variance Convexity Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constrained efficient-frontier form of the mean-variance handoff.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \Sigma\succeq0, a convex admissible set C, and target return \rho, \[\operatorname*{minimize}_{w\in C}\ \tfrac12w^\top\Sigma w\quad\text{subject to}\quad\mathbf1^\top w=1,\ \mu^\top w\geq\rho\] is a convex quadratic program. Every attained optimizer minimizes variance among admissible portfolios meeting the target.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum variance subject to a target expected return is a convex quadratic portfolio model.
assumptions_latex: The budget and target-return constraints are feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The displayed target-return problem is a convex quadratic program.}
review_flags: No optimizer-existence claim is made without closedness and an attainment condition.
knowledge_statements.title: Target-Return Portfolio Form

children.title: Engineering Domain Handoff
children.top_down_role: Covers transfer of convex templates into engineering analysis settings.

knowledge_statements.title: Engineering Domain Handoff
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robust convex engineering design under deterministic set-valued uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\in\mathbb N\). An uncertain engineering design problem is handed to convex programming as \[\operatorname*{minimize}_{z\in Z}\ f(z)\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sup_{q\in U}g_j(z,q)\leq0,\qquad j=1,\ldots,m.\] When every \(g_j(\cdot,q)\) is convex, these worst-case constraints define a convex feasible set and enforce the modeled engineering requirements for every \(q\in U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An engineering design problem with convex realization-wise constraints becomes a robust convex program by imposing each constraint for every modeled uncertainty realization.
assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb N\), the design variable lies in a nonempty convex set \(Z\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and the uncertainty set \(U\) is nonempty.
For every \(j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and \(q\in U\), the function \(z\mapsto g_j(z,q)\) is convex on \(Z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname*{minimize}_{z\in Z}\ f(z)\quad\text{subject to}\quad\sup_{q\in U}g_j(z,q)\leq0\quad(j=1,\ldots,m)\] is a convex robust engineering representation.

notation.meaning: Engineering design variable and its convex domain.

source_refs.locator: 5.1 Robust Counterpart representation of a safe convex approximation to a scalar chance constraint p. 111

source_witnesses.locator: 5.1 Robust Counterpart representation of a safe convex approximation to a scalar chance constraint p. 111

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Robust Convexity Does Not Ensure Tractability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computational boundary of the generic robust engineering handoff.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every g_j(\cdot,q) is convex, then z\mapsto\sup_{q\in U}g_j(z,q) is convex. This alone supplies neither a finite-dimensional representation nor an efficient evaluation or separation oracle; tractability requires additional structure in U and in the dependence on q.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointwise convexity guarantees a convex robust constraint but not a tractable representation or oracle.
assumptions_latex: For every q\in U, g_j(\cdot,q) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{q\in U}g_j(\cdot,q)\text{ is convex, but tractability does not follow without additional structure.}
knowledge_statements.title: Robust Convexity Does Not Ensure Tractability

children.title: Design Domain Handoff
children.top_down_role: Covers transfer of convex templates into design decision settings.

knowledge_statements.title: Design Domain Handoff
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-compliance truss sizing with affine positive-definite stiffness and a volume budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For member sizes \(a\), affine stiffness \(K(a)=\sum_{i=1}^p a_iK_i\), and load \(f\), the compliance-design handoff is \[\operatorname*{infimize}_{a\in D}\ f^\top K(a)^{-1}f,\qquad D=\{a\in\mathbb R_+^p:l^\top a\leq V,\ K(a)\succ0\}.\] This is a convex optimization representation on the positive-definite stiffness domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine-stiffness compliance design is a convex optimization problem over nonnegative member sizes satisfying the volume budget and positive-definite stiffness condition.
assumptions_latex: The design variables satisfy \(a\in\mathbb R_+^p\), and \(K(a)=\sum_{i=1}^p a_iK_i\) with \(K_i\in\mathbb S_+^n\).
The load is \(f\in\mathbb R^n\), the member-length vector is \(l\in\mathbb R_+^p\), and \(V>0\).
The domain \(D=\{a\in\mathbb R_+^p:l^\top a\leq V,\ K(a)\succ0\}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname*{infimize}_{a\in D}\ f^\top K(a)^{-1}f,\qquad D=\{a\in\mathbb R_+^p:l^\top a\leq V,\ K(a)\succ0\},\] is a convex compliance-design problem.

children.title: Analysis-to-Design Interface
children.top_down_role: Covers template roles linking engineering analysis to design choices.

assumptions_latex: The stiffness matrix is affine, \(K(a)=\sum_{i=1}^p a_iK_i\), and satisfies \(K(a)\succ0\).
The load vector is \(f\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(t\in\mathbb R\) is a compliance bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f^\top K(a)^{-1}f\leq t\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\begin{pmatrix}K(a)&f\\f^\top&t\end{pmatrix}\succeq0.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Schur-complement transfer from structural response analysis to semidefinite design constraints.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.5 Application: Truss topology design p. 21
2.3 Analysis with symmetric matrices p. 16

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(K(a)\succ0\), the structural-analysis inequality \(f^\top K(a)^{-1}f\leq t\) has the semidefinite representation \[f^\top K(a)^{-1}f\leq t\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\begin{pmatrix}K(a)&f\\f^\top&t\end{pmatrix}\succeq0.\] Thus a bound on analyzed compliance becomes a linear matrix inequality in the design variables whenever \(K(a)\) is affine. Minimizing \(t\) subject to this constraint and convex design restrictions transfers the response calculation into a convex design program.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compliance bound becomes a linear matrix inequality through the Schur complement, connecting structural analysis to semidefinite design optimization.
knowledge_statements.title: Analysis-to-Design Interface

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3.5 Application: Truss topology design p. 21
2.3 Analysis with symmetric matrices p. 16

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized Schur-complement boundary for positive-semidefinite stiffness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For K\succeq0, \[\begin{pmatrix}K&f\\f^\top&t\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f\in\operatorname{range}(K)\ \text{and}\ t\geq f^\top K^\dagger f.\] Thus merely replacing K^{-1} by K^\dagger without the range condition is not an exact extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With singular stiffness, the compliance LMI is exact only when the load lies in the stiffness range and the bound dominates pseudoinverse compliance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{pmatrix}K&f\\f^\top&t\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\iff f\in\operatorname{range}(K),\ t\geq f^\top K^\dagger f.

notation.meaning: Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of the stiffness matrix.

children.title: Discrete-Decision Boundary
children.top_down_role: Covers template limits caused by discrete decision structure.

assumptions_latex: At least two distinct feasible binary vectors are present; concretely take \(e_1,e_2\in\{0,1\}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\frac12e_1+\frac12e_2\notin\{0,1\}^n,\] so binary feasibility is nonconvex and its convex relaxation may admit fractional decisions.

notation.meaning: First and second standard basis vectors.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary integrality as a sharp boundary of direct convex modeling.

source_refs.locator: 1. Basic Concepts of Convex Analysis p. 1

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The binary decision set \(S=\{0,1\}^n\) is not convex when \(n\geq2\): both \(e_1\) and \(e_2\) belong to \(S\), but \(\tfrac12(e_1+e_2)\notin S\). Replacing \(S\) by its convex hull gives \(\operatorname{conv}(S)=[0,1]^n\), which admits fractional points. Therefore a convex relaxation can provide bounds or candidate solutions, but feasibility for the relaxation does not certify feasibility for the original discrete-decision problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary decisions destroy convexity; their box relaxation admits fractional points and therefore does not certify discrete feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Discrete-Decision Boundary

source_witnesses.locator: 1. Basic Concepts of Convex Analysis p. 1

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\text{ is convex as a subset of }\mathbb R^n\iff |D|\leq 1.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp convexity boundary for decision sets contained in an integer lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\). Viewed as a subset of \(\mathbb R^n\), \(D\) is convex if and only if it is empty or a singleton. In particular, every lattice-valued decision set containing two distinct decisions is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integer-lattice decision set is convex only when it is empty or contains one point.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Boundary for Lattice-Valued Decisions

children.title: Rank-Constraint Boundary
children.top_down_role: Covers template limits associated with rank restrictions.

assumptions_latex: The rank bound satisfies \(r\geq1\), and matrices lie in \(\mathbb S_+^{2r}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{rank}(X)=\operatorname{rank}(Y)=r,\qquad \operatorname{rank}\!\left(\frac{X+Y}{2}\right)=2r>r,\] so the rank-bounded set is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-semidefinite rank upper bounds as a nonconvex modeling boundary.

source_refs.locator: 2.3 Analysis with symmetric matrices p. 16

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(r\geq1\), let \(X=\operatorname{diag}(I_r,0_r)\) and \(Y=\operatorname{diag}(0_r,I_r)\) in \(\mathbb S_+^{2r}\). Both satisfy the constraint \(\operatorname{rank}(Z)\leq r\), whereas \[\frac{X+Y}{2}=\frac12I_{2r}\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{rank}\!\left(\frac{X+Y}{2}\right)=2r.\] Hence \(\{Z\in\mathbb S_+^{2r}:\operatorname{rank}(Z)\leq r\}\) is nonconvex. A rank upper bound therefore lies outside a direct convex template unless replaced by a relaxation or otherwise reformulated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two positive semidefinite rank-r matrices can have a full-rank midpoint, so an upper rank constraint is intrinsically nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Constraint Boundary

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3 Analysis with symmetric matrices p. 16

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{X\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}:\operatorname{rank}(X)\le r\}\text{ is convex}\iff r=0\text{ or }r\ge\min\{m,n\}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp degenerate, nontrivial, and inactive parameter regimes for rectangular and PSD upper-rank constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(M_r=\{X\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}:\operatorname{rank}(X)\le r\}\), convexity holds exactly when \(r=0\) or \(r\ge\min\{m,n\}\). Likewise, for \(S_r=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\operatorname{rank}(X)\le r\}\), convexity holds exactly when \(r=0\) or \(r\ge n\). Thus every nontrivial active upper-rank constraint is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rectangular or PSD upper-rank constraint is convex only when it forces the zero matrix or is inactive.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp Convexity Boundary for Rank Caps
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Convexity Boundary for Rank Caps

assumptions_latex: No normalization or additional side constraints are imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}(M_r)=\mathbb R^{m\times n},\qquad \operatorname{conv}(S_r)=\mathbb S_+^n.

notation.meaning: Matrices of rank at most r.
PSD matrices of rank at most r.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexification of nontrivial rank caps in the absence of normalization or other side constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M_r=\{X\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}:\operatorname{rank}(X)\le r\}\) with \(1\le r<\min\{m,n\}\), and let \(S_r=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\operatorname{rank}(X)\le r\}\) with \(1\le r<n\). Then \[\operatorname{conv}(M_r)=\mathbb R^{m\times n},\qquad \operatorname{conv}(S_r)=\mathbb S_+^n.\] Hence convexifying a bare positive rank cap removes the restriction entirely; normalization or side constraints materially change the convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without side constraints, the convex hull of a positive rectangular rank cap is the full matrix space, and the PSD counterpart is the full PSD cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Hulls of Unconstrained Rank Caps
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Hulls of Unconstrained Rank Caps

children.title: Cardinality-Constraint Boundary
children.top_down_role: Covers template limits associated with cardinality restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Cardinality-Constraint Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonconvexity of an upper cardinality constraint in Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\ge 2\), \(1\le k<n\), and \(S_k=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\|x\|_0\le k\}\). The set \(S_k\) is nonconvex. Thus an upper cardinality constraint on a decision vector is outside the ordinary convex feasible-set template.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nontrivial sparsity limit, the set of vectors having at most k nonzero coordinates is nonconvex, so an upper cardinality constraint is outside the ordinary convex feasible-set template.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The set \(S_k=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\|x\|_0\le k\}\) is nonconvex.

notation.meaning: Number of nonzero coordinates of x.
Set of vectors having at most k nonzero coordinates.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H_k(z)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x:\|x\|_0\le k}\|x-z\|_2.

notation.meaning: Hard-thresholding operator retaining k largest-magnitude coordinates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Euclidean projection onto an upper-cardinality set, including nonuniqueness from a positive tie at the cutoff.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S_k=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\|x\|_0\le k\}\) with \(1\le k<n\), retain any \(k\) indices of largest \(|z_i|\) and set all other coordinates to zero. Every resulting \(H_k(z)\) satisfies \[H_k(z)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S_k}\|x-z\|_2.\] The projection is unique if \(\|z\|_0\le k\) or \(|z|_{(k)}>|z|_{(k+1)}\); it is nonunique exactly when \(|z|_{(k)}=|z|_{(k+1)}>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Keeping the k largest-magnitude coordinates gives an exact Euclidean projection onto the sparsity set; only a positive tie across the cutoff causes nonuniqueness.
knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Projection by Hard Thresholding

assumptions_latex: The entries of \(A\) and \(b\) are rational and encoded in binary.
The sparsity limit \(k<n\) is part of the input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Computing a global solution of the displayed cardinality-constrained least-squares problem is NP-hard.}

notation.meaning: Rational regression data and sparsity limit.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case computational boundary for exact sparse least-squares optimization with binary-encoded rational data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given rational \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Q^m\), and an input sparsity limit \(k<n\), the problem \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\ \|Ax-b\|_2^2\quad\text{subject to}\quad\|x\|_0\le k\] is NP-hard in the binary input size. Thus easy projection onto the bare set \(S_k\) does not make general cardinality-constrained least-squares optimization polynomial-time solvable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: General exact sparse least squares is NP-hard even though Euclidean projection onto the bare sparsity set is easy.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: General Cardinality-Constrained Least Squares Is NP-Hard
knowledge_statements.title: General Cardinality-Constrained Least Squares Is NP-Hard

notation.meaning: Unit-box vectors with at most k nonzero coordinates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convex hull of the cardinality-constrained unit box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), let \(C_k=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\|x\|_0\le k,\ \|x\|_\infty\le1\}\). Then \[\operatorname{conv}C_k=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\|x\|_\infty\le1,\ \|x\|_1\le k\}.\] The right-hand side generally contains vectors with more than \(k\) nonzero coordinates, so it is the exact hull rather than an exact reformulation of the original set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Within the unit box, the convex hull of vectors having at most k nonzeros is exactly the intersection of that box with the l1 ball of radius k.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Hull of Box-Bounded Sparse Vectors

children.title: Bilinear Boundary
children.top_down_role: Covers template limits arising from bilinear structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Bilinear Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic bilinear constraints, excluding special reformulations that eliminate or convexify one factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(b:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\), defined by \(b(x,y)=xy\), is neither convex nor concave on \(\mathbb R^2\). The level set \(F=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:xy=1\}\) is nonconvex. Consequently, an unreformed product of two decision variables does not generally fit the convex objective or convex feasible-set template, although additional structure can permit a convex reformulation or relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A product of two unrestricted real decision variables is neither convex nor concave, and its unit-level set is nonconvex. Special structure may nevertheless permit reformulation or relaxation.
assumptions_latex: Variables are real and unrestricted unless the displayed set imposes bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A bilinear equality or inequality need not define a convex feasible set.

notation.meaning: The unit-level set of the product.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convex hull of one scalar bilinear graph over a finite rectangle; generally a relaxation of the graph itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=\{(x,y,w):\ell_x\le x\le u_x,\ \ell_y\le y\le u_y,\ w=xy\}\), where \(\ell_x<u_x\) and \(\ell_y<u_y\) are finite. Then \(\operatorname{conv}G\) is exactly the box bounds together with \[w\ge \ell_xy+\ell_yx-\ell_x\ell_y,\quad w\ge u_xy+u_yx-u_xu_y,\] \[w\le u_xy+\ell_yx-u_x\ell_y,\quad w\le \ell_xy+u_yx-\ell_xu_y.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Over a finite rectangle, four McCormick inequalities give the exact convex hull of a scalar bilinear graph, although generally not the graph itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: McCormick Hull of a Bounded Bilinear Graph
knowledge_statements.title: McCormick Hull of a Bounded Bilinear Graph

children.title: Fractional Boundary
children.top_down_role: Covers template limits arising from fractional structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic fractional expressions; linear-fractional objectives may retain quasiconvex or reformulable structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On the convex domain \(D=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:y>0\}\), the function \(f(x,y)=x/y\) is neither convex nor concave. Hence positivity of a decision-dependent denominator alone does not place a fractional expression within the convex-function template. Specialized linear-fractional transformations and quasiconvex methods remain separate admissible cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even with a positive denominator, x divided by y is neither convex nor concave on the positive-denominator half-plane. Specialized linear-fractional or quasiconvex methods are separate cases.
assumptions_latex: The denominator is positive on the stated domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A ratio of convex-compatible expressions need not be convex, even when its denominator is positive and affine.

notation.meaning: A linear-fractional example on the positive-denominator half-plane.
Domain on which the denominator is positive.

source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry
source_refs.locator: 1 What is Convex Algebraic Geometry? p. 1

source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is quasiconvex and quasiconcave on }C.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sublevel and superlevel geometry of a scalar affine ratio on a positive-denominator convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and \(d^Tx+\beta>0\) on \(C\). For \(f(x)=(c^Tx+\alpha)/(d^Tx+\beta)\) and every \(t\in\mathbb R\), \[\{x\in C:f(x)\le t\}=C\cap\{x:(c-td)^Tx+\alpha-t\beta\le0\},\] while the superlevel set is obtained by reversing the inequality. Thus \(f\) is both quasiconvex and quasiconcave, although it need not be convex or concave.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine ratio with a positive affine denominator has halfspace sublevel and superlevel sets, making it quasilinear even when it is not convex or concave.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Fractional Quasilinearity

assumptions_latex: The transformed domain retains the strict condition \(t>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\longleftrightarrow(y,t)=(x/(d^Tx+\beta),1/(d^Tx+\beta))\text{ is a feasibility- and value-preserving bijection.}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact reciprocal-scaling transformation for a positive-denominator linear-fractional program; no claim that the strict transformed feasible set is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[\min\left\{\frac{c^Tx+\alpha}{d^Tx+\beta}:Ax\le b,\ d^Tx+\beta>0\right\},\] set \(t=(d^Tx+\beta)^{-1}\) and \(y=tx\). Original feasible points correspond bijectively to \[(y,t):Ay\le bt,\quad d^Ty+\beta t=1,\quad t>0,\] the objective becomes \(c^Ty+\alpha t\), and the inverse map is \(x=y/t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-denominator linear-fractional program admits an exact reciprocal-scaling formulation with affine constraints and strict positive scaling; recovery is x=y/t.
knowledge_statements.title: Charnes-Cooper Reciprocal Scaling

children.title: Signomial Boundary
children.top_down_role: Covers template limits arising from signomial structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Signomial Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mixed-sign signomials on the positive orthant, contrasted with positive-coefficient geometric-programming forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A signomial on \(\mathbb R_{++}^n\) has the form \(s(x)=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{a_{ij}}\), where \(m,n\in\mathbb N\) and \(c_j,a_{ij}\in\mathbb R\). Mixed coefficient signs provide no general convexity guarantee: the signomial \(g(t)=t-t^2\) is strictly concave on \(\mathbb R_{++}\), and its logarithmically transformed expression \(e^z-e^{2z}\) is not convex on \(\mathbb R\). Thus unrestricted signomials lie outside the standard convex geometric-programming template.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A signomial may use real coefficients and exponents. Mixed coefficient signs provide no general convexity guarantee and can defeat the logarithmic convexification available for positive-coefficient geometric programs.
assumptions_latex: Decision variables lie in the positive orthant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Allowing coefficients of both signs in a signomial destroys the general convexity guarantee available to geometric-programming posynomials after logarithmic transformation.

notation.meaning: A finite sum of generalized monomials with real coefficients and exponents.

source_refs.locator: 4.10 Convex Forms p. 195
